 D=(1-x)^{-2}\equiv1+2x\pmod{16}.
\]
Hence $D+7+2x\equiv8\pmod{16}$, giving
$v_2(\widetilde A)=3$. Together with $v_2(B)=2$ these are precisely
the asserted valuations. In the second case $M\ge5$ so $a\ge4$;
all displayed denominator exponents are positive.
For odd $M$ this gives $q_M\ge2^{a-2}>N/8$. The even-parameter
theorem gives the stronger $q_M>N/2$ for even $M\ge4$.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Exact polynomial identities used in the proof}

For $j=0,1,2$, the bilinear values in the proof have the form
$\mathcal A(c^{[0]},c^{[j]})=P_j(D)H_D+R_j(D)$, where
\[
 P_0=\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(2D^2-11D-31)}{15},
\]
\[
 R_0=-\frac{D(334D^4-1915D^3-9660D^2-9425D-934)}{900},
\]
\[
 P_1=\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(D^3-13D^2-28D-20)}{60},
\]
\[
 R_1=-\frac{D(167D^5-3380D^4-8455D^3-2600D^2-2692D-4640)}{3600},
\]
\[
 P_2=\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(2D^4-55D^3-77D^2-254D-36)}{1260},
\]
\begin{align*}
R_2=-\frac{D}{176400}\bigl(&726D^6-41167D^5+1316D^4-12005D^3\\
                         &-472766D^2-109368D+280464\bigr).
\end{align*}
They follow by substitution into the displayed Gram entries, ordinary
finite sums of polynomials, and the elementary summation identity
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^D P(i)H_i
 =H_D\sum_{i=0}^D P(i)
  -\sum_{r=1}^D\frac1r\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}P(i).
\]
For off-diagonal gaps $d\ge2$ use
$a_{i,i+d}=1/(d-1)+2i/(d(d^2-1))$ and partial fractions in $d$.
These operations give polynomial identities, not interpolation claims.

To check the congruences, write $D=1+8u$. Then
\[
 P_0/16\equiv1+u\pmod2,\qquad v_2(R_0)\ge2,
\]
\[
 v_2(P_1)=v_2(P_2)=1,\qquad R_1,R_2\in\mathbb Z_2.
\]
There is a unique term of valuation $-a$ in $H_D$, so $2^aH_D$ is odd.
It follows that
$2^{a-1}(P_0H_D+R_0)\equiv8(1+u)=D+7\pmod{16}$,
while $2^{a-1}(P_jH_D+R_j)$ is odd for $j=1,2$.
These are the three base congruences used above.

\paragraph{What this establishes.}
This theorem closes a proposed route by proving a uniform arithmetic
obstruction. It supplies no irrationality proof for Euler's constant,
and says nothing about other cutoffs, rational node schedules, tapers,
or signed constructions.


% Research fragment: definitions and proofs are self-contained except for the PNT.
% Requires amsmath, amssymb, amsthm and theorem/lemma/corollary environments.
\section{Opposite Bessel limits: a nonzero accelerated family and its exact denominator obstruction}
\label{s2--alt:mirror-section}

Write $H_0=0$ and $H_m=\sum_{k=1}^m1/k$. For a rational number $x$,
$\operatorname{den}(x)$ denotes its positive reduced denominator, with
$\operatorname{den}(0)=1$. All logarithms below are natural.
The following argument concerns the actual rational approximants in
manuscript [044] \cite{corpus044}, not merely their limiting constants. It proves that
both their simple mirror average and a specified acceleration have
nonzero errors for all sufficiently large indices. Their reduced
integer errors nevertheless diverge. No assertion of historical
priority is made for the elementary denominator mechanism.

\subsection{Persistence of a harmonic denominator}

\begin{lemma}[A rational perturbation changes denominator size by at most its own size]
\label{s2--alt:den-perturbation}
For rational $x,y$,
\[
 \bigl|\log\operatorname{den}(x+y)-\log\operatorname{den}(x)\bigr|
 \le \log\operatorname{den}(y).
\]
For a fixed nonzero rational $c$, multiplying a rational number by $c$
changes its logarithmic denominator by a bounded amount depending only on $c$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If the reduced denominators of $x,y,x+y$ are $b,d,f$, respectively,
then $f\mid bd$ and $b\mid df$. Thus $b/d\le f\le bd$.
The scaling assertion follows by clearing the fixed numerator and
denominator of $c$ and applying the reverse scaling as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Harmonic cores with nonzero prime residues]
\label{s2--alt:harmonic-core}
Fix positive integers $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ and rational numbers
$\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_s$. Suppose
\[
 R(a):=\sum_{i=1}^s\alpha_i H_{\lfloor a/b_i\rfloor}\ne0
 \qquad\text{for every integer }a\ge1.
\]
Let $M$ tend to infinity through multiples of all the $b_i$, and put
\[
 A_M=\sum_{i=1}^s\alpha_i H_{M/b_i}.
\]
Then
\[
 \log\operatorname{den}(A_M)\sim M.
\]
The same conclusion holds for $A_M+z_M$ whenever $z_M\in\mathbb Q$ and
$\log\operatorname{den}(z_M)=o(M)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix a positive integer $K$. For sufficiently large $M$, every prime
$\ell$ with $M/(K+1)<\ell\le M$ exceeds $\sqrt M$ and is coprime
to the denominators of the fixed $\alpha_i$. Put $a=\lfloor M/\ell\rfloor$,
so $1\le a\le K$. Reduction in the local ring $\mathbb Z_{(\ell)}$ gives
\[
 \ell A_M\equiv
 \sum_i\alpha_i H_{\lfloor M/(b_i\ell)\rfloor}
 =R(a)\pmod\ell.
\]
Indeed only terms whose indices are multiples of $\ell$ survive, and
there are no multiples of $\ell^2$. The equality of the floors uses
$\lfloor x/b\rfloor=\lfloor\lfloor x\rfloor/b\rfloor$ for integral $b$.
The finitely many nonzero rationals $R(1),\ldots,R(K)$ have fixed
nonzero numerators. All sufficiently large $\ell$ therefore give
$\ell A_M\not\equiv0\pmod\ell$, hence $v_\ell(A_M)=-1$.

If $\vartheta(x)=\sum_{\ell\le x}\log\ell$, it follows that
\[
 \log\operatorname{den}(A_M)
 \ge\vartheta(M)-\vartheta(M/(K+1))
 =\left(1-\frac1{K+1}+o(1)\right)M
\]
by the prime number theorem. On the other hand, the denominator of
$A_M$ divides a fixed constant times $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,M)$,
whose logarithm is $\psi(M)\sim M$. First let $M\to\infty$ and then
$K\to\infty$ to prove the result. The perturbation assertion follows
from Lemma~\ref{s2--alt:den-perturbation}.
\end{proof}

In particular $\log\operatorname{den}(H_M)\sim M$. This lemma does not
say that every prime below $M$ survives: it obtains the asymptotic by
first considering a fixed range of the quotient $\lfloor M/\ell\rfloor$.

\subsection{The two exact rational families}

For integers $n,m\ge1$, retain the factorial approximants
\[
 r_{n,m}=
 \frac{\sum_{k=0}^n f_{n,m,k}(H_{m+k}-2H_k+2H_{n-k})}
      {\sum_{k=0}^n f_{n,m,k}},\qquad
 f_{n,m,k}=\frac{(m+k)!}{k!^2(n-k)!^2}.
\]
For $n\ge1$ and an integer $p\ge0$, define
\[
 T_{n,p}=
 \frac{\sum_{k=0}^n b_{n,p,k}((p+3)H_k-2H_{n-k}-pH_{n+k})}
      {\sum_{k=0}^n b_{n,p,k}},\qquad
 b_{n,p,k}=\frac{\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^{p}}{k!}.
\]
Set
\[
 n_j=2^j,\qquad p_j=3j,\qquad
 V_j=\frac{r_{n_j,n_j^2}+T_{n_j,p_j}}2,
 \qquad W_j=4V_{j+2}-4V_{j+1}+V_j.
\]
Thus $V_j,W_j$ are explicit rational numbers. Introduce the positive
constants
\[
 D=\sum_{a\ge0}\frac1{(a!)^2}=I_0(2),\qquad
 c=\frac{\sum_{a\ge0}a/(a!)^2}{D}=\frac{I_1(2)}{I_0(2)}.
\]
One has $0<c<1$, as also follows from the moment calculation below.

\begin{theorem}[Mirror averaging and a three-term acceleration]
\label{s2--alt:mirror-obstruction}
As $j\to\infty$, with $n=n_j$ and $p=p_j$,
\begin{align}
 V_j-\gamma
 &=\frac{p+6}{8nD^2}
   +\frac{(1-c)p^2}{32n^2D^2}
   +O\left(\frac p{n^2}+\frac{p^3}{n^3}\right),
 \label{s2--alt:V-expansion}\\
 W_j-\gamma
 &\sim\frac{(1-c)p^2}{128n^2D^2}>0.
 \label{s2--alt:W-expansion}
\end{align}
In particular both errors are strictly positive for all sufficiently
large $j$, and both rational families converge to $\gamma$.
Their actual reduced denominators satisfy
\begin{align}
 \log\operatorname{den}(V_j)&\sim n_j^2=4^j,
 \label{s2--alt:V-den}\\
 \log\operatorname{den}(W_j)&\sim16n_j^2=4^{j+2}.
 \label{s2--alt:W-den}
\end{align}
Consequently
\[
 \log\left(\operatorname{den}(V_j)|V_j-\gamma|\right)\sim4^j,
 \qquad
 \log\left(\operatorname{den}(W_j)|W_j-\gamma|\right)\sim4^{j+2}.
\]
Both denominator-normalized errors tend to $+\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the analytic assertions]
For $s\ge0$ put
\[
 D(s)=\sum_{a\ge0}\frac{s^a}{(a!)^2},\qquad
 F(s)=\sum_{a\ge0}\frac{H_as^a}{(a!)^2},\qquad
 \theta=s\frac{d}{ds}.
\]
The identities
\[
 \theta^2D=sD,\qquad \theta^2F=sF+\theta D
\]
follow by shifting the coefficients. Moreover
\[
 \theta\bigl(D\theta F-F\theta D\bigr)=D\theta D,
\]
so evaluation at $s=0$ yields
\[
 D\theta F-F\theta D=\frac{D^2-1}{2}.
\]
Use the probability distribution
$\Pr(J=a)=1/((a!)^2D(1))$, and write $h=\mathbb EH_J$.
At $s=1$ these identities give
\begin{gather*}
 \mathbb EJ=c,\quad \mathbb EJ^2=1,\quad
 \mathbb EJ^3=1+c,\quad \mathbb EJ^4=2+2c,\\
 u:=\operatorname{Cov}(H_J,J)=\frac{1-D^{-2}}2,\qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(H_J,J^2)=c,\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(H_J,J^3)=1+u,\qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(H_J,J^4)=1+2c+2u.
\end{gather*}
Since $J^2-J\ge0$ and its expectation is strictly positive, $c<1$.
For $X=J(J-1)$ and $Y=1-2J$, the displayed moments imply
\begin{gather}
 \mathbb EX=1-c,\qquad \mathbb EX^2=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(J,X)=c^2,\label{s2--alt:X-moments}\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(H_J,X)=c-u,\qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(H_J,X^2)=3c-1.\notag
\end{gather}

Reindex the factorial approximants by $a=n-k$ and divide all weights
by their term at $k=n$. On the square diagonal their weights are
\[
 w_{n,a}=\frac1{(a!)^2}
  \prod_{r=0}^{a-1}\frac{(1-r/n)^2}{1+1/n-r/n^2}.
\]
For $a\le n^{1/8}$, Taylor expansion gives
\[
 w_{n,a}=\frac1{(a!)^2}
 \left(1-\frac{a^2}{n}+O\left(\frac{(a+1)^4}{n^2}\right)\right),
\]
while the corresponding harmonic factor is
\[
 H_{n^2+n-a}-2H_{n-a}+2H_a
 =-\gamma+2H_a+\frac{2a}{n}
       +O\left(\frac{(a+1)^2}{n^2}\right).
\]
Thus the $1/n$ term in the quotient is
$2\mathbb EJ-2\operatorname{Cov}(H_J,J^2)=0$, and
\begin{equation}\label{s2--alt:r-leading}
 r_{n,n^2}=-\gamma+2h+O(n^{-2}).
\end{equation}

The normalized weights for $T_{n,p}$ are exactly
\[
 v_{n,p,a}=\frac{(n)_a^{p+3}}{(2n)_a^p(a!)^2}
 =\frac1{(a!)^2}
    \prod_{r=0}^{a-1}
       \frac{(1-r/n)^{p+3}}{(1-r/(2n))^p},
\]
where $(n)_a$ is the falling factorial and the second equality uses
$n^3=2^p$. Put $A=(p+6)/4$. Expanding the logarithm and then the
exponential gives, for $a\le n^{1/8}$,
\begin{align*}
 v_{n,p,a}
 =\frac1{(a!)^2}\biggl[1-\frac{A a(a-1)}n
 +\frac{A^2a^2(a-1)^2}{2n^2}
 +O\left(\frac{(p+1)(a+1)^3}{n^2}
          +\frac{(p+1)^3(a+1)^6}{n^3}\right)\biggr].
\end{align*}
The harmonic factor has the expansion
\[
 (p+3)H_{n-a}-pH_{2n-a}-2H_a
 =3\gamma-2H_a+\frac{A(1-2a)}n
       +O\left(\frac{(p+1)(a+1)^2}{n^2}\right).
\]
Here $3\log n-p\log2=0$ was used exactly.

Both exact families of normalized weights are bounded above by
$1/(a!)^2$. Their harmonic factors are $O((p+1)\log(n+1))$ uniformly
in $0\le a\le n$. The tails beyond $n^{1/8}$, including any fixed
polynomial weight, are smaller than every power of $n^{-1}$.
All expansions may therefore be summed and divided with the errors
shown above; $p=O(\log n)$ throughout.

For a weight perturbation $1-tX+t^2X^2/2$ and an observable $H+tY$,
the quotient expansion is
\[
 \mathbb EH+t\{\mathbb EY-\operatorname{Cov}(H,X)\}
 +t^2\left\{\tfrac12\operatorname{Cov}(H,X^2)
             -\mathbb EX\operatorname{Cov}(H,X)
             -\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)\right\}+O(t^3),
\]
with the preceding summable errors retained in our application.
Take $H=3\gamma-2H_J$ and $t=A/n$. The first coefficient is $D^{-2}$.
Using \eqref{s2--alt:X-moments}, the second coefficient is
\begin{align*}
 &-\operatorname{Cov}(H_J,X^2)
       +2\mathbb EX\operatorname{Cov}(H_J,X)
       +2\operatorname{Cov}(J,X)\\
 &\hspace{20mm}=-(3c-1)+2(1-c)(c-u)+2c^2
 =(1-c)D^{-2}.
\end{align*}
Consequently
\[
 T_{n,p}=3\gamma-2h+\frac{p+6}{4nD^2}
       +\frac{(1-c)p^2}{16n^2D^2}
       +O\left(\frac p{n^2}+\frac{p^3}{n^3}\right).
\]
Together with \eqref{s2--alt:r-leading} this proves
\eqref{s2--alt:V-expansion}.

The first correction in \eqref{s2--alt:V-expansion} is a constant
multiple of $(3j+6)2^{-j}$, which the operator
$V_j\mapsto4V_{j+2}-4V_{j+1}+V_j$ annihilates exactly.
For the next term, writing $C=(1-c)/(32D^2)$ gives
\[
 4\frac{C(p+6)^2}{(4n)^2}
 -4\frac{C(p+3)^2}{(2n)^2}
 +\frac{Cp^2}{n^2}
 =\frac C{n^2}\left(\frac{p^2}{4}-3p\right).
\]
The retained errors are $O(p/n^2+p^3/n^3)=o(p^2/n^2)$.
This proves \eqref{s2--alt:W-expansion}, including its eventual strict sign.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the denominator assertions]
For the factorial family, clear the common weight factor and put
\[
 a_{n,m,k}=\binom nk^2(m+1)(m+2)\cdots(m+k)\in\mathbb Z_{>0},
 \qquad Q_r=\sum_{k=0}^na_{n,m,k}.
\]
Then
\[
 r_{n,m}=H_m+z_{n,m},
\]
where the denominator of $z_{n,m}$ divides
\[
 Q_r\,\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,n)\prod_{h=1}^n(m+h).
\]
Indeed $H_{m+k}-H_m=\sum_{h=1}^k1/(m+h)$; all remaining harmonic
indices are at most $n$. Also
\[
 Q_r\le(n+1)4^n(m+n)^n.
\]
On $m=n^2$ this proves
$\log\operatorname{den}(z_{n,n^2})=O(n\log(n+1))$.

For $T_{n,p}$, multiply all weights by $n!$ and write
\[
 B_k=\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^p\frac{n!}{k!}\in\mathbb Z_{>0},
 \qquad Q_T=\sum_{k=0}^nB_k.
\]
Its denominator divides $Q_T\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,2n)$, and
\[
 Q_T\le(n+1)4^{n(p+1)}n!.
\]
For $p=3\log_2n$ this gives
$\log\operatorname{den}(T_{n,p})=O(n\log(n+1))$.
Therefore
\[
 V_j=\tfrac12H_{n_j^2}+\varepsilon_j,
 \qquad
 \log\operatorname{den}(\varepsilon_j)=O(n_j\log(n_j+1)).
\]
The harmonic-core and perturbation lemmas prove
\eqref{s2--alt:V-den}.

For the accelerated sequence, put $M=16n_j^2$. Its harmonic core is
\[
 W_j=2H_M-2H_{M/4}+\tfrac12H_{M/16}+\widetilde\varepsilon_j,
 \qquad
 \log\operatorname{den}(\widetilde\varepsilon_j)=O(n_j\log(n_j+1)).
\]
The residue function of this core is
\[
 R(a)=2\bigl(H_a-H_{\lfloor a/4\rfloor}\bigr)
                  +\tfrac12H_{\lfloor a/16\rfloor}>0
 \qquad(a\ge1).
\]
Lemma~\ref{s2--alt:harmonic-core} therefore gives
\eqref{s2--alt:W-den}. Finally the logarithms of the positive analytic
errors are $O(\log n_j)$, so adding them does not change either
quadratic denominator asymptotic.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The five-condition test for these two families.}
Their reduced pairs give logarithm-free integer linear forms.
The analytic expansions prove nonvanishing for all sufficiently large
indices, hence for infinitely many indices without an unproved
hypothesis. However, multiplying the error by the actual reduced
denominator makes it diverge exponentially on the $n_j^2$ scale.
Thus condition 3 fails for both $V_j$ and $W_j$. The theorem concerns
these specified constructions; it is not a universal obstruction to
all gamma approximations or to all nonlinear combinations of the corpus.


\section{An exact escape from the large harmonic core}
\label{s2--alt:escape-section}

Retain $r_{n,m},T_{n,p},V_j,D,c$ from the mirror construction, and write
$\operatorname{den}(x)$ for the positive denominator of a reduced rational
number $x$.  The following construction cancels $H_{n^2}$ exactly in the
finite rational formula.  It therefore lies outside the preceding
harmonic-core denominator obstruction.

\begin{theorem}[Exact core cancellation and a further acceleration]
\label{s2--alt:core-escape}
For $j\ge1$, put $n=2^j$, $p=3j$, and define
\[
 U_j=\frac{r_{n,n^2}+T_{n,p}-H_{n^2}+2H_n}{3},
 \qquad X_j=4U_{j+2}-4U_{j+1}+U_j.
\]
Both are explicitly defined rational numbers.  Their asymptotic expansions
are
\begin{align}
 U_j-\gamma
 &=\frac{1}{n}\left(\frac{p+6}{12D^2}+\frac13\right)
   +\frac{(1-c)p^2}{48D^2n^2}
   +O\left(\frac p{n^2}+\frac{p^3}{n^3}\right),
   \label{s2--alt:U-expand}\\
 X_j-\gamma
 &\sim\frac{(1-c)p^2}{192D^2n^2}>0.
   \label{s2--alt:X-expand}
\end{align}
In particular, both converge to $\gamma$ and both exceed $\gamma$ for all
sufficiently large $j$.  Their reduced denominators satisfy
\begin{align}
 \log\operatorname{den}(U_j)&\le8n\log n+O(n),
   \label{s2--alt:U-den-upper}\\
 \log\operatorname{den}(X_j)&\le56n\log n+O(n).
   \label{s2--alt:X-den-upper}
\end{align}
Writing $q_{U,j}=\operatorname{den}(U_j)$ and
$q_{X,j}=\operatorname{den}(X_j)$, their exact asymptotic arithmetic
thresholds are
\[
 q_{U,j}|U_j-\gamma|\sim\frac{q_{U,j}p}{12D^2n},\qquad
 q_{X,j}|X_j-\gamma|\sim\frac{(1-c)q_{X,j}p^2}{192D^2n^2}.
\]
Thus primitive-error decay along any infinite subsequence is equivalent,
respectively, to $q_{U,j}=o(n/p)$ and $q_{X,j}=o(n^2/p^2)$ along that
subsequence.  These are conclusions about the exact threshold, not
assumed or proved denominator estimates.
For $U_j$ there is also the following exact arithmetic obstruction:
\[
 v_2(U_j)=
 \begin{cases}
 -j,&j\ge3\text{ is odd},\\
 1-j,&j\ge8,\ j\equiv0\pmod4,\\
 2-j,&j\ge6,\ j\equiv6\pmod8.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{\(\ast\)}\label{s2--alt:U-valuations}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{den}(U_j)(U_j-\gamma)\longrightarrow+\infty
\]
along any sequence of indices tending to infinity outside the residue
class $j\equiv2\pmod8$.  Thus the full sequence $U_j$ does not satisfy
primitive-error decay.  The theorem does not settle that decay for the
remaining residue class or for the accelerated sequence $X_j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Analytic expansion and exact denominator clearing]
First observe the exact identity
\[
 U_j=\frac{2V_j+G_j}{3},\qquad
 G_j=2H_n-H_{n^2}.
\]
The elementary harmonic expansion gives
\[
 G_j=\gamma+\frac1n-\frac{2}{3n^2}+O(n^{-4}).
\]
Combining this with the two-term expansion of $V_j$ proves
\eqref{s2--alt:U-expand}.  The displayed first correction is a linear
polynomial in $j$ multiplied by $2^{-j}$, so the operator
$U_j\mapsto4U_{j+2}-4U_{j+1}+U_j$ annihilates it exactly.  If
$C=(1-c)/(48D^2)$, its action on the second term is
\[
 \frac C{n^2}\left(\frac{p^2}{4}-3p\right).
\]
The retained errors are $O(p/n^2+p^3/n^3)=o(p^2/n^2)$, proving
\eqref{s2--alt:X-expand}.  The coefficient is positive because $0<c<1$.

For the arithmetic bound set
\[
 a_{n,m,k}=\binom nk^2(m+1)_k,
 \qquad Q_r=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{n,m,k},
 \qquad d_s=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,s).
\]
Here $(m+1)_k=(m+1)(m+2)\cdots(m+k)$ is a rising factorial, with
$(m+1)_0=1$.
These weights are polynomials in $m$ with integer coefficients, and
\[
 \partial_m a_{n,m,k}
   =a_{n,m,k}(H_{m+k}-H_m).
\]
Their derivatives are integers at integer $m$.  Therefore the exact
finite cancellation has the stronger denominator statement
\[
 \operatorname{den}(r_{n,m}-H_m)\mid Q_r d_n.
\]
No product of the integers $m+1,\ldots,m+n$ is needed.
For the second family put
\[
 B_k=\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^{p}\frac{n!}{k!},
 \qquad Q_T=\sum_{k=0}^n B_k.
\]
Then $B_k$ are integers and
$\operatorname{den}(T_{n,p})\mid Q_Td_{2n}$.  It follows that
\[
 \operatorname{den}(U_j)\mid 3Q_rQ_Td_{2n}.
 \tag{\(\dagger\)}\label{s2--alt:U-clearing}
\]
This is an upper bound for the actual reduced denominator; it makes no
assumption about the gcd of the displayed integerized pair.

The normalized positive weights used in the mirror proof give the exact
bounds
\[
 Q_r\le D(n^2+1)_n,
 \qquad Q_T\le D\binom{2n}{n}^{p}.
\]
Indeed their ratios to the respective final summands are bounded by
$1/(a!)^2$ after the change of index $a=n-k$.  Hence
\[
 \log Q_r\le2n\log n+O(1),\qquad
 \log Q_T\le6n\log n+O(1),
\]
where the second bound uses $\binom{2n}{n}\le4^n$ and
$p=3\log_2n$.  The standard bound $\log d_{2n}=O(n)$ proves
\eqref{s2--alt:U-den-upper}.  An integer linear combination of rationals has
denominator dividing the product of their denominators.  Applying this
to $X_j$ yields
\[
 8\bigl(n\log n+2n\log(2n)+4n\log(4n)\bigr)+O(n)
 =56n\log n+O(n),
\]
as asserted.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[The two-adic obstruction]
All congruences below are in $\mathbb Z_2$, after the indicated scaling.
Put
\[
 R_j=r_{n,n^2}-H_{n^2}+2H_n,\qquad U_j=(R_j+T_{n,p})/3.
\]
For $1\le k<n$, $\binom nk$ is even; for $k=n$ one has
$v_2((n^2+1)_n)=v_2(n!)=n-1$.  Thus, for $j\ge3$, all $a_{n,n^2,k}$
with $k\ge1$ are divisible by $4$, and $Q_r\equiv1\pmod4$.
Using the integer-derivative identity above and the fact that
$nH_k\in\mathbb Z_2$ for $k\le n$ gives
\[
 nR_j\equiv2nH_n(1+Q_r^{-1})\equiv4\pmod8.
 \tag{\(\ddagger\)}\label{s2--alt:R-mod8}
\]
Here $nH_n$ is odd, since precisely one summand in $H_n$ has denominator
of two-adic valuation $j$.  In particular $v_2(R_j)=2-j$.

We next locate the unique minimum among the valuations of the integer
weights $B_k$.  For $1\le k<n$,
\[
 v_2\binom nk=j-v_2(k),\qquad
 v_2\binom{n+k}{k}=0.
\]
If $a=n-k$ and $s_2$ denotes the number of ones in a binary expansion,
Legendre's factorial formula therefore gives
\[
 v_2(B_{n-a})=p+g(a),\qquad
 g(a)=a-1-2v_2(a)-s_2(a-1),\quad 1\le a<n.
\]
For a power $a=2^t$,
$g(a)=2^t-1-3t$; its only negative values are
\[
 g(2)=-2,\qquad g(4)=-3,\qquad g(8)=-2.
\]
For completeness, if $a=2^tu$ with odd $u\ge3$, then
\[
 g(a)=2^tu-1-3t-s_2(u-1)
       \ge(2^t-1)u-3t\ge0.
\]
The endpoint weights have valuations
$v_2(B_n)=p$ and $v_2(B_0)=n-1$.  For $j\ge3$ the latter is strictly
greater than $p-3$.  Thus $a=4$ is the unique minimum, and
\[
 v_2(Q_T)=p-3.
 \tag{\(\S\)}\label{s2--alt:QT-valuation}
\]
Write $\widetilde B_a=B_{n-a}/2^{p-3}$ and
$\widetilde Q=Q_T/2^{p-3}$, an odd integer.  Also put
\[
 h'_a=n\bigl((p+3)H_{n-a}-2H_a-pH_{2n-a}\bigr).
\]
For $a\ge1$, $h'_a$ is two-adically integral.  If $j$ is odd, then
$p$ is odd, and $h'_4$ is odd: $nH_{n-4}$ is even,
$2nH_4$ is even, and $nH_{2n-4}$ is odd.  All other normalized weights
are even.  The only possible nonintegral $h'_a$ is at $a=0$, where
$v_2(h'_0)\ge-1$ but $v_2(\widetilde B_0)=3$.
Consequently $nT_{n,p}$ is odd.  Together with
\eqref{s2--alt:R-mod8}, this proves $v_2(U_j)=-j$ for odd $j\ge3$.

Suppose next that $j$ is even and $j\ge6$.  Then every $h'_a$ is
two-adically integral, including $a=0$ because $p$ is even.
Modulo $8$ only the normalized weights at $a=2,4,8$ can contribute:
their valuations are respectively $1,0,1$, and all other weights have
valuation at least $3$.  For each of these three values of $a$,
grouping harmonic summands by their two-adic denominator gives
\[
 nH_{n-a}\equiv2\pmod8,\qquad
 nH_{2n-a}\equiv1\pmod8,\qquad
 2nH_a\equiv0\pmod8.
\]
For the first congruence, the $k=n/2$ summand gives $2$, and the two
$k=n/4,3n/4$ summands sum to a multiple of $8$; all remaining
summands are multiples of $8$.  For the second, $k=n$ gives $1$,
the pair $k=n/2,3n/2$ sums to $8/3$, and the four terms with
$v_2(k)=j-2$ also sum to a multiple of $8$.  The omission of at most
seven terms near either upper endpoint changes neither congruence.
It follows that $h'_a\equiv p+6\pmod8$ for $a=2,4,8$, and hence
\[
 nT_{n,p}\equiv p+6\pmod8,
 \qquad nU_j\equiv(p+10)/3\pmod8.
\]
When $j\equiv0\pmod4$, $p+10$ has valuation $1$; when
$j\equiv6\pmod8$, it has valuation $2$.  This proves the remaining
parts of \eqref{s2--alt:U-valuations}.

Outside $j\equiv2\pmod8$, these formulas imply
$\operatorname{den}(U_j)\ge n/4$ for all sufficiently large $j$.
Since \eqref{s2--alt:U-expand} gives
$U_j-\gamma\sim p/(12D^2n)$, the primitive error tends to infinity
along any such sequence of indices.  No statement about the remaining
residue class is inferred from this calculation.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What has and has not been gained.}
The large harmonic core has been removed from an actual finite rational
formula, and the proven denominator upper scale improves from $n^2$ to
$n\log n$.  A further exact acceleration preserves eventual strict
positivity.  Nevertheless the first escaped family still fails the
primitive-error test on seven residue classes out of eight.  For its
remaining class, and for the accelerated family, the displayed upper
denominator bounds are far too large to establish primitive-error decay.
They provide explicit candidates and exact arithmetic constraints, not
an irrationality proof or an assumption that the unknown gcd is large.






\paragraph{Notation for the accelerated family.}
In this part, $U_j$ denotes the core-cancelled rational approximant defined
above, and
\begin{equation}\label{s3--seq:definition}
 X_j=4U_{j+2}-4U_{j+1}+U_j.
\end{equation}
In the kernel parts below the rational
integral majorant is always written $\mathcal U_j$.
\section{The accelerated sequence has no factor of two in its denominator}
\label{s3--sec:padic-acceleration}

The approximation $X_j$ is defined by \eqref{s3--seq:definition}. The new result below determines its two-adic valuation at every
sufficiently large index. In particular, the large two-primary
denominator of the unaccelerated family does not survive acceleration.
All assertions concern reduced fractions.

Write $O_2(2^r)$ for an element of $2^r\mathbb Z_2$, allowing negative
integers $r$. Constants introduced by convergent two-adic series below
are not assumed to agree with any real constants bearing similar
descriptions.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform removal of the two-primary denominator]
\label{s3--thm:X-two-adic}
For every integer $j\ge6$,
\[
 \boxed{v_2(X_j)=2.}
\]
Equivalently, if $X_j=P_j/Q_j$ in lowest terms with $Q_j>0$, then $Q_j$
is odd and $P_j$ is divisible by $4$ but not by $8$. This result does not
bound the odd part $Q_j$ and does not prove primitive-error decay.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Three convergent factorial series}
Put
\[
 t_0=1,\qquad t_a=(-1)^{a-1}\frac{(a-1)!}{a^2}\quad(a\ge1),
\]
\[
 \mathfrak F=1+\sum_{a\ge1}t_a,\qquad
 \mathfrak G=\sum_{a\ge1}t_aH_{a-1},\qquad
 \mathfrak W=\sum_{a\ge1}t_a\left(H_{a-1}-\frac2a\right).
\]
For $a\ge2$ let $b(a)=\lfloor\log_2(a-1)\rfloor$, and let $b(1)=0$.
Legendre's factorial identity gives
\[
 g(a):=v_2(t_a)=a-1-s_2(a-1)-2v_2(a).
\]
The following elementary bounds will control all remainders:
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:g-bounds}
 g(a)-b(a)\ge-4,\qquad g(a)-2b(a)\ge-6.
\end{equation}
For $1\le a<32$ they follow from the finite table
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
 a&1&2\text{--}3&4\text{--}7&8\text{--}15&16\text{--}31\\\hline
 \min(g-b)&0&-2&-4&-4&0\\
 \min(g-2b)&0&-2&-5&-6&-3
\end{array}
\]
and for $a\ge32$ one uses, with $d=\lfloor\log_2a\rfloor\ge5$,
\[
 g(a)-2b(a)\ge a-1-5d\ge2^d-1-5d\ge6.
\]
The same estimates show convergence of the three factorial series.

\begin{lemma}[Exact valuations of the factorial series]
\label{s3--lem:factorial-series-values}
One has
\[
 v_2(\mathfrak F)=-3,\qquad
 v_2(\mathfrak G)=-3,\qquad
 v_2(\mathfrak W)=-1.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The unique minimum of $g(a)$ is $g(4)=-3$, proving the first assertion.
For the second, the only terms below valuation $-2$ occur at $a=4,8$.
Their sum is
\[
 t_4H_3+t_8H_7=-\frac{11}{16}-\frac{3267}{16}
              =-\frac{1639}{8}.
\]
Every remaining term has valuation at least $-2$; this follows from
the displayed bounds for $a\ge32$ and direct substitution for $a<32$.
Thus the sum has valuation exactly $-3$.

For the third assertion, the only negative-valuation terms are at
$a=4,6,8$. They sum to
\[
 t_4\left(H_3-\frac24\right)
 +t_6\left(H_5-\frac26\right)
 +t_8\left(H_7-\frac28\right)
 =-\frac12-\frac{13}{2}-\frac{369}{2}
 =-\frac{383}{2}.
\]
All other terms are two-adically integral, again by the bounds and the
finite range $a<32$. This proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A uniform two-adic expansion of the rational weights}
For $n=2^j$, $p=3j$, reindex the $T_{n,p}$ weights by $a=n-k$ and divide
by their final weight. Exactly as in the real analysis,
\[
 v_{n,p,a}=\frac{(n)_a^{p+3}}{(2n)_a^p(a!)^2},
 \qquad 0\le a\le n,
\]
where the factorials $(n)_a$ in this display are falling. For $a\ge1$,
the identity $n^3=2^p$ gives the exact factorization
\[
 v_{n,p,a}=t_a\prod_{r=1}^{a-1}
       \frac{(1-n/r)^{p+3}}{(1-2n/r)^p}.
\]
For $r<n$, $v_2(n/r)\ge1$, so these factors are units.
Their convergent expansions over $\mathbb Z_2$ have first coefficient
$(p-3)n/r$. Since all binomial coefficients involved are integers,
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:padic-weight-expansion}
 v_{n,p,a}
 =t_a\bigl(1+n(p-3)H_{a-1}
       +O_2(2^{2(j-b(a))})\bigr).
\end{equation}
The weaker first-order difference is
$v_{n,p,a}-t_a=t_aO_2(2^{j-b(a)})$.

Put $S=\sum_{a=0}^nv_{n,p,a}$. Summing
\eqref{s3--eq:padic-weight-expansion} and using \eqref{s3--eq:g-bounds} yields,
for $j\ge6$,
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:S-padic}
 S=\mathfrak F+n(p-3)\mathfrak G+O_2(2^{2j-6}).
\end{equation}
The omitted tails beyond $n$ satisfy the same bounds. Indeed, for
$a>n=2^j$ and $d=\lfloor\log_2a\rfloor\ge j$, the lower bound
$a-1-5d$ is at least $2j-6$ when $j\ge6$; it also controls the harmonic
factors. In particular $v_2(S)=-3$. Expanding its inverse gives
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:inverse-S-padic}
 \frac1S=\frac1{\mathfrak F}
       -\frac{n(p-3)\mathfrak G}{\mathfrak F^2}
       +O_2(2^{2j}).
\end{equation}
To check the last error, the remainder in \eqref{s3--eq:S-padic} divided by
$\mathfrak F^2$ has valuation at least $2j$, while the quadratic
inverse remainder has valuation at least $2j+3$.

\subsection{The harmonic terms and the affine pole}
The sequence $K_j=2^jH_{2^j}$ converges in $\mathbb Z_2$ to a unit
\[
 \mathfrak K=\lim_{j\to\infty}2^jH_{2^j},
 \qquad \mathfrak K-K_j\in2^{2j+2}\mathbb Z_2\quad(j\ge1).
\]
In fact, separating the odd and even terms gives
\[
 K_{j+1}-K_j=2^{j+1}
 \sum_{\substack{1\le r<2^{j+1}\\r\text{ odd}}}\frac1r.
\]
Pair $r$ with $2^{j+1}-r$ to see that the last sum is divisible by
$2^{j+1}$ for $j\ge1$. This proves convergence and the stated error.

Set
\[
 A=\frac p2+3,\qquad
 C=\mathfrak K-1+\frac1{\mathfrak F}.
\]
For $a\ge1$, the harmonic observable multiplied by $n$ can be written
exactly as
\[
 n\bigl((p+3)H_{n-a}-2H_a-pH_{2n-a}\bigr)=C_j+nL_a,
\]
where
\[
 C_j=(p+3)(K_j-1)-\frac p2(K_{j+1}-1),
\]
\[
 L_a=-(p+3)\sum_{r=1}^{a-1}\frac1{n-r}
       +p\sum_{r=1}^{a-1}\frac1{2n-r}-2H_a.
\]
For $a=0$, the observable is $C_j+A$. Since $v_2(A)\ge-1$,
\[
 C_j=A(\mathfrak K-1)+O_2(2^{2j+1}).
\]
Expanding the two reciprocal sums gives, uniformly in $1\le a\le n$,
\[
 L_a=H_{a-1}-\frac2a+O_2(2^{j-2b(a)}).
\]
Together with \eqref{s3--eq:g-bounds} and the first-order weight bound,
this implies
\[
 \sum_{a=1}^nv_{n,p,a}L_a
       =\mathfrak W+O_2(2^{j-6}),
 \qquad
 \frac{\sum_{a=1}^nv_{n,p,a}L_a}{S}
       =\frac{\mathfrak W}{\mathfrak F}+O_2(2^{j-3}).
\]
Combining these identities with \eqref{s3--eq:inverse-S-padic} proves
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:T-padic-expanded}
 T_{n,p}=
 \frac{AC}{n}
 -\frac{A(p-3)\mathfrak G}{\mathfrak F^2}
 +\frac{\mathfrak W}{\mathfrak F}
 +O_2(2^{j-3}).
\end{equation}

The other component
$R_j=r_{n,n^2}-H_{n^2}+2H_n$ has the simpler expansion
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:R-padic-expanded}
 R_j=\frac{4\mathfrak K}{n}+O_2(2^{j-1}).
\end{equation}
To prove it, use the integer weights
$a_k=\binom nk^2(n^2+1)_k$, now with a rising factorial, and $Q_r=\sum a_k$.
For $1\le k<n$,
\[
 v_2(a_k)=2j-2v_2(k)+k-s_2(k)\ge2j-1.
\]
The elementary bound used here is
$k-s_2(k)-2v_2(k)\ge-1$: writing $k=2^tu$ with $u$ odd, the case
$u=1$ reduces to $2^t-1-2t\ge-1$, and $u\ge3$ follows from
$(2^t-1)u-2t\ge-1$.
At $k=n$ the valuation is $n-1\ge2j-1$. Thus
$Q_r=1+O_2(2^{2j-1})$.
The derivative identity
$a_k'=a_k\sum_{h=1}^k1/(n^2+h)$ gives
$v_2(a_k')\ge j-1$, since $v_2(n^2+h)\le j$.
The remaining noninitial harmonic terms have valuation at least $j$.
Hence $R_j=4H_n+O_2(2^{j-1})$, and the estimate for $K_j$ proves
\eqref{s3--eq:R-padic-expanded}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{s3--thm:X-two-adic}]
Since $U_j=(R_j+T_{n,p})/3$, the two expansions give
\[
 U_j=\frac{AC+4\mathfrak K}{3n}
 -\frac{A(p-3)\mathfrak G}{3\mathfrak F^2}
 +\frac{\mathfrak W}{3\mathfrak F}
 +O_2(2^{j-3}).
\]
The first term is an affine polynomial in $j$ divided by $2^j$.
The operator $U_j\mapsto4U_{j+2}-4U_{j+1}+U_j$ annihilates it exactly.
Since $2A(p-3)=p^2+3p-18$, its action on the remaining polynomial gives
\begin{equation}\label{s3--eq:X-padic-congruence}
 X_j=
 \frac{\mathfrak W}{3\mathfrak F}
 -\frac{\mathfrak G}{6\mathfrak F^2}
       (p^2+27p+126)
 +O_2(2^{j-3}).
\end{equation}
The first term has valuation $2$. The coefficient
$\mathfrak G/(6\mathfrak F^2)$ has valuation $2$, and the integer
$p^2+27p+126$ is even, so the second term is divisible by $8$.
For $j\ge6$ the error is also divisible by $8$. Consequently
\[
 X_j\equiv4\pmod8,
\]
proving $v_2(X_j)=2$ and the assertion about its reduced fraction.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Arithmetic meaning.}
This is a proved infinite cancellation in the actual denominator, not
a cancellation of a chosen common multiplier. The theorem removes the
two-primary obstacle completely from $X_j$. It leaves the odd
denominator unconstrained, and therefore does not by itself establish
condition 3.
\section{An exact odd-prime certificate for the reduced denominator}
\label{s3--sec:odd-prime-certificate}

The removal of the two-primary denominator does not control the odd
denominator.  The following result gives an exact, finite certificate
for prime divisors of the reduced denominator of $X_j$.  It also isolates
one specific distribution estimate that would prove failure of
condition 3.  No such distribution estimate is assumed.

For integers $N,m\ge1$ and $q\ge1$, define the positive integers
\[
 Q_r(N,m)=\sum_{k=0}^N\binom Nk^2(m+1)_k,
 \qquad
 Q_T(N,q)=\sum_{k=0}^N
 \binom Nk^2\binom{N+k}{k}^q\frac{N!}{k!}.
\]
Here $(m+1)_k=(m+1)\cdots(m+k)$ is a rising factorial, and the empty
product is $1$.  Write $\widehat R_N=r_{N,N^2}-H_{N^2}+2H_N$; the additional
parameter of $T_{N,q}$ remains explicit.

\begin{lemma}[Upper-half prime residues]
\label{s3--lem:upper-half-prime-residue}
Let $N\ge2$, $q\ge1$, and let $\ell$ be an odd prime with
$N/2<\ell\le N$ and $\ell^2>2N$.  If
$\ell\nmid Q_r(N,N^2)Q_T(N,q)$, then
\[
 \ell \widehat R_N\equiv4\pmod\ell,
 \qquad
 \ell T_{N,q}\equiv3-\frac q2\pmod\ell.
\]
In these formulas all denominators after multiplication by $\ell$ are
coprime to $\ell$.  If instead $N<\ell$, $\ell^2>2N$, and
$\ell\nmid Q_r(N,N^2)Q_T(N,q)$, then both $\widehat R_N$ and $T_{N,q}$ are
$\ell$-adically integral.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First suppose $N=\ell+s$ with $0\le s<\ell$.  Put
$a_k=\binom Nk^2(N^2+1)_k$.  The integer-derivative identity proved in Section~\ref{s2--alt:escape-section} gives
\[
 \widehat R_N=\frac{\sum_{k=0}^N\left(a'_k+
       2a_k(H_{N-k}-H_k+H_N)\right)}{Q_r(N,N^2)},
\]
where $a'_k$ is the derivative with respect to the rising-factorial
parameter, evaluated at the integer $N^2$.  Each $a'_k$ is an integer.
For $s<k<\ell$, the binomial coefficient $\binom Nk$ is divisible by
$\ell$.  For $k\ge\ell$, the rising factorial $(N^2+1)_k$ is divisible
by $\ell$.  Consequently
\[
 Q_r(N,N^2)\equiv\sum_{k=0}^s a_k\pmod\ell.
\]
For $k\le s$, multiplying the harmonic expression
$2(H_{N-k}-H_k+H_N)$ by $\ell$ gives residue $4$.
All terms with $k>s$ have zero residue after multiplication by $\ell$,
and the integer derivative terms also have zero residue.  Division by
the unit $Q_r(N,N^2)$ proves the first congruence.

For the other family put
\[
 B_k=\binom Nk^2\binom{N+k}{k}^{q}\frac{N!}{k!},
 \qquad h_k=(q+3)H_k-2H_{N-k}-qH_{N+k}.
\]
If $k<\ell$, the quotient $N!/k!$ is divisible by $\ell$, so
$\ell B_kh_k$ has zero residue.  If $k=\ell+t$, $0\le t\le s$, and
$s+t\ge\ell$, the binomial coefficient $\binom{N+k}{k}$ is divisible
by $\ell$, and the same conclusion holds.  In every remaining case
$k=\ell+t$ with $s+t<\ell$,
\[
 \ell H_k\equiv1,
 \qquad \ell H_{N-k}\equiv0,
 \qquad \ell H_{N+k}\equiv H_2=\frac32\pmod\ell.
\]
Thus $\ell h_k\equiv3-q/2$ on every weight that can survive modulo
$\ell$.  Dividing the resulting numerator congruence by the unit
$Q_T(N,q)$ proves the second formula.  The assumption $\ell^2>2N$
ensures that all harmonic poles used here are at most simple.

Finally suppose $N<\ell$.  The derivative formula shows that $\widehat R_N$ is
$\ell$-adically integral whenever $Q_r(N,N^2)$ is a unit.  In $T_{N,q}$
the only possible harmonic pole is in $H_{N+k}$ when $N+k\ge\ell$.
For exactly those indices $\binom{N+k}{k}$ is divisible by $\ell$,
and its positive power $q$ clears that simple pole.  Division by the
unit $Q_T(N,q)$ therefore gives an integral value.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Certified prime product in the actual denominator]
\label{s3--thm:actual-odd-prime-product}
Let $j\ge2$, $n=2^j$, $p=3j$, and put
\[
 \Pi_j=\prod_{r=0}^2
 Q_r(2^{j+r},2^{2(j+r)})
 Q_T(2^{j+r},3(j+r)),
\]
\[
 P_j^{\rm band}=\prod_{\substack{2n<\ell\le4n\\\ell\text{ prime}}}\ell,
 \qquad
 D_j=\frac{P_j^{\rm band}}{\gcd(P_j^{\rm band},\Pi_j)}.
\]
Then $D_j$ divides the actual reduced denominator of $X_j$.  More
precisely, every prime $\ell\mid D_j$ satisfies
\[
 v_\ell(X_j)=-1,
 \qquad \ell X_j\equiv\frac{2(8-p)}3\pmod\ell.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \log\operatorname{den}(X_j)
 \ge\vartheta(4n)-\vartheta(2n)
       -\log\gcd(P_j^{\rm band},\Pi_j),
\]
where $\vartheta(x)=\sum_{\ell\le x,\ \ell\text{ prime}}\log\ell$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix a prime $\ell\mid D_j$.  Since $2n<\ell$, both $U_j$ and
$U_{j+1}$ are $\ell$-adically integral by the last assertion of
Lemma~\ref{s3--lem:upper-half-prime-residue}.  For $U_{j+2}$ take
$N=4n$ and $q=p+6$ in the first part of that lemma.  It gives
\[
 \ell U_{j+2}
 \equiv\frac{4+3-(p+6)/2}{3}
 =\frac{8-p}{6}\pmod\ell.
\]
Therefore $X_j=4U_{j+2}-4U_{j+1}+U_j$ has the claimed residue.
For $j\ge2$ one has $0<|p-8|<2n<\ell$, so this residue is nonzero.
The poles are at most simple, proving $v_\ell(X_j)=-1$.  Multiplying
the distinct certified primes proves $D_j\mid\operatorname{den}(X_j)$,
and taking logarithms gives the displayed inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two certified primes suffice]
\label{s3--cor:two-certified-primes}
Let $\mathcal J$ be an infinite set of indices $j\ge2$.  Suppose that
for each sufficiently large $j\in\mathcal J$ there are at least two
distinct primes $\ell\in(2n,4n]$ with $\ell\nmid\Pi_j$.  Then, at every
index in $\mathcal J$ satisfying this two-prime hypothesis,
\[
 \operatorname{den}(X_j)>4n^2,
\]
and, for all sufficiently large $j\in\mathcal J$,
\[
 \operatorname{den}(X_j)|X_j-\gamma|
 >\frac{1-c}{96\mathcal D^2}\,p^2.
\]
Consequently the primitive errors tend to infinity along $\mathcal J$.
An infinite set of such indices implies that the full sequence has
infinite limsup; this alone does not exclude a different successful
subsequence.  If the two-prime hypothesis holds for every sufficiently
large index, the primitive errors tend to infinity along the full
sequence and along every infinite subsequence.

The existence of two certified primes is established here only for the
finite checked indices.  No infinite existence assertion is included
in this corollary.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The two distinct certified primes both exceed $2n$ and their product
divides the actual reduced denominator by
Theorem~\ref{s3--thm:actual-odd-prime-product}.  Thus that denominator is
strictly greater than $4n^2$.  The real asymptotic established for this
same sequence is
\[
 X_j-\gamma\sim C_\infty\frac{p^2}{n^2},\qquad
 C_\infty=\frac{1-c}{192\mathcal D^2}>0.
\]
For all sufficiently large $j$ its left side is at least
$(C_\infty/2)p^2/n^2$.  Multiplication by the denominator lower bound
gives the assertion.  Since $p=3j$, the lower bound tends to infinity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A sufficient obstruction stated entirely in integers]
\label{s3--cor:bad-prime-mass}
Along any sequence of indices tending to infinity on which
\[
 \log\gcd(P_j^{\rm band},\Pi_j)=o(n),
\]
one has
\[
 \liminf\frac{\log\operatorname{den}(X_j)}n\ge2,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{den}(X_j)|X_j-\gamma|\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
More generally, if the gcd logarithm is at most $(2-\varepsilon)n$
eventually for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the primitive errors diverge
exponentially.  These gcd estimates are sufficient hypotheses; neither
is asserted for an infinite sequence here.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The prime number theorem \cite{dlmf-primes} gives
$\vartheta(4n)-\vartheta(2n)=2n+o(n)$.  Apply the theorem, and use the
asymptotic $X_j-\gamma\sim C_\infty p^2/n^2$ with
$C_\infty=(1-c)/(192\mathcal D^2)>0$.
Its logarithm is $O(\log n)$ and hence cannot offset a positive linear
lower bound for the logarithm of the reduced denominator.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Finite exact checks and their limitation.}
For $j=2,\ldots,10$, the numbers of primes in $(2n,4n]$ certified by
the theorem are respectively
\[
 2,\ 5,\ 7,\ 12,\ 22,\ 43,\ 74,\ 137,\ 254,
\]
out of total prime counts
\[
 2,\ 5,\ 7,\ 13,\ 23,\ 43,\ 75,\ 137,\ 255.
\]
The omitted primes in those checks are $67$, $131$, $653$, and $2113$,
one at each of $j=5,6,8,10$.  Direct reduction shows that these four
primes also divide the corresponding reduced denominators, although
the unit-denominator hypothesis does not certify them.  These are
exact finite computations.  They establish no asymptotic bound on
the omitted prime product and therefore do not close condition 3.

\subsection{Rational certificates for the finite primitive errors}
\label{s3--subsec:finite-error-certificates}

The large finite primitive errors can be certified without inserting a
decimal approximation to $\gamma$.  The following classical enclosure
is sufficient; its proof records the sign of the remainder explicitly.

\begin{lemma}[A rationally usable enclosure for Euler's constant]
\label{s3--lem:rational-gamma-enclosure}
For every positive integer $M$,
\[
 H_M-\log M-\frac1{2M}+\frac1{12M^2}-\frac1{120M^4}
 <\gamma<
 H_M-\log M-\frac1{2M}+\frac1{12M^2}.
\]
Define the rational numbers
\[
 \lambda=2\sum_{a=0}^{30}\frac1{(2a+1)3^{2a+1}},
 \qquad \rho=\frac9{4\cdot63\cdot3^{63}},
\]
\[
 G_-=H_{64}-6(\lambda+\rho)-\frac1{128}
       +\frac1{12\cdot64^2}-\frac1{120\cdot64^4},
 \quad
 G_+=H_{64}-6\lambda-\frac1{128}+\frac1{12\cdot64^2}.
\]
Then $G_-<\gamma<G_+$, and both endpoints are given by finite rational
arithmetic.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
% Primary source for Binet's digamma identity: https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.9.E15 .
Binet's digamma identity \cite{dlmf-binet}, together with
$\psi(M+1)=H_M-\gamma$ and $\psi(M+1)=\psi(M)+1/M$, gives
\[
 H_M-\log M-\gamma
 =\frac1{2M}-2\int_0^\infty
       \frac{t}{(M^2+t^2)(e^{2\pi t}-1)}\,dt.
\]
For $t>0$,
\[
 \frac{t}{M^2}-\frac{t^3}{M^4}
 <\frac{t}{M^2+t^2}<\frac{t}{M^2}.
\]
The two needed positive integrals are
\[
 \int_0^\infty\frac{t}{e^{2\pi t}-1}\,dt=\frac1{24},
 \qquad
 \int_0^\infty\frac{t^3}{e^{2\pi t}-1}\,dt=\frac1{240};
\]
they follow by expanding the positive geometric series and using
$\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6$ and $\zeta(4)=\pi^4/90$.
Integration of the strict kernel inequalities proves the first claim.
Finally
\[
 \log2=2\sum_{a\ge0}\frac1{(2a+1)3^{2a+1}},
 \qquad 0<\log2-\lambda<\rho,
\]
where the upper bound follows by replacing every tail denominator
$2a+1$ by $63$ and summing the geometric series.  Take $M=64$ and
$\log64=6\log2$ in the first enclosure.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{How the finite certificates are verified.}
The exact finite sums define a reduced fraction $X_j=A_j/B_j$ with
$B_j>0$.  If $X_j>G_+$, rational comparison proves
$X_j-\gamma>X_j-G_+$.  If $X_j<G_-$, it proves
$\gamma-X_j>G_--X_j$.  If the relevant positive rational gap exceeds
$2^{-k}$ and $B_j$ has bit length $b$, then
\[
 B_j|X_j-\gamma|>2^{b-1-k}.
\]
The supplied exact-arithmetic certificate program performs these
comparisons with the displayed rational endpoints and gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|c|r|r}
 j&b&\operatorname{sign}(X_j-\gamma)&k&b-1-k\\\hline
 8&135056&-&25&135030\\
 9&299332&+&23&299308\\
 10&656413&+&24&656388
\end{array}
\]
All entries in this table concern actual reduced fractions and exact
rational inequalities.  They are finite verification results and do
not assert any infinite denominator growth.



\section{Fixed-shift localization and explicit node identities}
\label{s3--sec:fixed-shift-foundation}
The following calculation extends the shift $1-1/M$ to every fixed
$1-k/M$, $k>0$. The forms $A(Q)$ and $B(Q)$ retain their Laguerre
normalization from Part~\ref{part:positive}.
\subsection{The finite polynomial schedule at the node zero}

At $x=0$, define the unnormalized polynomial
\[
 Q_D^\circ=\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}(D-j)^2(j+1)(L_j-L_{j+1}).
\]
Its ordinary Laguerre coefficient at index $j$, $0\le j\le D$, is
$C_D(j)=3j^2-(4D+1)j+D^2$. Direct finite summation yields
\begin{equation}\label{s3--foundation-polynomial-schedule}
 A(Q_D^\circ)=P(D)H_D+R(D),\qquad B(Q_D^\circ)=V(D),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align*}
 P(D)&=\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(2D^2-11D-31)}{15},\\
 V(D)&=-\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(2D^2-11D-1)}{15}.
\end{align*}
\[
 R(D)=-\frac{D(334D^4-1915D^3-9660D^2-9425D-934)}{900}.
\]
Here is a finite-sum verification, including enough intermediate
identities to check the polynomials without numerical interpolation.
Substitution of $C_D$ into the tridiagonal form gives
\[
 2\sum_{j=0}^D jC_D(j)^2
 -2\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}(j+1)C_D(j)C_D(j+1)=V(D).
\]
For the diagonal and adjacent terms of $A$, use
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^m f(j)H_j
 =H_m\sum_{j=0}^m f(j)
 -\sum_{r=1}^m\frac1r\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}f(j).
\]
The inner sum is a polynomial divisible by $r$, so the final sum is
an ordinary polynomial sum. With $m=D,D-1$ and
$H_{D-1}=H_D-1/D$, this gives the near-diagonal contribution
\[
 V(D)H_D-
 \frac{D(30D^5-334D^4-785D^3+810D^2-55D-3266)}{900}.
\]
For the remaining gaps $2\le d\le D$, the summand after summing in $j$ is
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{D-d}2C_D(j)C_D(j+d)A_{j,j+d}
 =G_D(d)+\frac{r_-}{d+1}+\frac{r_0}{d}+\frac{r_+}{d-1},
\]
where
\[
 G_D(d)=-\frac{9d^4-(20D^2+28D-7)d^2
                    +15D^4+20D^3-55D^2-78D-12}{15},
\]
\[
 r_- =\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(D+4)(D^2-D-7)}{15},
 \quad r_0=-\frac{2D(D+1)(D+2)(D^3+D^2+3)}{15},
\]
\[
 r_+=\frac{D(D-2)(D+1)(D+2)(D^2+5D-1)}{15}.
\]
These are obtained by expanding the degree-five polynomial in $j$
and taking the three residues at $d=-1,0,1$.
Sum the polynomial part using
\[
 \sum_{d=1}^D d^2=\frac{D(D+1)(2D+1)}6,\qquad
 \sum_{d=1}^D d^4=\frac{D(D+1)(2D+1)(3D^2+3D-1)}{30}.
\]
The rational parts sum respectively to
$r_-(H_D+1/(D+1)-3/2)$, $r_0(H_D-1)$, and $r_+(H_D-1/D)$.
Adding the near contribution gives exactly
\eqref{s3--foundation-polynomial-schedule}. All these steps are finite
polynomial identities and harmonic telescoping identities.

\subsection{Normalized shifted nodes and exact rational sandwiches}

Fix a positive integer $k$. For integers $M\ge2k$, put
\[
 D=M^2,\quad N=D-1,\quad x=1-k/M,\quad
 w_j=(1-j/D)^2\ (0\le j\le N),\quad w_{N+1}=0,
\]
\[
 p_M(t)=\sum_{j=0}^N\frac{w_jL_j^{(1)}(x)L_j^{(1)}(t)}{j+1},
 \qquad Q_M(t)=t p_M(t).
\]
These are the \emph{normalized} polynomials. The identity
$tL_j^{(1)}=(j+1)(L_j-L_{j+1})$ gives
\[
 Q_M=D^{-2}Q_{D,x}^\circ,
 \qquad Q_{D,x}^\circ=
 \sum_{j=0}^{D-1}(D-j)^2L_j^{(1)}(x)(L_j-L_{j+1}).
\]
Consequently
\[
 (A(Q_{D,x}^\circ),B(Q_{D,x}^\circ),I(Q_{D,x}^\circ))
 =D^4(A(Q_M),B(Q_M),I(Q_M)).
\]
All asymptotics below refer to $Q_M$, not to $Q_{D,x}^\circ$;
their target ratios, reduced denominators, and primitive errors agree.
The ordinary Laguerre coefficient of $Q_M$ at index zero is $1$,
so these polynomials are nonzero.

Use $\langle f,g\rangle_1=\int_0^\infty f(t)g(t)t e^{-t}dt$ and put
\[
 \mathsf H_r=\langle p_M,t^rp_M\rangle_1,\qquad
 T_M=\mathsf H_2+\mathsf H_1,\qquad
 U_M=\mathsf H_3-\mathsf H_2-\mathsf H_1+\mathsf H_0.
\]
These are rational, $B_M=B(Q_M)=\mathsf H_2-\mathsf H_1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{s3--foundation-sandwich}
 \frac{2B_M^2}{T_M}\le I_M\le\frac{U_M}{2},\qquad
 \frac{2q_M|B_M|}{T_M}\le\mathcal E_M
       \le\frac{q_MU_M}{2|B_M|}\quad(B_M\ne0).
\end{equation}
Here $I_M=I(Q_M)>0$ and $q_M$ is the actual reduced denominator of
$A(Q_M)/B(Q_M)$.

To prove these inequalities, for $t>0$ use
\[
 \frac{2(t-1)^2}{t+1}\le(t-1)\log t
 \le\frac{(t-1)^2(t+1)}{2t}.
\]
The first follows from $\log t=2\operatorname{artanh}((t-1)/(t+1))$.
For the second, differentiate $(t-t^{-1})/2-\log t$ and multiply
its sign by that of $t-1$.  The upper bound integrates to $U_M/2$.
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 B_M^2\le
 \left\langle p_M,\frac{t(t-1)^2}{t+1}p_M\right\rangle_1
 \left\langle p_M,t(t+1)p_M\right\rangle_1
 \le I_MT_M/2.
\]
Finally use $\mathcal E_M=q_MI_M/|B_M|$.

\subsection{Uniform real localization for every fixed shift}

\begin{theorem}[The real scale and the exact denominator threshold]
For fixed $k>0$ and the normalized polynomials above, as $M\to\infty$,
\[
 B_M=-k\kappa+O_k(\log M/M),\quad
 T_M=2\kappa M+O_k(\log M),\quad U_M=O_k(M^{-1}),
 \qquad \kappa=\frac{128e}{315\pi}>0.
\]
In particular $B_M<0$ eventually and
\[
 I_M=\Theta_k(M^{-1}),\qquad
 \gamma-A(Q_M)/B(Q_M)=\Theta_k(M^{-1}),\qquad
 \mathcal E_M=\Theta_k(q_M/M).
\]
Thus primitive-error decay in this family is equivalent to $q_M=o(M)$.
These assertions make no assumption about the arithmetic nature of $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The compact-$x$ Laguerre expansion, for $\alpha=0,1$, is
\begin{equation}\label{s3--foundation-PR}
 L_j^{(\alpha)}(x)=
 \frac{e^{x/2}j^{\alpha/2-1/4}}{\sqrt\pi\,x^{\alpha/2+1/4}}
 \left[\cos\!\left(2\sqrt{jx}-(\alpha/2+1/4)\pi\right)
       +O(j^{-1/2})\right].
\end{equation}
Its error is uniform for $x\in[1/2,1]$; see the standard Laguerre
asymptotic expansion \cite{dlmf-laguerre-asymptotic}.
This compact uniformity applies to $x=1-k/M$.

The basis $\phi_j=L_j^{(1)}/\sqrt{j+1}$ is orthonormal for
$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_1$. Multiplication by $t$ has Jacobi matrix
\[
 J_{jj}=2j+2,\qquad J_{j,j+1}=-\sqrt{(j+1)(j+2)}.
\]
The coefficient vector of $p_M$ is
$b_j=w_jL_j^{(1)}(x)/\sqrt{j+1}$ for $j\le N$, zero afterwards.
Set $S=\|b\|^2$, $g=(J-x)b$, and $\delta=\langle b,g\rangle$.
Squaring \eqref{s3--foundation-PR} gives
\begin{equation}\label{s3--foundation-norm}
 S=\kappa(x)\sqrt N+O(\log(N+2)),\qquad
 \kappa(x)=\frac{128e^x}{315\pi x^{3/2}}.
\end{equation}
Indeed the nonoscillating sum is
$e^x/(2\pi x^{3/2})\sum_{j=1}^N j^{-1/2}(1-j/D)^4$.
Integral comparison uses
$\int_0^1u^{-1/2}(1-u)^4du=256/315$.
The squared asymptotic remainders sum to $O(\log(N+2))$.
For the oscillating sum, comparison with its integral has the same
error: the phase derivative contributes $O(1/t)$ to the absolute
derivative.  Substitution $t=y^2$ makes the integral bounded by
integration by parts, since $4\sqrt x$ stays away from zero and
the amplitude $(1-y^2/D)^4$ has bounded variation.
All constants are uniform on the stated compact interval.

The eigenvector recurrence for $L_j^{(1)}(x)$ gives the exact identity
\[
 \delta=\sum_{j=0}^N L_j^{(1)}(x)L_{j+1}^{(1)}(x)
                          (w_j-w_{j+1})^2.
\]
It follows either by expanding both sides or by summing the Jacobi
recurrence with the finitely supported weights $w_j$.
Since $|w_j-w_{j+1}|\le2/D$ and
$L_j^{(1)}(x)L_{j+1}^{(1)}(x)=O((j+1)^{1/2})$,
\begin{equation}\label{s3--foundation-delta}
 \delta=O(N^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
No sign of the individual Laguerre products is assumed.

A weighted residual estimate is needed to control the unbounded
moment in $U_M$. Put $L_{-1}^{(1)}=0$ and
\[
 U_j^*=L_j(x)+L_{j+1}(x),\qquad
 V_j^*=L_{j-1}^{(1)}(x)+L_{j+1}^{(1)}(x).
\]
Direct substitution of the quadratic taper gives
\[
 g_j=\sqrt{j+1}\left[\frac{2(D-j)}{D^2}U_j^*
                              -\frac1{D^2}V_j^*\right]\ (0\le j\le N),
 \qquad
 g_{N+1}=-\frac{\sqrt{N+2}}{D^2}L_N^{(1)}(x).
\]
All later entries vanish. The identities
$L_{j+1}^{(1)}-L_j^{(1)}=L_{j+1}$ and
$L_{j+1}-L_j=-xL_j^{(1)}/(j+1)$, together with
\eqref{s3--foundation-PR}, imply
\[
 U_j^*=O((j+1)^{-1/4}),\quad \Delta U_j^*=O((j+1)^{-3/4}),
 \qquad
 V_j^*=O((j+1)^{1/4}),\quad \Delta V_j^*=O((j+1)^{-1/4}).
\]
Hence $g_j=O((j+1)^{1/4}/D)$ in the bulk and
$g_N,g_{N+1}=O(D^{-5/4})$. Summing squares gives
$\|g\|^2=O(N^{-1/2})$.
Moreover the Jacobi energy identity is
\[
 \langle g,Jg\rangle=g_0^2+
 \sum_{j\ge0}(\sqrt{j+1}\,g_j-\sqrt{j+2}\,g_{j+1})^2.
\]
In the bulk the displayed difference is $O((j+1)^{1/4}/D)$:
apply the bounds on $\Delta U_j^*,\Delta V_j^*$ and the elementary
first differences of $(j+1)(D-j)$ and $j+1$.
The two endpoint differences are $O(D^{-3/4})$.
Their squared sum therefore proves
\begin{equation}\label{s3--foundation-energy}
 \langle g,(J+1)g\rangle=O(N^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}

The exact moment identities now give
\[
 B_M=(x^2-x)S+(2x-1)\delta+\|g\|^2,\qquad
 T_M=(x^2+x)S+(2x+1)\delta+\|g\|^2.
\]
Using $\sqrt N=M+O(M^{-1})$, $x=1-k/M$, and
$\kappa(1)=\kappa$, equations \eqref{s3--foundation-norm}--
\eqref{s3--foundation-energy} give the asserted $B_M,T_M$ asymptotics.
Finally, since $(J-1)b=g+(x-1)b$ and $J+1$ is positive,
\[
 U_M=\langle(J-1)b,(J+1)(J-1)b\rangle
 \le2\langle g,(J+1)g\rangle
       +2(x-1)^2\langle b,(J+1)b\rangle=O_k(M^{-1}).
\]
The last inner product is $(x+1)S+\delta=O(M)$.
The lower sandwich in \eqref{s3--foundation-sandwich} is asymptotic
to $k^2\kappa/M$, and the upper sandwich is $O_k(M^{-1})$.
This proves $I_M=\Theta_k(M^{-1})$. Since $|B_M|\to k\kappa$,
the remaining assertions follow, including the exact primitive
denominator threshold.
\end{proof}


\section{Odd primes at a zero of the rational node}
\label{s3--sec:node-primes}
The rational forms $A,B$, their Laguerre Gram matrices, the exact
polynomial-schedule identities, and the real localization threshold
are derived in Section~\ref{s3--sec:fixed-shift-foundation}.

The earlier two-adic theorem concerns the particular node $1-1/M$.
Changing it to $1-3/M$ can cancel that leading two-adic residue.
The following result tracks primes in the numerator of the new node
and proves that such a cancellation can leave a much larger factor
in the actual reduced denominator.

For an integer $D\ge2$ and a rational $x$, put
\[
 z_j(x)=(D-j)^2L_j^{(1)}(x),\qquad
 Q_{D,x}=\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}z_j(x)(L_j-L_{j+1}).
\]
The common factor $D^{-2}$ in the normalized localization family is
omitted: it has no effect on $A(Q)/B(Q)$ or its primitive error.
The rational forms satisfy
\[
 A(Q)-\gamma B(Q)=\int_0^\infty Q(t)^2(t-1)\log t\,e^{-t}\,dt>0.
\]

Define three rational polynomials
\[
 P(D)=\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(2D^2-11D-31)}{15},
\]
\[
 R(D)=-\frac{D(334D^4-1915D^3-9660D^2-9425D-934)}{900},
\]
\[
 V(D)=-\frac{D(D+1)(D+2)(2D^2-11D-1)}{15}.
\]
The finite-sum identities proved in Section~\ref{s3--sec:fixed-shift-foundation} give
\[
 A(Q_{D,0})=P(D)H_D+R(D),\qquad B(Q_{D,0})=V(D).
\]
Indeed the ordinary Laguerre coefficients at $x=0$ are
$c_j=3j^2-(4D+1)j+D^2$, and substitution into the exact Gram
matrices gives these identities by finite sums.

\begin{theorem}[A node-zero prime survives the complete gcd]
Let $p\ge7$ be prime, assume $D\ge p$, let $v_p(x)=s\ge1$, and put
\[
 a=\lfloor\log_pD\rfloor,\qquad h=\lfloor D/p^a\rfloor.
\]
Suppose $P(D)$, $V(D)$, and $H_h$ are $p$-adic units.
Then $B(Q_{D,x})\ne0$, and
\[
 v_p(A(Q_{D,x}))=-a,\qquad v_p(B(Q_{D,x}))=0.
\]
Consequently the actual reduced denominator satisfies
\[
 \boxed{v_p\!\left(\operatorname{den}(A(Q_{D,x})/B(Q_{D,x}))\right)=a.}
\]
This is a valuation after complete reduction, not a common-denominator
estimate.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For every integer $r\ge1$,
$v_p(x^r/r!)\ge s$, since $v_p(r!)\le r-1$ and $s\ge1$.
The finite Laguerre formula therefore gives, uniformly in $j$,
\[
 L_j^{(1)}(x)\equiv j+1\pmod{p^s\mathbb Z_p}.
\]
Thus every ordinary Laguerre coefficient of $Q_{D,x}-Q_{D,0}$
belongs to $p^s\mathbb Z_p$.
The half-lcm clearing theorem~\ref{s1--next-square-normalization} says that $p^aA$ has $p$-integral quadratic
coefficients; $B$ has integral quadratic coefficients. It follows that
\[
 v_p(A(Q_{D,x})-A(Q_{D,0}))\ge s-a,
 \qquad
 v_p(B(Q_{D,x})-B(Q_{D,0}))\ge s.
\]
In $H_D$, the terms with denominator divisible by $p^a$ sum to
$p^{-a}H_h$. All other terms have valuation at least $1-a$.
The unit hypothesis gives $v_p(H_D)=-a$.
Since $a\ge1$, $P(D)$ is a unit and $R(D)$ is $p$-integral, so
$v_p(A(Q_{D,0}))=-a$; its perturbation has strictly larger valuation.
Likewise $V(D)$ is a unit and its perturbation is divisible by $p$.
These facts prove the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary harmonic exception for a shifted node]
Fix a positive integer $k$ and an integer $M>k$, and use
$D=M^2$, $x=1-k/M$.
Let $p\ge7$ divide $M-k$, with $p\nmid k$, and set
$a=\lfloor\log_p(M^2)\rfloor$, $h=\lfloor M^2/p^a\rfloor$.
If $P(k^2)$, $V(k^2)$, and $H_h$ are $p$-adic units, then
\[
 v_p(q_M)=a,\qquad
 q_M\ge p^a>\frac{M^2}{p}>M.
\]
Thus any sequence satisfying $q_M=o(M)$ must eventually arrange,
at every such numerator prime except the fixed coefficient exceptions,
the congruence $H_h\equiv0\pmod p$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Here $v_p(x)=v_p(M-k)\ge1$, since $M\equiv k\not\equiv0\pmod p$.
The polynomial unit hypotheses reduce to their values at $k^2$.
Also $p\le M-k<M$, so $D>p^2$ and the theorem applies with $a\ge2$.
Finally $M^2<p^{a+1}$ proves the displayed lower bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An all-exponent obstruction for bounded cofactors]
Fix positive integers $k,c$. Apart from an explicit finite set of primes,
every prime
\[
 p>\max\{c^2,2kc+k^2,5\}
\]
has the following property. For every $e\ge1$, let $M=k+cp^e$ and
$x=1-k/M$. Then
\[
 \boxed{v_p(q_M)=2e,\qquad q_M\ge p^{2e}=((M-k)/c)^2.}
\]
The excluded primes are precisely those additionally dividing the
numerators of $H_{c^2}$, $P(k^2)$, or $V(k^2)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The size condition gives
$c^2<M^2/p^{2e}<c^2+1\le p$.
Therefore $a=2e$ and $h=c^2$, while $v_p(x)=e$.
The preceding theorem proves the result.
The two fixed polynomial values are nonzero, since neither
$2D^2-11D-31$ nor $2D^2-11D-1$ has an integer root.
Hence the exceptional prime set is finite.
\end{proof}

For example, for $k=3,c=4$,
\[
 P(9)=2112=2^6\cdot3\cdot11,\qquad
 V(9)=-4092=-2^2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot31,
\]
\[
 H_{16}=\frac{2436559}{720720},\qquad2436559=17^2\cdot8431.
\]
Thus every prime $p\ge37$, $p\ne8431$, and every $e\ge1$ gives
$v_p(q_{3+4p^e})=2e$. In particular primes $p\equiv3\pmod4$
at $e=1$ give infinitely many obstructed parameters
$M\equiv15\pmod{16}$, a class in which the leading two-adic residue
had canceled. Infinitude of primes $3$ modulo $4$ follows from the
usual Euclid argument and is unaffected by deleting a finite set.

\begin{corollary}[The full dyadic $k=3$ schedule does not have decaying error]
Take $k=3$ and $M_s=2^s-1$. Along infinitely many $s$,
\[
 q_{M_s}>M_s^2/7.
\]
The primitive errors of this full schedule therefore have infinite
limsup; in particular they do not tend to zero. This statement does
not exclude every further subsequence of the schedule.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For $s\equiv2\pmod3$, $7\mid M_s-3$.
The numbers $P(9)$ and $V(9)$ are $7$-adic units, and
\[
 (H_1,H_2,H_3,H_4,H_5,H_6)\equiv(1,5,3,5,1,0)\pmod7.
\]
Consequently, if the leading base-$7$ digit of $M_s^2$ is at most $5$,
the theorem gives $v_7(q_{M_s})=\lfloor\log_7(M_s^2)\rfloor$
and $q_{M_s}>M_s^2/7$.

There are infinitely many such $s\equiv2\pmod3$. Indeed, for $s=3n+2$,
\[
 \log_7(M_s^2)=6n\log_7 2+4\log_7 2+o(1).
\]
The number $6\log_7 2$ is irrational by unique factorization.
Density of an irrational rotation supplies infinitely many $n$ for
which the fractional part of the main term belongs to $(1/4,1/2)$.
The vanishing perturbation preserves membership in a slightly larger
interval strictly contained in $(0,\log_7 6)$; this is exactly the
required leading-digit condition. Density can be proved by the
elementary pigeonhole argument already used in the Farey-selection
theorem, and every tail of the orbit is dense.

For any fixed $k>0$, the normalized localization proof in Section~\ref{s3--sec:fixed-shift-foundation}
applies to $D^{-2}Q_{D,x}$ at $x=1-k/M$ and gives
\[
 B_M=-k\kappa+O(\log M/M),\quad T_M=2\kappa M+O(\log M),
 \quad U_M=O(M^{-1}),\qquad \kappa=128e/(315\pi).
\]
The exact rational sandwich then gives
$\gamma-A_M/B_M=\Theta(M^{-1})$ and primitive error
$\mathcal E_M=\Theta(q_M/M)$.
The lower bound $q_{M_s}>M_s^2/7$ on the stated infinite subsequence
therefore makes $\mathcal E_{M_s}$ tend to infinity on that subsequence.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Relation to the existing target-realization results.}
Positive rational mixing of two nearby certificates can cancel all
their old denominator factors. That observation is already contained
in the earlier exact target-realization theorem, its determinant/gcd
identity, and the Farey optimization theorems; it is not a new solution
to condition 3. The new contribution here is the local survival
criterion at numerator primes, including its all-exponent and dyadic
consequences. It concerns this single localized-square family and
does not exclude arbitrary positive mixtures or other constructions.

\paragraph{A finite full-denominator audit of the apparent two-adic escape.}
For $k=3$, $M=11$, $D=121$, $x=8/11$, the earlier modular computation
gave $v_2(q)=0$. Complete rational evaluation of $A/B$ gives an odd
reduced denominator with $633$ decimal digits:
\[
 10^{632}\le q<10^{633}.
\]
The exact moment calculation also gives $10|B|>T$, where
$T=\mathsf H_2+\mathsf H_1$ is the rational moment quantity from the localization
sandwich. Consequently
\[
 \mathcal E\ge\frac{2q|B|}{T}>\frac q5>10^{631}.
\]
The accompanying exact-arithmetic script and its full integer/rational
certificate record the complete denominator and both error bounds.
No decimal value of $\gamma$ enters this calculation. This finite audit
is not an infinite obstruction theorem; it shows concretely why
eliminating the factor $2$ at one parameter did not satisfy condition 3.



\clearpage
\part{Proper kernels, prime support, and exact cancellation}\label{part:kernels}


\section{Kernel identities and analytic inputs}\label{s6--sec:foundations}
\subsection{Proper Binet kernels and rational error bounds}
We reproduce the kernel calculation to fix the normalization of these certificates.
Put
\[
 d\mu(u)=\frac{du}{e^{2\pi\sqrt u}-1}.
\]
Binet's identity \cite{dlmf-binet} gives, for every integer $j\ge1$,
\[
 \int_0^\infty\frac{d\mu(u)}{u+j^2}
 =\gamma+\log j-H_j+\frac1{2j}.
\]
For $n\ge1$, define
\[
 R_n(u)=\frac{\prod_{k=0}^{2n-1}(4u+k^2)}
              {\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(u+j^2)},\qquad
 I_n=\int_0^\infty R_n(u)\,d\mu(u)>0.
\]
The residues, constant coefficient, and prime-log coefficients are
\begin{align*}
 A_{n,j}&=(-1)^{j-n}
 \frac{4j^2(2j+2n-1)!(n+j-1)!}
 {(2j-2n)!(j-n)!(3n-j)!(3n+j)!},\\
 p_n&=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}\left(H_j-\frac1{2j}\right),\qquad
 E_{n,\ell}=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}v_\ell(j).
\end{align*}
There is no polynomial part in the partial fraction decomposition, and
$\sum_j A_{n,j}=16^n$. Thus Binet's formula gives exactly
\begin{equation}\label{s6--stage3-proper-linear-form}
 I_n=16^n\gamma-p_n+\sum_{\ell\le3n}E_{n,\ell}\log\ell.
\end{equation}
Only primes occur in the last sum.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform height and raw integral bounds]
\label{s6--stage3-proper-bounds}
For every $n\ge1$ and $n\le j\le3n$,
\[
 2A_{n,j}\in\mathbb Z,\qquad
 2|A_{n,j}|\le6\,2^{12n}.
\]
Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{s6--stage3-proper-U}
 0<I_n<\mathcal U_n:=
 \frac{(4n)!((n-1)!)^2}{8\,16^n((3n)!)^2},
 \qquad \mathcal U_{n+1}<\mathcal U_n,
\end{equation}
and, with $\kappa_0=\log(729/16)$,
\[
 \log \mathcal U_n=-\kappa_0 n+O(\log(n+1)).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $a=j+n$ and $b=j-n$. With
\[
 B=\binom{2a}{b},\quad C=\binom a{2b},\quad
 B'=\binom{2a-1}{b-1},\quad C'=\binom{a-1}{2b-1},
\]
where $B'=C'=0$ at $b=0$, direct factorial simplification gives
\[
 2|A_{n,j}|=BC+4B'C+B'C'.
\]
This proves integrality. Every product in this expression is at most
$2^{3a}\le2^{12n}$, proving the stated height bound.

For the integral estimate, put
$d\nu(u)=du/(2\sinh(2\pi\sqrt u))$. Then
$1<d\mu/d\nu=1+e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}<2$.
Let $T_j(u)=P_{2j}^{(1)}(2\sqrt u;\pi/2)$ be the even
Meixner--Pollaczek polynomials in their usual normalization.
Their generating function and orthogonality
\cite{dlmf-mp,dlmf-mp-generating} imply
\[
 S_r(u):=\sum_{j=0}^r\binom rj T_j(u)
       =\frac{4^r}{(2r)!}\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}(4u+k^2),
 \qquad \int_0^\infty S_r\,d\nu=\frac1{16}.
\]
For clarity, the generating function of the binomial transform is
$\cosh(4\sqrt u\arcsin\sqrt z)$, whose coefficient gives the displayed
product. In the integral, all $T_j$ with $j>0$ vanish by orthogonality;
the constant norm is $\int d\nu=1/16$. The product is positive for
$u>0$, so $\int S_r d\mu<1/8$.
Since
\[
 R_n(u)=\frac{(4n)!}{16^n}
          \frac{S_{2n}(u)}{\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(u+j^2)},
\]
replacing each denominator factor by $j^2$ gives
\eqref{s6--stage3-proper-U}. A direct quotient estimate gives
\[
 \frac{\mathcal U_{n+1}}{\mathcal U_n}
 =\frac{(4n+1)(4n+2)(4n+3)(4n+4)n^2}
 {16(3n+1)^2(3n+2)^2(3n+3)^2}
 \le\frac{16}{729}\left(1+\frac1n\right)^4
 \le\frac{256}{729}<1.
\]
Finally Stirling's formula \cite{dlmf-stirling} gives the logarithmic estimate.
\end{proof}



We use
$L_j=\sum_\ell E_{j,\ell}\log\ell$. The latter denotes a logarithmic
value, not a least common multiple. The factor-two denominator
result proved in Section~\ref{s6--adic:section} gives
$d_jp_j,d_jE_{j,\ell}\in\Z$ for
$d_j=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3j)$.
The asymptotic formula, including its prefactor, is
\begin{equation}\label{s6--eq:r-asymptotic}
 r_n:=\frac{\mathcal U_n}{16^n}
 \sim\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\,n^{-3/2}729^{-n}.
\end{equation}
This follows directly from Stirling's formula \cite{dlmf-stirling}.
The quotient bound above also gives
$r_{n+1}\le(16/729)r_n$.


\subsection{Positive kernels from weighted prefixes}
\label{s6--sec:cumulative-positive-kernel}

Write $f_j=16^{-j}R_j$, and retain
$L_j=\sum_\ell E_{j,\ell}\log\ell$ and $\rho_j=16^{-j}L_j$.

\begin{lemma}[Pointwise ordering and logarithmic ordering]
For every $j\ge1$ and every $u>0$,
\[
 0<\frac{f_{j+1}(u)}{f_j(u)}
 =\frac{(u+j^2)^2(u+(j+\tfrac12)^2)}
 {(u+(3j+1)^2)(u+(3j+2)^2)(u+(3j+3)^2)}<1.
\]
Moreover $\rho_{j+1}>\rho_j$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Cancel the common numerator and denominator factors in $R_{j+1}/R_j$.
Each of the three resulting numerator factors is smaller than its
paired denominator factor. The strict inequality follows.
The partial fractions and $\sum_kA_{j,k}=16^j$ give
\[
 2\rho_j=\int_0^\infty\left(\frac1{u+1}-f_j(u)\right)\,du,
\]
since $\int_0^\infty((u+1)^{-1}-(u+k^2)^{-1})\,du=2\log k$.
Subtracting consecutive identities gives
\[
 2(\rho_j-\rho_{j+1})
 =-\int_0^\infty(f_j(u)-f_{j+1}(u))\,du<0.
\]
This integral converges: each $f_j$ has leading term $1/u$ at infinity,
and each is regular at zero. Its integrand is strictly positive.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The cumulative positivity cone]
\label{s6--thm:cumulative-cone}
Let $c=(c_n,\ldots,c_M)$ be a finite real vector and set
\[
 a_j=16^jc_j,\qquad S_k=\sum_{j=n}^k a_j,
 \qquad K_c(u)=\sum_{j=n}^M c_jR_j(u).
\]
Then
\[
 K_c(u)=\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(f_k(u)-f_{k+1}(u))+S_M f_M(u).
\]
If $c\ne0$ and every $S_k\ge0$, then $K_c(u)>0$ for every $u>0$.
If in addition $c$ cancels all prime-log coordinates, then necessarily
$S_M>0$, and
\[
 0<\int_0^\infty K_c\,d\mu
   =S_M\gamma-\sum_{j=n}^M c_jp_j
   <\sum_{j=n}^M |c_j|\mathcal U_j.
\]
No arithmetic assumption about $\gamma$ is used.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The displayed decomposition is finite summation by parts. Every
function appearing there is strictly positive on $(0,\infty)$.
Not all $S_k$ vanish unless $c=0$, proving positivity of $K_c$.
Log cancellation and a second summation by parts give
\[
 0=\sum_{j=n}^M a_j\rho_j
   =\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(\rho_k-\rho_{k+1})+S_M\rho_M.
\]
If $S_M=0$, one of the earlier $S_k$ is positive and the strict
increase of $\rho_j$ makes the right-hand side negative. This proves
$S_M>0$. Binet's identity, positivity, and the strict individual upper
bounds $0<I_j<\mathcal U_j$ finish the proof.
\end{proof}



\subsection{Quantitative logarithmic increments}
Retain $f_k=R_k/16^k$, $\rho_k=L_k/16^k$, and put
\[
 \Delta_k=\rho_{k+1}-\rho_k,
 \qquad
 T_k=2+\frac32H_{k-1},\qquad H_0=0.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Explicit rational bounds for the logarithmic increments]
\label{s6--lem:rho-increments-rational}
For every integer $k\ge1$,
\[
 \boxed{\Delta_k>\frac1{66k},\qquad 0<\rho_k<T_k.}
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set
\[
 B_k=\sum_{j=k}^{3k}j^2
     =\frac{26k^3+15k^2+k}{3}\le14k^3.
\]
Factoring powers of $u$ out of numerator and denominator gives
\[
 f_k(u)=\frac1u
 \frac{\prod_{h=0}^{2k-1}(1+(h/2)^2/u)}
      {\prod_{j=k}^{3k}(1+j^2/u)}.
\]
For $u\ge14k^3$, the numerator factors are at least one and
$\prod_j(1+j^2/u)\le\exp(B_k/u)\le e<3$. Hence
\[
 f_k(u)>\frac1{3u}.
\]
The exact ratio from the preceding positivity lemma satisfies
\[
 \frac{f_{k+1}(u)}{f_k(u)}
 \le\frac{u+k^2}{u+(3k+1)^2}.
\]
On $14k^3\le u\le28k^3$, it follows that
\[
 1-\frac{f_{k+1}(u)}{f_k(u)}
 \ge\frac{8k^2+6k+1}{u+(3k+1)^2}
 \ge\frac{8k^2}{44k^3}=\frac2{11k}.
\]
Frullani's identity therefore yields
\begin{align*}
 \Delta_k
 &=\frac12\int_0^\infty(f_k-f_{k+1})\,du\\
 &>\frac12\,(14k^3)\frac1{84k^3}\frac2{11k}
 =\frac1{66k}.
\end{align*}

For the upper bound, the elementary product inequality
$\prod_i(1-t_i)\ge1-\sum_i t_i$ for $0\le t_i\le1$ gives
\[
 \prod_{j=k}^{3k}\frac1{1+j^2/u}
 \ge1-\sum_{j=k}^{3k}\frac{j^2}{u+j^2}
 \ge1-\frac{B_k}{u}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 f_k(u)\ge\frac1u-\frac{B_k}{u^2}\qquad(u>0).
\]
Here, if the right-hand side is negative, the inequality follows
already from $f_k(u)>0$; if it is nonnegative, multiplying the product
bound by the numerator factors preserves it.
Split the Frullani integral at $B_k$. On its first part drop the
nonnegative $f_k$; on its second part use the last estimate. This gives
\begin{align*}
 2\rho_k
 &=\int_0^\infty\left(\frac1{u+1}-f_k(u)\right)du\\
 &<\log(B_k+1)+\int_{B_k}^\infty\frac{B_k}{u^2}\,du
 =\log(B_k+1)+1\\
 &\le\log(15k^3)+1
 <4+3H_{k-1}=2T_k.
\end{align*}
The last strict inequality uses $\log15<3$ and
$\log k\le H_{k-1}$. The elementary estimate $e>5/2$ proves
$\log15<3$. Positivity of $\rho_k$ was proved by the earlier
Frullani separation bound, and also follows directly from
$f_k(u)<1/(u+9k^2)\le1/(u+1)$.
\end{proof}


For later compactness, exact cancellation gives
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k\Delta_k=q\rho_M.
\]
If $S_k\ge0$ and $q=S_M>0$, each term on the left is nonnegative,
so $S_k<66kT_Mq$ for $k<M$. Thus all normalized prefixes $q=1$
are bounded in every fixed window.


\subsection{A sharper uniform residue height}
\begin{lemma}[A sharper uniform residue height]
\label{s6--reverse:residue-height}
Put
\[
 G=\frac{16399}{1296},\qquad \beta=G^2.
\]
For all $m\le j\le3m$,
\[
 2|A_{m,j}|\le6\beta^m,\qquad \beta^3<2^{22}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $a=j+m$, $b=j-m$, so $a-b=2m$ and $0\le2b\le a$.
The exact binomial identity used to prove residue integrality is
\[
 2|A_{m,j}|=BC+4B'C+B'C',
\]
where
\[
 B=\binom{2a}{b},\quad C=\binom a{2b},\quad
 B'=\binom{2a-1}{b-1},\quad C'=\binom{a-1}{2b-1};
\]
put $B'=C'=0$ when $b=0$. Since $B'\le B$ and $C'\le C$,
the right side is at most $6BC$.

For any positive $t,s$, the binomial theorem gives
\[
 BC\le \frac{(1+t)^{2a}(1+s)^a}{t^b s^{2b}}.
\]
Choose $t=5/18$ and $s=27/4$. Then
\[
 (1+t)^2(1+s)=G,\qquad
 \frac{G}{ts^2}=\frac{32798}{32805}<1.
\]
Consequently
\[
 BC\le G^{a-b}\left(\frac{G}{ts^2}\right)^b
       \le G^{2m}=\beta^m.
\]
The remaining strict inequality is an exact integer comparison:
\[
 2^{22}1296^6-16399^6
 =424901949697141879058783>0.
\]
\end{proof}





\subsection{The matrices and the two arithmetic coordinates}
For each $N$, set
\[
 V_N=(2E_{n,\ell})_{\substack{\ell\le3N\ {\rm prime}\\1\le n\le N}},
 \qquad
 \Psi_N(c)=
 \left(\sum_{n=1}^N16^nc_n,\ \sum_{n=1}^Np_nc_n\right).
\]
Rows of $V_N$ are ordered by increasing prime.
All entries of $V_N$ are integers; those of $\Psi_N$ are rational.
The phrase \emph{log-null} means $V_Nc=0$, coordinate by coordinate.
It is stronger than a numerical cancellation test on a real sum of
logarithms. For such a vector,
\[
 \sum_{n=1}^Nc_nI_n=L_\gamma(\Psi_N(c)),
 \qquad L_\gamma(q,p)=q\gamma-p.
\]
For rational $x$, $\operatorname{den}(x)$ denotes its positive reduced
denominator, with $\operatorname{den}(0)=1$.
\section{Exact rank and a recursive basis for logarithm cancellation}
\label{s4--sec:rank}

This section gives an infinite construction of all finite logarithm
cancellations. The rank certificates at its two starting indices use
only arithmetic in finite fields. No numerical value of $\gamma$ is
used.

\begin{lemma}[One new prime at a time]
\label{s4--lem:newprime}
For $N\ge2$, the interval $(3N-3,3N]$ contains at most one prime.
If it contains a prime $\ell_N$, then
\[
 V_{\ell_N,n}=0\quad(n<N),\qquad
 V_{\ell_N,N}=2A_{N,\ell_N}\ne0.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The integer $3N$ is composite, and one of the consecutive integers
$3N-2,3N-1$ is even and greater than two. Thus at most one is prime.
If $\ell_N$ occurs, then $\ell_N>3(N-1)\ge N$ and
$2\ell_N>3N$. Earlier pole intervals contain no multiple of $\ell_N$,
whereas the current pole interval contains exactly the single multiple
$j=\ell_N$. The residue formula shows that its coefficient is nonzero.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact logarithm rank]
\label{s4--thm:rank}
For every $N\ge9$,
\[
 \boxed{\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}V_N=\pi(3N),\qquad
        \dim_{\mathbb Q}\ker V_N=N-\pi(3N).}
\]
The same rank holds over $\mathbb R$. Here $\pi(x)$ denotes the number
of primes not exceeding $x$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The $9$ by $9$ matrix $V_9$ is nonsingular: the exact finite-field
certificate in Appendix~\ref{s4--app:rankcert} gives
$\det V_9\equiv97\pmod {101}$.
Suppose the claimed row rank holds for $N-1$. If no new prime occurs,
the old matrix is a full-row-rank submatrix of $V_N$. If a new prime
occurs, its new row is zero in all old columns and nonzero in the new
column by Lemma~\ref{s4--lem:newprime}, so the rank increases by one.
This proves the assertion by induction. Rational and real rank agree
for a rational matrix.
\end{proof}

The starting index is minimal: for $1\le N\le8$ one has
$\pi(3N)=N+1$, so full row rank is impossible. The kernel dimension
increases by exactly one at every index with no new prime, and stays
unchanged at every index with a new prime.

\begin{theorem}[Exact rank of the arithmetic output]
\label{s4--thm:outputrank}
Put
\[
 W_N=\begin{pmatrix} V_N\\ (16^n)_{n=1}^N\\ (p_n)_{n=1}^N\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For every $N\ge17$,
\[
 \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}W_N=\pi(3N)+2,\qquad
 \Psi_N(\ker_{\mathbb Q}V_N)=\mathbb Q^2.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The matrix $W_{17}$ is square. Its entries have denominators prime to
$211$, and the exact certificate in Appendix~\ref{s4--app:rankcert} gives
$\det W_{17}\equiv65\pmod {211}$. Thus the output rank is two at
$N=17$. This rank cannot decrease when zero coordinates are appended
to old kernel vectors. Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:rank}, together with the
elementary rank identity
\[
 \operatorname{rank}\begin{pmatrix}V_N\\ \Psi_N\end{pmatrix}
 =\operatorname{rank}V_N+
   \operatorname{rank}(\Psi_N|_{\ker V_N}),
\]
proves both assertions.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A canonical recursion with growing support}
Let $\mathcal P_9=\{1,\ldots,9\}$. For $N>9$, define the pivot set by
\[
 \mathcal P_N=
 \begin{cases}
  \mathcal P_{N-1}\cup\{N\},&\pi(3N)>\pi(3N-3),\\
  \mathcal P_{N-1},&\pi(3N)=\pi(3N-3).
 \end{cases}
\]
Rows are ordered by increasing prime and columns by increasing index.
The square matrix $B_N=V_N[:,\mathcal P_N]$ is invertible. More
precisely,
\begin{equation}
 \det B_N=\det V_9
 \prod_{\substack{10\le k\le N\\
                  \pi(3k)>\pi(3k-3)}}2A_{k,\ell_k}.
 \label{s4--eq:pivotdet}
\end{equation}
This follows from the block upper triangular form at every new-prime
step.

At an index $m\ge10$ with no new prime, write $v_m$ for the new column,
with the same row set as $V_{m-1}$. Define a rational vector $h^{(m)}$
by
\begin{equation}
 h^{(m)}_m=1,\qquad
 h^{(m)}_{\mathcal P_{m-1}}=-B_{m-1}^{-1}v_m,\qquad
 h^{(m)}_j=0\quad
 (j\notin\mathcal P_{m-1}\cup\{m\}).
 \label{s4--eq:kernelrecursion}
\end{equation}
Append zeros when this vector is regarded as a vector in a larger
block.

\begin{theorem}[All finite cancellations from a triangular recursion]
\label{s4--thm:kernelrecursion}
For every $N\ge9$, the vectors
\[
 \left\{h^{(m)}:
 10\le m\le N,\ \pi(3m)=\pi(3m-3)\right\}
\]
form a rational basis of $\ker V_N$.
Their number is exactly $N-\pi(3N)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At its creation, \eqref{s4--eq:kernelrecursion} cancels every existing
prime row. A later prime row is identically zero on its support, so
the vector remains in every larger kernel. Its coordinate at the
nonpivot index $m$ is one, while all other displayed basis vectors
have zero in that coordinate. The vectors are therefore independent.
Their number is $N-|\mathcal P_N|=N-\pi(3N)$, the full kernel
dimension from Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:rank}.
\end{proof}

This is a constructive infinite recursion for exact logarithm
cancellation. All matrices and residues are rational and explicitly
given. Multiplying any $h^{(m)}$ by the least common multiple of its
entry denominators gives an integer vector. A second finite clearing
factor makes both arithmetic output coordinates integral. These
operations prove exact integrality; they do not bound the resulting
primitive error. In particular, neither the growth of the kernel
dimension nor the determinant product \eqref{s4--eq:pivotdet} implies
that the second primitive minimum tends to zero.

\section{What kind of recurrence the integrals cannot satisfy}
\label{s4--sec:nonprec}

\begin{theorem}[The exact rational span of the integrals]
\label{s4--thm:span}
For every $N\ge17$,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{I_1,\ldots,I_N\}
 =
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}
 \bigl(\{1,\gamma\}\cup\{\log\ell:\ell\le3N,\ \ell\text{ prime}\}\bigr).
 \label{s4--eq:span}
\end{equation}
In particular the dimension of the left side is at least $\pi(3N)$
and tends to infinity.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The Binet identity gives the inclusion from left to right. For the
other inclusion, Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:outputrank} says that the formal
coefficient columns, whose coordinates correspond to
$\{1,\gamma,\log\ell\}$, span the full rational coordinate space.
The factors $2$ in $V_N$ and the sign of the $p_n$ row are invertible
rational row scalings. Thus a rational combination of the $I_n$
recovers each displayed generator separately.

The logarithms of distinct primes are rationally independent. Indeed,
clearing denominators in $\sum_\ell a_\ell\log\ell=0$ and
exponentiating gives $\prod_\ell\ell^{a_\ell}=1$ with integral
exponents; unique factorization gives $a_\ell=0$ for every $\ell$.
No assertion about the independence of $\gamma$, $1$, and the
logarithms is required.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No eventually nonsingular rational recurrence]
\label{s4--thm:nonprec}
There do not exist a fixed $r\ge0$, an index $n_0$, and rational
numbers $a_{k,n}$, for $0\le k\le r$ and $n\ge n_0$, satisfying
\[
 a_{r,n}\ne0,\qquad
 \sum_{k=0}^r a_{k,n}I_{n+k}=0
 \quad\text{for every }n\ge n_0.
\]
Consequently $(I_n)$ is not P-recursive over $\mathbb Q$, and its
ordinary generating series is not D-finite over $\mathbb Q(z)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Such a recurrence would express each subsequent term as a rational
linear combination of the preceding $r$ terms. Including the finite
initial segment, all terms would lie in a fixed finite-dimensional
rational vector space, contrary to Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:span}.
The case $r=0$ would give $I_n=0$, also impossible.

In a polynomial-coefficient recurrence over $\mathbb Q$, the highest
nonzero coefficient polynomial has only finitely many integer zeros.
It would therefore give the excluded recurrence after a finite
starting index. Finally, a differential equation with coefficients in
$\mathbb Q[z]$ for the generating series gives a polynomial-coefficient
recurrence by equating coefficients. This is the usual
P-recursive/D-finite correspondence; see Stanley
\cite[Theorem 1.5]{stanley1980}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No closed finite rational state]
A representation of $(I_n)$ by a fixed finite-dimensional state,
updated by rational matrices and read by rational linear output maps, is
impossible if the initial state has finitely many real coordinates.
The same conclusion holds if fixed finitely many real constants
appear as inhomogeneous inputs.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every state and output lies in the rational span of the initial
coordinates and the finitely many fixed inputs. This contradicts
Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:span}.
\end{proof}

The restriction to rational coefficients is essential. These results
concern this particular family of proper Binet integrals. Other
families of approximants to $\gamma$ can satisfy polynomial
recurrences; see, for example, \cite{pilehrood2013}. The recursive
