kernel construction in Section~\ref{s4--sec:rank} is not excluded,
because its dimension and support increase.

\section{Total positivity and the necessary cancellation bandwidth}
\label{s4--sec:chebyshev-bandwidth}

The polynomial degree bound in the prime-band argument can be replaced
by the dimension bound.  The reason is that the cleared residue
polynomials belong to a strictly totally positive generalized Bernstein
basis.  We include an elementary proof of the required total positivity;
in particular, no numerical sign test is used.

\begin{lemma}[Positive solid minors imply strict total positivity]
\label{s4--lem:solid-fekete}
Let $X$ be a finite real matrix. If every square minor with consecutive
rows and consecutive columns is strictly positive, then every square
minor of $X$ is strictly positive.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We first prove the following completion step for an $N\times m$ matrix
$Y$, with $N\ge m$. Suppose all its $(m-1)$-minors on its first $m-1$
columns are positive, and all its $m$-minors with consecutive rows are
positive. Then all its $m$-minors are positive. For $m=1$ there is
nothing to prove. For $m\ge2$, induct on the dispersion
$i_m-i_1-m+1$ of a row set $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_m\}$.
If this dispersion is nonzero, insert a missing interior index to obtain
$J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_{m+1}\}$ with $I=J\setminus\{j_t\}$,
$1<t<m+1$. Set
\[
 \Delta_s=\det Y[J\setminus\{j_s\},\{1,\ldots,m\}],
 \qquad
 \delta_{uv}=\det Y[J\setminus\{j_u,j_v\},\{1,\ldots,m-1\}].
\]
The determinantal identity
\[
 \delta_{1,m+1}\Delta_t
 =\delta_{t,m+1}\Delta_1+\delta_{1,t}\Delta_{m+1}
\]
is the elementary three-term Pl\"ucker identity (and also follows by
expanding each determinant in its last column).
All $\delta$'s are positive by hypothesis; $\Delta_1$ and
$\Delta_{m+1}$ have smaller dispersion, so they are positive by
induction. This proves the completion step.

Now induct on the order $m$ of minors of $X$. All smaller minors may
be assumed positive. Apply the completion step first to every submatrix
formed by $m$ consecutive columns: its full-size minors are positive.
Next fix any $m$ rows and apply the completion step to the transpose of
the submatrix on those rows. Its consecutive-row full-size minors are
precisely the minors just proved positive. Hence all $m$-minors of $X$
are positive, completing the induction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Separated-knot Bernstein basis]
\label{s4--lem:separated-bernstein}
Let $N\ge0$ and let $a_1,\ldots,a_N,b_1,\ldots,b_N$ be real numbers
such that the interval
\[
\mathcal I=(\max_i a_i,\min_i b_i)
\]
is nonempty; when $N=0$, take any nonempty open interval instead.
Repeated knots on the same side are allowed. Define
\[
 B_j(x)=\prod_{i=1}^j(x-a_i)\prod_{i=j+1}^N(b_i-x),
 \qquad 0\le j\le N.
\]
For every finite increasing list of distinct nodes in $\mathcal I$,
the collocation matrix with rows indexed by nodes and columns indexed
by $j$ is strictly totally positive. Consequently every subfamily of
$s+1$ of the $B_j$ is a Chebyshev system: a nonzero real linear
combination has at most $s$ distinct zeros in $\mathcal I$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a block of consecutive columns $j=v,v+1,\ldots,v+k$, factor the
positive common function
\[
 W(x)=\prod_{i\le v}(x-a_i)\prod_{i>v+k}(b_i-x)
\]
out of each row. The remaining $k+1$ polynomials are
\[
 g_j(x)=\prod_{i=v+1}^{v+j}(x-a_i)
              \prod_{i=v+j+1}^{v+k}(b_i-x),\qquad0\le j\le k.
\]
Their coefficient determinant, in increasing monomial order, is
\[
 \det\bigl([x^i]g_j(x)\bigr)_{0\le i,j\le k}
 =\prod_{v<i\le j\le v+k}(b_j-a_i)>0.                 \tag{CB}
\]
For completeness, evaluate the polynomials at $a_{v+1}$ and express
the remainder in the basis
$1,(x-a_{v+1}),\ldots,(x-a_{v+1})^k$.
The monomial change of basis has determinant one. Only the first
polynomial has a nonzero constant coefficient, namely
$\prod_{j=v+1}^{v+k}(b_j-a_{v+1})$. Deleting its row and column and
dividing the remaining polynomials by $x-a_{v+1}$ leaves the same
problem with $k-1$ pairs of knots. Induction proves (CB), including
repeated $a_i$.

At any $k+1$ increasing nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_k$ in $\mathcal I$, the
minor on these consecutive columns is therefore
\[
 \left(\prod_{h=0}^kW(x_h)\right)
 \left(\prod_{0\le h<l\le k}(x_l-x_h)\right)
 \left(\prod_{v<i\le j\le v+k}(b_j-a_i)\right)>0.
\]
In particular all solid minors are positive, so
Lemma~\ref{s4--lem:solid-fekete} proves strict total positivity.
If a combination of $s+1$ selected columns vanished at $s+1$ distinct
nodes, their strictly positive square collocation determinant would
make every coefficient zero. This gives the zero bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp dimension bound for the prime band]
\label{s4--thm:chebyshev-bandwidth}
Let $n\ge1$, $r\ge0$, and suppose a nonzero vector
$(c_0,\ldots,c_r)\in\mathbb R^{r+1}$ cancels every prime-log
coordinate of the proper kernels $R_n,\ldots,R_{n+r}$.
Then
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 r\ge\pi(3n)-\pi\!\left(\frac{3(n+r)}2\right).
 \quad}                                                     \tag{PB}
\]
In particular, along any such sequence of cancellations with
$n\to\infty$ and $r=o(n)$,
\[
 r\ge\left(\frac32+o(1)\right)\frac{n}{\log n}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For primes $3(n+r)/2<\ell\le3n$, the only multiple of $\ell$ in
each pole interval $[n+k,3(n+k)]$ is $\ell$ itself. The corresponding
log coefficient equals $A_{n+k,\ell}$. Write $x=\ell^2$.
The exact residue ratio is
\[
 \frac{A_{m+1,\ell}}{A_{m,\ell}}
 =\frac{-16(x-m^2)^2(x-(m+\tfrac12)^2)}
 {( (3m+1)^2-x)((3m+2)^2-x)((3m+3)^2-x)}.
\]
Use $N=3r$ pairs of knots, indexed in blocks $m=n,\ldots,n+r-1$:
\[
 (a_{3(m-n)+1},a_{3(m-n)+2},a_{3(m-n)+3})
       =(m^2,m^2,(m+\tfrac12)^2),
\]
\[
 (b_{3(m-n)+1},b_{3(m-n)+2},b_{3(m-n)+3})
       =((3m+1)^2,(3m+2)^2,(3m+3)^2).
\]
Every prime-band node $x=\ell^2$ lies strictly between every $a_i$
and every $b_i$. If this band contains no primes, (PB) is immediate.
Otherwise this separation interval is nonempty, and
Lemma~\ref{s4--lem:separated-bernstein} applies. Clearing the common
positive denominator from the residue ratios converts the cancellation
equation at each prime into
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^r c_k(-16)^k B_{3k}(\ell^2)=0.
\]
The subfamily $B_0,B_3,\ldots,B_{3r}$ is a Chebyshev system, so a
nonzero combination has at most $r$ distinct roots there. This proves
(PB). The case $r=0$ is the same assertion for one positive constant
polynomial and may also be checked directly.
For $r=o(n)$ the prime number theorem \cite{dlmf-primes} gives
\[
 \pi(3n)-\pi\!\left(\frac{3(n+r)}2\right)
   =\left(\frac32+o(1)\right)\frac{n}{\log n},
\]
as claimed. The term ``sharp dimension bound'' refers to the number
$r$ of possible zeros of a system of dimension $r+1$; it makes no
claim that a logarithm-free vector exists at this bandwidth.
\end{proof}

The proof of Lemma~\ref{s4--lem:solid-fekete} is the classical Fekete
solid-minor criterion, included to make the application self-contained; see also \cite[Section 4.6]{fomin-zelevinsky}.
Total positivity itself is not a new principle; its consequence here is
the stronger necessary bandwidth for exact prime-log cancellation.
\section{The exact asymptotic size of the positive integral}
\label{s4--dual:ratio-section}

Retain the proper Binet kernels and their rational upper weights:
\[
 R_n(u)=\frac{\prod_{k=0}^{2n-1}(4u+k^2)}
                 {\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(u+j^2)},\qquad
 I_n=\int_0^\infty\frac{R_n(u)}{e^{2\pi\sqrt u}-1}\,du,
 \qquad
 \mathcal U_n=\frac{(4n)!((n-1)!)^2}
                    {8\,16^n((3n)!)^2}.
\]
Both the integrals and the upper weights are positive.  The previously
proved inequality is $I_n<\mathcal U_n$.  The next theorem determines
their precise asymptotic ratio.  It makes no assumption about the
arithmetic nature of Euler's constant.

\begin{theorem}[Exact limiting ratio and the first corrections]
\label{s4--dual:ratio-theorem}
As $n\to\infty$,
\[
 \boxed{\frac{I_n}{\mathcal U_n}
 =\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}
   -\frac{13\sqrt3}{256n}
   +\frac{\sqrt2}{\pi^{7/2}n^{3/2}}
   +O(n^{-2}).}
\]
In particular the rational bound $\mathcal U_n$ and the actual integral
$I_n$ have the same exponential decay rate, and
$I_n/\mathcal U_n\to3\sqrt3/16$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Euler's product for the hyperbolic sine \cite{dlmf-sinh} gives
\[
 \prod_{k=1}^\infty\left(1+\frac{4u}{k^2}\right)
       =\frac{\sinh(2\pi\sqrt u)}{2\pi\sqrt u}.
\]
% Primary source: DLMF 4.36.1, https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.36.E1 .
Define
\[
 a_n=\frac{8\,16^n}{n^2\binom{4n}{2n}},\qquad
 E_n(u)=
 \prod_{k=2n}^\infty\left(1+\frac{4u}{k^2}\right)^{-1}
 \prod_{j=n}^{3n}\left(1+\frac{u}{j^2}\right)^{-1}.
\]
The infinite product converges for each $u\ge0$. Direct cancellation of
the factorials in $R_n/\mathcal U_n$, followed by the displayed Euler
product, gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{s4--dual:ratio-exact}
 \frac{I_n}{\mathcal U_n}
 =\frac{a_n}{4\pi}\int_0^\infty
    \sqrt u\left(1+e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}\right)E_n(u)\,du.
\end{equation}
For example, before using Euler's product the prefactor is
$32u\,16^n((2n-1)!)^2/(4n)!=a_nu$; this records the normalization.

Put $e_n(x)=E_n(nx)$.  For every fixed $x\ge0$,
\[
 \log e_n(x)\longrightarrow-\frac83x.
\]
Indeed, the linear terms in the two logarithmic products are
$4nx\sum_{k\ge2n}k^{-2}\to2x$ and
$nx\sum_{j=n}^{3n}j^{-2}\to2x/3$, and their total quadratic remainder
is $O(x^2/n)$.  A uniform integrable majorant is available without
an asymptotic assumption on $x$.  The $2n$ factors with
$2n\le k<4n$ give
\[
 0<e_n(x)\le\left(1+\frac{x}{4n}\right)^{-2n}
           \le\left(1+\frac x8\right)^{-4}\qquad(n\ge2).
\]
The last inequality follows because $(1+y/t)^t$ increases with $t>0$.
Stirling's formula \cite{dlmf-stirling} yields
\begin{equation}\label{s4--dual:ratio-prefactor}
 \frac{a_nn^{3/2}}{4\pi}
 =2\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\left(1+\frac1{16n}+O(n^{-2})\right).
\end{equation}
Thus dominated convergence already proves
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{I_n}{\mathcal U_n}
 =2\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty\sqrt x\,e^{-8x/3}\,dx
 =\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}.
\]

For the corrections, let $L_n(x)=-\log e_n(x)$.  Elementary tail-sum
expansions, obtainable from Euler--Maclaurin with its remainder, give
\begin{align*}
 4n\sum_{k=2n}^\infty\frac1{k^2}
 +n\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac1{j^2}
 &=\frac83+\frac{19}{18n}+O(n^{-2}),\\
 16n^2\sum_{k=2n}^\infty\frac1{k^4}
 +n^2\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac1{j^4}
 &=\frac{80}{81n}+O(n^{-2}),\\
 64n^3\sum_{k=2n}^\infty\frac1{k^6}
 +n^3\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac1{j^6}
 &=O(n^{-2}).
\end{align*}
The first two identities can be checked from
\[
 \sum_{k=2n}^\infty k^{-2}
 =\frac1{2n}+\frac1{8n^2}+O(n^{-3}),\qquad
 \sum_{j=n}^{3n}j^{-2}
 =\frac2{3n}+\frac5{9n^2}+O(n^{-3}),
\]
and the corresponding leading fourth-power integrals.
Since every argument of the logarithms is at most $x/n$,
Taylor's formula is uniform for $0\le x\le n^{1/4}$ and gives
\[
 L_n(x)=\frac83x+
       \frac1n\left(\frac{19}{18}x-\frac{40}{81}x^2\right)
       +O\left(\frac{x+x^2+x^3}{n^2}\right).
\]
Consequently on the same range
\[
 e_n(x)=e^{-8x/3}\left[
 1-\frac1n\left(\frac{19}{18}x-\frac{40}{81}x^2\right)
 +O\left(\frac{(1+x)^4}{n^2}\right)\right].
\]
These expansions may be integrated with error $O(n^{-2})$.  To justify
this assertion explicitly, for $n^{1/4}\le x\le n$ the earlier product
bound is at most $e^{-2x/5}$.  For $x\ge n$,
\[
 \int_n^\infty\sqrt x\left(1+\frac{x}{4n}\right)^{-2n}dx
 \le Cn^{3/2}(5/4)^{-n}\qquad(n\ge4),
\]
by putting $x=ny$ and retaining four powers for the integrable factor.
Both tails are smaller than every negative power of $n$.

Under the density proportional to $\sqrt x\,e^{-8x/3}$, the first two
moments are $9/16$ and $135/256$. Combining the integrated expansion
with \eqref{s4--dual:ratio-prefactor}, the relative coefficient of $1/n$
is
\[
 \frac1{16}-\frac{19}{18}\frac9{16}
                   +\frac{40}{81}\frac{135}{256}
 =-\frac{13}{48}.
\]
This yields the first correction $-13\sqrt3/(256n)$.

The part of \eqref{s4--dual:ratio-exact} containing the extra exponential
can be handled before the substitution $u=nx$.  Positivity of the
product factors implies
\[
 0\le1-E_n(u)
 \le u\left(4\sum_{k=2n}^\infty k^{-2}
                +\sum_{j=n}^{3n}j^{-2}\right)\le\frac{Cu}{n}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \int_0^\infty\sqrt u\,e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}E_n(u)\,du
 =\int_0^\infty\sqrt u\,e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}\,du+O(n^{-1})
 =\frac1{2\pi^3}+O(n^{-1}).
\]
Multiplication by $a_n/(4\pi)$ gives
$\sqrt2/(\pi^{7/2}n^{3/2})+O(n^{-5/2})$.
This proves the complete stated expansion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[An explicit uniform rational improvement]
\label{s4--dual:uniform-ratio}
For every $n\ge1$,
\[
 0<\frac{I_n}{\mathcal U_n}<\frac{488}{945}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the polynomials and measure from the proper-kernel bound:
\[
 S_r(u)=\frac{4^r}{(2r)!}\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}(4u+k^2),
 \qquad d\nu(u)=\frac{du}{2\sinh(2\pi\sqrt u)},
 \qquad \int_0^\infty S_r\,d\nu=\frac1{16}.
\]
The last normalization is the identity already proved in establishing
$I_n<\mathcal U_n$.  Thus $dP_r=16S_r\,d\nu$ is a probability
measure.  The likelihood ratio
\[
 g_r(u)=\frac{S_{r+1}(u)}{S_r(u)}
       =\frac{4(4u+r^2)}{(2r+2)(2r+1)}
\]
is strictly increasing in $u$, and its $P_r$-mean is one.
For the strictly decreasing function $f(u)=e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}$,
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_{r+1}}f-\mathbb E_{P_r}f
 =\operatorname{Cov}_{P_r}(g_r,f)<0.
\]
Indeed, twice this covariance is the expectation of
$(g_r(u)-g_r(v))(f(u)-f(v))$ for two independent $P_r$ samples;
the product is negative off the diagonal.  Hence
$J_r=\int S_r e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}\,d\nu$ decreases with $r$.

Since $e^{-2\pi\sqrt u}d\nu=du/(e^{4\pi\sqrt u}-1)$ and
$S_2(u)=32u^2/3+8u/3$, the elementary Bose moments give
\[
 J_2=\frac{32}{3}\frac1{16128}
       +\frac83\frac1{1920}
     =\frac1{1512}+\frac1{720}
     =\frac{31}{15120}.
\]
For completeness, the moments here follow from
\[
 \int_0^\infty\frac{u^k\,du}{e^{4\pi\sqrt u}-1}
 =\frac{2\Gamma(2k+2)\zeta(2k+2)}{(4\pi)^{2k+2}}
\]
at $k=1,2$, with $\zeta(4)=\pi^4/90$ and
$\zeta(6)=\pi^6/945$.
Writing $D_n(u)=\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(u+j^2)$, exact normalization yields
\[
 \frac{I_n}{\mathcal U_n}
 =8\int_0^\infty S_{2n}(u)\frac{D_n(0)}{D_n(u)}
              (1+e^{-2\pi\sqrt u})\,d\nu(u)
 <\frac12+8J_{2n}
 \le\frac12+8J_2=\frac{488}{945}.
\]
The first inequality is strict because $D_n(0)<D_n(u)$ for $u>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A constant improvement and its precise scope]
\label{s4--dual:ratio-scope}
Put $\rho_n=I_n/\mathcal U_n$ and
$\rho_*=\sup_{n\ge1}\rho_n$.  Then
\[
 \frac{3\sqrt3}{16}\le\rho_*<\frac{488}{945}<1.
\]
For every finite real coefficient vector $c$,
\[
 \left|\sum_n c_nI_n\right|
 \le\rho_*\sum_n\mathcal U_n|c_n|.
\]
For vectors supported on indices $n\ge M$, the best universal constant
in this inequality is $\sup_{n\ge M}\rho_n$, and it converges to
$3\sqrt3/16$ as $M\to\infty$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{s4--dual:uniform-ratio} and the limit strictly below $488/945$
give $\rho_*<488/945$ by separating a finite prefix from a tail.
The triangle inequality proves the estimate.  Single-coordinate vectors show that
the stated constants are optimal for the indicated unrestricted
coefficient spaces.  This last optimality assertion does not impose
prime-log cancellation and hence is not an optimality assertion for
the quotient norms.
\end{proof}




\section{Thin-block cancellation and the formal-zero obstruction}
\label{s1--sec:thin-counting}
The coefficients $E_{n,\ell}$ and $p_n$ are those of the common kernel
identity. The sufficient clearing factor $4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M)$
used in this construction can be replaced by the factor two proved
below; the exponential rates are unchanged.
\begin{theorem}[Thin-block cancellation with an exponential bound, possibly zero]
\label{s1--stage3-counting-main}
For integers $N\ge2$, define using integer operations
\[
 h_N=\max\left(1,\left\lfloor\sqrt{\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor}\right\rfloor\right),
 \quad M=N+\left\lceil\frac N{h_N}\right\rceil,
 \quad d=M-N+1,
\]
\[
 D_N=4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M),\qquad
 \delta_* =\log(729/16)-3>0.
\]
For every sufficiently large $N$, there is a nonzero integer vector
$c=(c_N,\ldots,c_M)$ satisfying
\[
 \sum_{n=N}^M c_n E_{n,\ell}=0\quad\hbox{for every prime }\ell,
 \qquad
 \log\max(1,\|c\|_\infty)
       =O\!\left(\frac N{\sqrt{\log N}}\right).
\]
Its exactly log-free form is
\begin{equation}\label{s1--stage3-counting-small-form}
 F_N=D_N\sum_{n=N}^M c_n I_n=Q_N\gamma-P_N,
 \qquad Q_N,P_N\in\mathbb Z,
\end{equation}
and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{s1--stage3-counting-upper-bound}
 |F_N|\le\exp(-\delta_*N+o(N)).
\end{equation}
This is an upper bound; $F_N$ is allowed to be exactly zero.

Indeed, for every sufficiently large $N$, there also exists a nonzero
integer vector of the same height order for which all prime-log
coefficients, $Q_N$, and $P_N$ are zero simultaneously. Its rational
kernel $\sum c_nR_n$ is nonzero and changes sign on $(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the integer log matrix
\[
 V_{\ell,n}=2E_{n,\ell},\qquad
 \ell\le3M\hbox{ prime},\quad N\le n\le M.
\]
It has $r=\pi(3M)$ rows and $d$ columns, and its entries have absolute
value at most the integer
\[
 H_N=6(2M+1)\lceil\log_2(3M)\rceil 2^{12M}.
\]
The prime number theorem \cite{dlmf-primes} and the chosen block give
\[
 M/N\to1,\quad d\asymp\frac N{\sqrt{\log N}},\quad
 r\asymp\frac N{\log N},\quad
 \log H_N=O(N).
\]
Thus $d>r$ for all sufficiently large $N$.

Here is the full counting argument. For any $r$-by-$d$ integer matrix
with entries bounded by $H$, let $K$ be a positive integer such that
\[
 K^{d-r}>(3dH)^r.
\]
The $(K+1)^d$ vectors in $\{0,\ldots,K\}^d$ have images with at most
$(2dKH+1)^r\le(3dKH)^r<K^d$ possible values. Two images coincide.
Subtracting the input vectors gives a nonzero integer null vector of
supremum norm at most $K$. Taking the smallest admissible integer $K$
yields
\[
 \log K\le
 \frac r{d-r}\log(3dH)+O(1)
 =O\!\left(\frac N{\sqrt{\log N}}\right).
\]
This proves exact log cancellation and the height estimate. It also
gives a finite, though not efficient, construction by enumeration.

Since $2A_{n,j}$ is integral, every denominator in $p_n$ divides
$4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M)=D_N$. Thus the coefficients
\[
 Q_N=D_N\sum c_n16^n,\qquad P_N=D_N\sum c_np_n
\]
in \eqref{s1--stage3-counting-small-form} are integers. Positivity and
monotonicity of the raw bounds give
\[
 |F_N|\le D_NdK \mathcal U_N.
\]
The same prime number theorem gives
$\log D_N=3M+o(M)=3N+o(N)$, while
$\log(dK)=o(N)$. Lemma~\ref{s6--stage3-proper-bounds} therefore proves
\eqref{s1--stage3-counting-upper-bound}. The margin is positive since
$e<3$ gives $e^3<27<729/16$.

To see exactly why nonvanishing is missing, append to $V$ the two
integer rows $(16^n)_{n=N}^M$ and $(D_Np_n)_{n=N}^M$.
Their entries still have logarithmic height $O(N)$: the residue bound,
$H_j\le j$, and $\log D_N=O(N)$ suffice. Replacing $r$ by $r+2$
does not change the asymptotic height estimate. The same counting
argument therefore gives a nonzero vector annihilating all three
types of coefficients. Its integral is exactly zero, as a formal
identity, independently of the arithmetic nature of $\gamma$.

Let $n_*$ be the largest index with nonzero coefficient. The pole at
$u=-(3n_*)^2$ occurs in $R_{n_*}$ with nonzero residue and in none of
the smaller-index kernels. Hence $\sum c_nR_n$ is not the zero
rational function. It is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ and has zero
integral against a strictly positive measure with full support.
It must take both signs there. This proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A fixed-degree positive construction from two independent pairs}
Let $\mathcal K_N=\ker_{\mathbb Z}V$ and define the integer coefficient
map
\[
 \Phi_N(c)=\left(D_N\sum c_n16^n,\ D_N\sum c_np_n\right).
\]
For $c\in\mathcal K_N$, the corresponding form is
$F_c(\gamma)=Q_c\gamma-P_c$. Define $\sigma_2(N)$ as the least value of
$\max(\|c^{(1)}\|_\infty,\|c^{(2)}\|_\infty)$ among pairs in
$\mathcal K_N$ with
\[
 \det\begin{pmatrix}Q_1&P_1\\Q_2&P_2\end{pmatrix}\ne0.
\]
Set $\sigma_2(N)=\infty$ if no such pair exists. This definition is a
property of explicitly given integer and rational matrices. It does
not compare any computed value to $\gamma$.

\begin{proposition}[A positive quadratic certificate and its exact missing bound]
\label{s1--stage3-counting-independent-pair}
For every pair with nonzero determinant, the integer polynomial
\[
 W_N(X)=(Q_1X-P_1)^2+(Q_2X-P_2)^2
\]
is strictly positive for every real $X$. If, along an infinite sequence
of indices tending to infinity,
\begin{equation}\label{s1--stage3-counting-sigma-target}
 \limsup\frac{\log\sigma_2(N)}N<\delta_*,
\end{equation}
then, choosing a pair attaining $\sigma_2(N)$ at each of those indices,
the resulting polynomials satisfy $W_N(\gamma)\to0$, and $\gamma$ is irrational.
No estimate \eqref{s1--stage3-counting-sigma-target} is proved here.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Two independent coefficient pairs cannot vanish at the same real
argument. Equivalently the leading coefficient is positive and the
discriminant of $W_N$ is
\[
 -4(Q_1P_2-Q_2P_1)^2<0.
\]
For a pair attaining $\sigma_2(N)$, the raw estimates give
\[
 |F_{c^{(i)}}(\gamma)|\le D_Nd\sigma_2(N)\mathcal U_N.
\]
The logarithm of this upper bound is
$-\delta_*N+\log\sigma_2(N)+o(N)$. Under
\eqref{s1--stage3-counting-sigma-target} both forms tend to zero, and so
does their sum of squares. If $\gamma=a/b$ were rational, then
\[
 b^2W_N(\gamma)
 =(aQ_1-bP_1)^2+(aQ_2-bP_2)^2\in\mathbb Z_{>0},
\]
contradicting convergence to zero. The degree is the fixed number $2$,
so this integerization introduces the fixed factor $b^2$ only.
\end{proof}

The preceding construction separates positivity from the sign of an
integral kernel. It replaces that sign problem by an exact determinant
test. It does not supply cheap independent pairs: the counting theorem
controls a short null vector, which can lie in $\ker\Phi_N$.

\begin{proposition}[Why dimension and entry height alone do not bound the pair]
\label{s1--stage3-counting-countermodel}
For integers $H\ge2$, $s\ge1$, and any number of free coordinates
$z_1,\ldots,z_k$ with $k\ge1$, impose
\[
 x_i-Hx_{i+1}=0,\quad y_i-Hy_{i+1}=0\quad(0\le i<s),
 \qquad\Phi(x,y,z)=(x_s,y_s).
\]
The constraint matrix has rank $2s$, entries of absolute value at most
$H$, and arbitrarily many independent null vectors of height $1$ with
$\Phi=0$. Appending the two rows of $\Phi$ raises its rank by $2$.
Nevertheless the least height of two null vectors with independent
$\Phi$-images is exactly $H^s$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Every null vector has
$x_i=H^{s-i}x_s$ and $y_i=H^{s-i}y_s$. If its height is less than
$H^s$, both $x_s$ and $y_s$ are zero. The free coordinate vectors have
height $1$, and the two choices $(x_s,y_s)=(1,0),(0,1)$ give independent
images at height exactly $H^s$. The rank assertions follow directly
from the independent chain constraints.
\end{proof}

This is not a failure theorem for the specific proper-kernel matrix.
It proves that its additional arithmetic structure must be used:
dimension, entry size, and formal rank alone cannot upgrade the
counting theorem to the required independent-pair estimate.


% Additional synthesis result, independently derived 31 October 2026.
% This fragment uses the theorem/lemma environments of the unified manuscript.
% Only this owned fragment was created; the source manuscripts are unchanged.

\section{An actual-matrix height barrier for independent signed outputs}
\label{s1--unified-signed-height-section}

The counting theorem produces short vectors in the integer kernel of the
prime-log matrix, but it does not provide two independent coefficient
pairs.  The following additional synthesis result shows that this
distinction is unavoidable for the actual matrices considered here:
subexponential-height log-null vectors can have formal outputs of rank
at most one.  The proof combines the common gamma-coefficient factor
with the integral estimate already established above.  The underlying
integer determinant argument and Smith normal form are standard tools;
no historical-priority claim is made for them.

\begin{lemma}[An integer-output determinant bound]
\label{s1--unified-signed-determinant-lemma}
Let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be a lattice, let
$a,b:\Lambda\to\mathbb Z$ be homomorphisms, and let $\theta$ be real.
Suppose that, for constants $A,E>0$ and every $c\in\Lambda$,
\[
 |a(c)|\le A\|c\|_\infty,
 \qquad
 |\theta a(c)-b(c)|\le E\|c\|_\infty.
\]
Put $\mathcal L=\{(a(c),b(c)):c\in\Lambda\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$.
If $\mathcal L$ has rank two, let
$j=[\mathbb Z^2:\mathcal L]$.  Then every pair with independent
outputs satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{s1--unified-signed-height-product}
 \|c_1\|_\infty\|c_2\|_\infty\ge\frac{j}{2AE}.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $2AEK^2<1$, all outputs with
$\|c\|_\infty\le K$ span a space of dimension at most one,
whether or not the full image has rank two.

When the full image has rank two, $j$ is the greatest common divisor
of the determinants of all pairs of image vectors.  Thus it concerns
the actual image lattice, which need not be saturated in $\mathbb Z^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set $e_i=\theta a(c_i)-b(c_i)$.  Cancellation of $\theta$ gives
\[
 a(c_1)b(c_2)-a(c_2)b(c_1)
   =a(c_2)e_1-a(c_1)e_2.
\]
Its absolute value is at most
$2AE\|c_1\|_\infty\|c_2\|_\infty$.
A nonzero determinant of two vectors of $\mathcal L$ is a nonzero
integer multiple of the covolume $j$, proving
\eqref{s1--unified-signed-height-product}.

For completeness, a rank-two sublattice of $\mathbb Z^2$ has a basis
$(a_0,b_0),(0,b_1)$ with $a_0,b_1>0$: choose $a_0$ as the positive
generator of its first-coordinate image, choose a vector above it,
and choose $b_1$ as the positive generator of its vertical kernel.
Subtracting a multiple of the first vector proves generation by these
two vectors.  The index and the absolute basis determinant are both
$a_0b_1$.  Every pair determinant is a multiple of this number, and
the basis pair attains it, proving the gcd assertion.

Finally, if $2AEK^2<1$, every determinant of two outputs in the
specified height ball is an integer of absolute value less than one,
and therefore is zero.  If one such output is nonzero, every other
one is collinear with it; if none is nonzero, the assertion is
immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The exact image index and the fibres of the output map]
\label{s1--unified-signed-image-index}
Let $C\in\mathbb Z^{r\times d}$ have row rank $r$, let
$B\in\mathbb Z^{2\times d}$, and suppose
$\operatorname{rank}\binom CB=r+2$.
For a full-row-rank integer matrix $T$ with $s$ rows, write
$\Delta_s(T)$ for the positive gcd of its $s$-by-$s$ minors;
use $\Delta_0(C)=1$ when $r=0$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{s1--unified-signed-index-formula}
 \left[\mathbb Z^2:B(\ker_{\mathbb Z}C)\right]
 =\frac{\Delta_{r+2}\!\left(\binom CB\right)}{\Delta_r(C)}.
\end{equation}
For any attained output $y=Bc_0$ with $Cc_0=0$, its entire fibre is
\[
 \{c\in\mathbb Z^d:Cc=0,\ Bc=y\}
 =c_0+\ker_{\mathbb Z}\binom CB.
\]
Both integer kernels in this statement are saturated in
$\mathbb Z^d$.  This does not assert that the image
$B(\ker_{\mathbb Z}C)$ is saturated in $\mathbb Z^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $\mathcal H=\binom CB\mathbb Z^d$,
$\mathcal C=C\mathbb Z^d$, and
$\mathcal L=B(\ker_{\mathbb Z}C)$.
Projection to the first $r$ coordinates gives the exact sequence
of finite abelian groups
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^2/\mathcal L
 \longrightarrow\mathbb Z^{r+2}/\mathcal H
 \longrightarrow\mathbb Z^r/\mathcal C
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
Indeed, a class whose first coordinate lies in $\mathcal C$ can
be represented by $(0,y)$ after subtracting a vector of
$\mathcal H$, and $(0,y)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ exactly when
$y\in\mathcal L$.  Taking group orders gives the ratio of the
two image indices.

For a full-row-rank integer matrix, its image index is the gcd of
its maximal minors.  To see this, apply integer unimodular row and
column operations to obtain Smith normal form.  Such operations
preserve the image index and the gcd of the maximal minors; on
the diagonal form both are the product of the nonzero diagonal
entries.  This proves \eqref{s1--unified-signed-index-formula}.
The fibre identity follows by subtracting $c_0$.
An integer kernel is saturated because $kTc=0$, for a nonzero
integer $k$, implies $Tc=0$ in the torsion-free group
$\mathbb Z^s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Independent signed outputs have an exponential height cost]
\label{s1--unified-signed-actual-barrier}
Use the proper kernels, their rational bounds $\mathcal U_n$ in
\eqref{s6--stage3-proper-U}, and the thin blocks of
Theorem~\ref{s1--stage3-counting-main}.  Thus
\[
 \mathcal K_N=\ker_{\mathbb Z}V,
 \quad D_N=4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M),
 \quad \delta_*=\log(729/16)-3.
\]
Set the explicit positive rational quantities
\[
 \mathcal S_N=\sum_{n=N}^M16^{n-N}
     =\frac{16^{M-N+1}-1}{15},
 \qquad
 \mathcal T_N=\sum_{n=N}^M \mathcal U_n,
 \qquad G_N=D_N16^N.
\]
For $c\in\mathcal K_N$, write the integer form as
\[
 F_c(\gamma)=Q_c\gamma-P_c,
 \qquad
 a_N(c)=\frac{Q_c}{G_N}
       =\sum_{n=N}^M c_n16^{n-N}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Let $\sigma_2(N)$ be the least possible maximum input height of
two vectors whose original coefficient pairs $(Q_c,P_c)$ are
independent, and set it to $\infty$ if no such pair exists.
Then, for every $N$ for which the block is defined,
\begin{equation}\label{s1--unified-signed-actual-finite}
 \sigma_2(N)\ge
 \bigl(2D_N\mathcal S_N\mathcal T_N\bigr)^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}
If the normalized image
\[
 \mathcal L_N
   =\{(a_N(c),P_c):c\in\mathcal K_N\}
\]
has rank two and index $j_N$ in $\mathbb Z^2$, the sharper bound is
\begin{equation}\label{s1--unified-signed-actual-index}
 \sigma_2(N)\ge
 \sqrt{\frac{j_N}{2D_N\mathcal S_N\mathcal T_N}}.
\end{equation}
In particular, with the extended-real convention for $\log\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{s1--unified-signed-actual-rate}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log\sigma_2(N)}N
 \ge\frac{\delta_*}{2}
 =\frac{\log(729/16)-3}{2}>0.
\end{equation}

More strongly, if $K_N\ge1$ and
\[
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log K_N}{N}
 <\frac{\delta_*}{2},
\]
then, for all sufficiently large $N$, the formal outputs of
\emph{all} $c\in\mathcal K_N$ with $\|c\|_\infty\le K_N$
span a space of dimension at most one.  In particular this holds
for every subexponential height schedule $K_N=\exp(o(N))$,
including the heights produced by the counting argument.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The exact formulas preceding
\eqref{s1--stage3-counting-upper-bound} give
\[
 P_c=D_N\sum_{n=N}^M c_np_n\in\mathbb Z,
 \qquad F_c(\gamma)=D_N\sum_{n=N}^M c_nI_n.
\]
Consequently
\[
 |a_N(c)|\le\mathcal S_N\|c\|_\infty,
 \qquad
 |G_N\gamma a_N(c)-P_c|
 \le D_N\mathcal T_N\|c\|_\infty.
\]
The two original pairs are independent exactly when the normalized
pairs are independent, since their first coordinates differ by
the same nonzero factor $G_N$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{s1--unified-signed-determinant-lemma} with
\[
 \theta=G_N\gamma,\quad A=\mathcal S_N,
 \quad E=D_N\mathcal T_N.
\]
Every nonzero normalized determinant is an integer, and in the
rank-two case it is a nonzero multiple of $j_N$.
This proves both finite bounds; if there is no independent pair,
\eqref{s1--unified-signed-actual-finite} holds by the convention
$\sigma_2(N)=\infty$.

The thin-block choice gives $M-N=o(N)$, so
\[
 \log\mathcal S_N=o(N).
\]
Since $\mathcal U_n$ decreases,
$\mathcal U_N\le\mathcal T_N\le(M-N+1)\mathcal U_N$.  The proved asymptotic for
$\mathcal U_N$ therefore gives
\[
 \log\mathcal T_N=-\log(729/16)N+o(N).
\]
The already used least-common-multiple asymptotic gives
$\log D_N=3N+o(N)$.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{s1--unified-signed-determinant-scale}
 2D_N\mathcal S_N\mathcal T_N
 =\exp\{-\delta_*N+o(N)\}.
\end{equation}
Taking logarithms of \eqref{s1--unified-signed-actual-finite}
proves \eqref{s1--unified-signed-actual-rate}.
Under the stated hypothesis on $K_N$, the product of
\eqref{s1--unified-signed-determinant-scale} with $K_N^2$ tends to zero.
The final conclusion follows from the last assertion of
Lemma~\ref{s1--unified-signed-determinant-lemma}.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Exact arithmetic and scope.}
The index $j_N$, whenever the normalized image has rank two, can be
computed without any evaluation of $\gamma$.
Choose a maximal independent set of rows of the integer log matrix
as $C$, and let the two rows of $B$ be
$(16^{n-N})_{n=N}^M$ and $(D_Np_n)_{n=N}^M$.
Then Lemma~\ref{s1--unified-signed-image-index} gives its exact value.
All vectors with a fixed formal output differ by the saturated
integer kernel of the stacked matrix; changing a vector inside
that fibre changes neither its formal linear form nor its
primitive arithmetic error.

The new conclusion is a lower height bound for the actual
proper-kernel matrices, not just for an unrelated model matrix.
It does not prove that every short output is zero, and it does
not exclude independent outputs at larger heights.
In particular, the previously stated sufficient target
$\limsup\log\sigma_2(N)/N<\delta_*$ is not contradicted:
an exponential-rate window between $\delta_*/2$ and $\delta_*$
remains.  Neither existence of suitable pairs in that window nor
irrationality of $\gamma$ is established here.



\section{A separation obstruction across different cancellation blocks}
\label{s2--sec:cross-block-stabilization}

Put $\kappa_0=\log(729/16)$ and $\delta_*=\kappa_0-3$.
Retain the proper-kernel identity
\[
 I_n=16^n\gamma-p_n+\sum_\ell E_{n,\ell}\log\ell,
 \qquad 0<I_n<\mathcal U_n,
 \qquad \log \mathcal U_n=-\kappa_0n+O(\log(n+1)).
\]
The constants and kernels in this section are exactly those of the
proper-kernel construction. In particular $4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M)$
clears all $p_n$ for $n\le M$.

\begin{lemma}[An exact comparison of two blocks]
\label{s2--lem:cross-block-determinant}
Let $N_1\le N_2$ and let $c^{(i)}$ be integer vectors supported on
$[N_i,M_i]$ whose prime-log coefficients vanish. Put
\[
 H_i=\max(1,\|c^{(i)}\|_\infty),\quad
 S_i=\sum_{n=N_i}^{M_i}16^{n-N_i},\quad
 T_i=\sum_{n=N_i}^{M_i}\mathcal U_n,
\]
\[
 a_i=\sum_{n=N_i}^{M_i}c_n^{(i)}16^{n-N_i},\qquad
 b_i=\sum_{n=N_i}^{M_i}c_n^{(i)}p_n,\qquad
 D=4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3\max(M_1,M_2)).
\]
If
\begin{equation}\label{s2--eq:cross-block-cost}
 D H_1H_2\left(16^{N_2-N_1}S_2T_1+S_1T_2\right)<1,
\end{equation}
then the two coefficient pairs $(16^{N_i}a_i,b_i)$ are proportional.
If both $a_i$ are nonzero, this means exactly
\[
 \frac{b_1}{16^{N_1}a_1}=
 \frac{b_2}{16^{N_2}a_2}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $J_i=\sum_n c_n^{(i)}I_n$. Log cancellation gives
$J_i=16^{N_i}a_i\gamma-b_i$, while $|J_i|\le H_iT_i$.
The integer
\[
 \Delta=a_1(Db_2)-16^{N_2-N_1}a_2(Db_1)
   =D\left(16^{N_2-N_1}a_2J_1-a_1J_2\right)
\]
has absolute value at most the left side of
\eqref{s2--eq:cross-block-cost}, since $|a_i|\le H_iS_i$.
It must therefore vanish. Scaling its first coordinates back by the
nonzero common factor $16^{N_1}$ gives the asserted proportionality.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Persistent short outputs force a rational limiting slope]
\label{s2--thm:cross-block-stabilization}
Fix $0\le\alpha<\delta_*/2$ and set
\[
 \rho_\alpha=
 \frac{\log729-\alpha}{3+\log16+\alpha}>1.
\]
Let $N_k\to\infty$ be strictly increasing integers. Suppose that
integer prime-log-null vectors $c^{(k)}$ are supported on
$[N_k,M_k]$, where
\[
 M_k=N_k+o(N_k),\qquad
 \log\max(1,\|c^{(k)}\|_\infty)\le\alpha N_k+o(N_k),
\]
and that every formal output
\[
 \left(\sum_n c_n^{(k)}16^n,\ \sum_n c_n^{(k)}p_n\right)
\]
is nonzero. If
\begin{equation}\label{s2--eq:cross-block-gap}
 \limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{N_{k+1}}{N_k}<\rho_\alpha,
\end{equation}
then $\gamma$ is rational. More precisely, the rational slopes of the
formal outputs are eventually equal to $\gamma$, so all their evaluated
linear forms are eventually exactly zero.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $D_k=4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M_k)$ and
$J_k=\sum_n c_n^{(k)}I_n$. The least-common-multiple asymptotic and
the integral bound give
\[
 |D_kJ_k|\le
 \exp\{-(\delta_*-\alpha)N_k+o(N_k)\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
If the first formal coefficient were zero, $D_kJ_k$ would be an
integer. It would vanish for sufficiently large $k$, contradicting
nonzero formal output. Hence $a_k=\sum c_n^{(k)}16^{n-N_k}\ne0$
for all sufficiently large $k$.

For two consecutive blocks, write $N=N_k$ and $N'=N_{k+1}$.
Condition \eqref{s2--eq:cross-block-gap} bounds $N'/N$, and
$\max(M_k,M_{k+1})=N'+o(N)$. In Lemma~\ref{s2--lem:cross-block-determinant},
\[
 \log D=3N'+o(N),\quad \log S_i=o(N),\quad
 \log T_1=-\kappa_0N+o(N),\quad
 \log T_2=-\kappa_0N'+o(N).
\]
The larger of the two exponents on the left of
\eqref{s2--eq:cross-block-cost} is
\[
 (3+\log16+\alpha)N'-(\log729-\alpha)N+o(N).
\]
Indeed its difference from the other exponent is
$\log729\,(N'-N)\ge0$. By \eqref{s2--eq:cross-block-gap} this larger
exponent tends to minus infinity linearly in $N$.
Thus consecutive rational slopes are equal for every sufficiently
large $k$; call the eventual rational value $r$.

Since $a_k$ is a nonzero integer,
\[
 |\gamma-r|
 =\frac{|J_k|}{16^{N_k}|a_k|}
 \le\frac{H_kT_k}{16^{N_k}}
 \le\exp\{-(\log729-\alpha)N_k+o(N_k)\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore $r=\gamma$. The claimed eventual zero evaluation follows
from the exact identities.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary separation for successful short forms]
Suppose the vectors in Theorem~\ref{s2--thm:cross-block-stabilization}
instead satisfy $J_k\ne0$ at every index. Then necessarily
\[
 \limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{N_{k+1}}{N_k}\ge\rho_\alpha.
\]
In particular, at subexponential height ($\alpha=0$), the threshold is
\[
 \rho_0=\frac{\log729}{3+\log16}=1.141892147\ldots.
\]
Thus a subexponential-height nonzero-valued form at every sufficiently
large block is impossible for this construction. This conclusion does
not rule out sufficiently separated infinite subsequences or larger
coefficient heights.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The opposite strict inequality would make the evaluated forms eventually
zero by the theorem, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Scope.}
The displayed separation threshold is sufficient for this determinant
argument; no optimality is claimed. The theorem does not show that
$\gamma$ is rational, because persistent nonzero formal outputs have
not been constructed. It does not show that $\gamma$ is irrational,
because nonzero evaluated forms on an infinite admissible subsequence
have not been constructed. It strengthens the single-block rank
obstruction by comparing different blocks.


\section{Primitive lifts and the remaining quantitative target}
\label{s2--primlift:section}

The following formulation specializes the primitive quotient optimization
of corpus manuscript [019].  It is included to state the remaining target
after division by the actual output gcd; no new general optimization
theorem is claimed.

Fix a finite set of indices and an exact identity
\[
 e_j=a_j\gamma-b_j+\sum_{\ell}V_{\ell j}\log\ell,
 \qquad a_j,b_j,V_{\ell j}\in\mathbb Z,
 \qquad |e_j|\le\varepsilon_j\in\mathbb Q_{>0}.
\]
Put
\[
 \Lambda=\ker V\cap\mathbb Z^s,\qquad
 \Phi(w)=(a^Tw,b^Tw),\qquad
 C(w)=\sum_{j=1}^s\varepsilon_j|w_j|.
\]
Assume that $\Phi:\ker_{\mathbb Q}V\longrightarrow\mathbb Q^2$
has rank two.  A nonzero integer pair $v=(q,p)$ is called primitive
when $\gcd(|q|,|p|)=1$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact primitive lifting]
\label{s2--primlift:lemma}
For a primitive pair $v$, define the rational quotient cost
\[
 F(v)=\min_{Vw=0,\ \Phi(w)=v}C(w),
 \qquad w\in\mathbb R^s.
\]
The minimum has a rational optimizer, and
\begin{equation}\label{s2--primlift:gcd-equality}
 F(v)=
 \min_{\substack{c\in\Lambda,\ \Phi(c)=gv\\g\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}}
 \frac{C(c)}{g},
 \qquad
 g=\gcd(|a^Tc|,|b^Tc|).
\end{equation}
In particular $|q\gamma-p|\le F(v)$.

There is also an explicit lift from any independent output pair.
If $u_1,u_2\in\Lambda$, $\Phi(u_i)=(Q_i,P_i)$, and
$\Delta=Q_1P_2-Q_2P_1\ne0$, then
\[
 c=\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta)
 \bigl((P_2q-Q_2p)u_1+(Q_1p-P_1q)u_2\bigr)
\]
satisfies $\Phi(c)=|\Delta|v$.  Its actual output gcd is exactly
$|\Delta|$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{s2--primlift:adjugate-bound}
 F(v)\le
 \frac{|P_2q-Q_2p|C(u_1)+|Q_1p-P_1q|C(u_2)}{|\Delta|}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The feasible fiber is nonempty by the rank assumption.  Positive weights
make its intersections with sublevel sets of $C$ compact.  The minimum
exists and can be attained rationally: after writing $w=w^+-w^-$,
this is a feasible rational linear program with an attained optimum.
Every integral lift in \eqref{s2--primlift:gcd-equality} gives the rational
lift $c/g$.  Conversely, multiply a rational optimizer by a positive
common denominator $g$ of its coordinates.  Its output is $gv$;
primitivity of $v$ makes the output gcd exactly $g$.  Homogeneity of
$C$ proves the equality, including attainment.  Log cancellation gives
$e^Tw=q\gamma-p$, proving the error bound.  Direct multiplication of
the two output columns proves the adjugate lift formula and its bound.
\end{proof}

The same proof with the supremum norm gives the exact normalized
coefficient cost
\begin{equation}\label{s2--primlift:tau}
 \tau(v):=\min_{Vw=0,\ \Phi(w)=v}\|w\|_\infty
 =\min_{\substack{c\in\Lambda,\ \Phi(c)=gv\\g\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}}
       \frac{\|c\|_\infty}{g},
 \qquad
 F(v)\le\left(\sum_j\varepsilon_j\right)\tau(v).
\end{equation}
Thus $\tau$ charges the coefficient size \emph{after} the exact output
gcd has been removed.  It is not the raw coefficient height.

\begin{proposition}[A sufficient test in the primitive quotient cost]
\label{s2--primlift:success-test}
For an unbounded sequence of blocks, let $F_N$ be the cost above.
If there are primitive pairs $v_N^{(1)},v_N^{(2)}$ such that
\[
 \det(v_N^{(1)},v_N^{(2)})\ne0,
 \qquad
 \max_{i=1,2}F_N(v_N^{(i)})\longrightarrow0,
\]
then $\gamma$ is irrational.  Alternatively, one primitive pair per
block suffices if its evaluated form is proved nonzero and its cost
tends to zero.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Two independent pairs cannot both lie in the kernel of the nonzero
linear functional $(q,p)\mapsto q\gamma-p$.  Hence at each block
at least one evaluated integer form is nonzero and has absolute value
at most the displayed maximum.  If $\gamma=A/B$ with integers $A,B$,
$B>0$, every nonzero integer form has absolute value at least $1/B$,
which is a contradiction.  The one-pair version is identical.
\end{proof}

For the proper kernels on $[N,M]$, take
\begin{gather*}
 D_M=4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M),\qquad e_n=D_MI_n,
 \qquad \varepsilon_n=D_M\mathcal U_n,\\
 \Phi_N(c)=\left(D_M\sum c_n16^n,\ D_M\sum c_np_n\right).
\end{gather*}
The log matrix is $(D_ME_{n,\ell})_{\ell,n}$; it has exactly the
same rational and integer kernels as $(2E_{n,\ell})_{\ell,n}$.
For $M=N+o(N)$ the established bounds imply
\[
 \sum_{n=N}^{M}\varepsilon_n
 =\exp\{-(\log(729/16)-3)N+o(N)\}
 =\exp\{-\delta_*N+o(N)\}.
\]
Consequently a sufficient concrete target is an infinite sequence of
such blocks with independent primitive pairs and, for one fixed
$\eta>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{s2--primlift:concrete-target}
 \max_{i=1,2}\tau_N(v_N^{(i)})
 \le\exp\{(\delta_*-\eta)N\}.
\end{equation}
Equations \eqref{s2--primlift:tau} and \eqref{s2--primlift:concrete-target}
would give primitive integer errors tending to zero, while independence
would supply the required nonvanishing.

\paragraph{Scope.}
Rank two makes every primitive rational slope accessible through a
multiple, as the explicit adjugate lift shows.  It proves neither a
small quotient cost nor \eqref{s2--primlift:concrete-target}.  The latter is
an unproved sufficient target, not an irrationality result.  A lower
bound for the raw height of two independent integer lifts cannot be
transferred to $F_N$ or $\tau_N$ without controlling their actual output
gcds.  Conversely, merely allowing large gcds gives no quantitative
upper bound for these costs.





\section{Reverse design from a denominator-cleared decay budget}
\label{jr--reverse:budget-section}

Put
\[
 \kappa=\log(729/16),\qquad
 \delta=\kappa-3>0,\qquad
 \varepsilon_2=\delta-\log2=\log(729/32)-3>0.
\]
All logarithms in asymptotic expressions are natural.  The last
positivity follows, for example, from
$e<11/4$ and $(11/4)^3=1331/64<729/32$.
For $m\ge1$ define
\[
 D_m=4\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3m).
\]
The proper kernels, integrals, and rational bounds are
\[
 R_m(u)=\frac{\prod_{k=0}^{2m-1}(4u+k^2)}
                   {\prod_{j=m}^{3m}(u+j^2)},\qquad
 I_m=\int_0^\infty\frac{R_m(u)}{e^{2\pi\sqrt u}-1}\,du,
 \qquad
 \mathcal U_m=\frac{(4m)!((m-1)!)^2}{8\,16^m((3m)!)^2}.
\]
Retain the exact identity
\[
 I_m=16^m\gamma-p_m+\sum_\ell E_{m,\ell}\log\ell,
 \qquad
 p_m=\sum_{j=m}^{3m}A_{m,j}\left(H_j-\frac1{2j}\right),
 \quad E_{m,\ell}=\sum_{j=m}^{3m}A_{m,j}v_\ell(j),
\]
where
\[
 A_{m,j}=(-1)^{j-m}
 \frac{4j^2(2j+2m-1)!(m+j-1)!}
 {(2j-2m)!(j-m)!(3m-j)!(3m+j)!}.
\]
The established bounds used below are
\[
 2A_{m,j}\in\mathbb Z,\qquad
 0<I_m<\frac{488}{945}\mathcal U_m,\qquad
 \frac{\mathcal U_{m+1}}{\mathcal U_m}\le\frac{256}{729}.
\]
The weaker inequality $I_m<\mathcal U_m$ would give all the same exponential
conclusions; the improved constant only sharpens the finite budget.

\begin{theorem}[An unconditional positive seed after denominator clearing]
\label{jr--reverse:raw-seed}
For every $n\ge1$, all coefficients in
\[
 D_nI_n=(D_n16^n)\gamma-D_np_n
            +\sum_\ell D_nE_{n,\ell}\log\ell
\]
are integers.  Moreover
\[
 0<D_nI_n=\exp\{-\delta n+o(n)\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus denominator-cleared decay and nonvanishing are already available
for this raw family.  Its prime-logarithm terms have not been removed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each $A_{n,j}$ is a half-integer.  Harmonic denominators divide
$\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3n)$, while the additional $1/(2j)$
requires at most one further factor two.  Hence $D_np_n$ is integral,
as are $D_nE_{n,\ell}$ and $D_n16^n$.

Writing
$\psi(x)=\sum_{\ell^a\le x,\ \ell\text{ prime}}\log\ell$, one has
$\log D_n=\log4+\psi(3n)=3n+o(n)$ by the prime number theorem.
Stirling's formula gives
\[
 \mathcal U_n=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\,
      n^{-3/2}\left(\frac{16}{729}\right)^n
      (1+O(n^{-1})).
\]
The proved limit $I_n/\mathcal U_n\to3\sqrt3/16>0$ therefore gives the
claimed exponential rate.  Positivity follows directly from the
integral.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A uniform budget fixed before cancellation]
\label{jr--reverse:uniform-budget}
Let $n\ge1$, $r\ge0$, $M=n+r$, and $H\ge1$. For every integer
vector $c=(c_0,\ldots,c_r)$ with $\|c\|_\infty\le H$, define
\[
 F_c=D_M\sum_{k=0}^r c_kI_{n+k}.
\]
All coefficients of $\gamma$, $1$, and the prime logarithms in
$F_c$ are integers, and
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 |F_c|<\frac{13176}{16555}\,D_MH\mathcal U_n.
 \quad}                                                     \tag{RB}
\]
If $\sum_{k=0}^r c_kE_{n+k,\ell}=0$ for every prime, then
\[
 F_c=Q_c\gamma-P_c,\qquad
 Q_c=D_M\sum_{k=0}^r c_k16^{n+k},\quad
 P_c=D_M\sum_{k=0}^r c_kp_{n+k}\in\mathbb Z,
\]
with precisely the same bound.

Suppose along an infinite sequence $n\to\infty$ that
$r/n\le\rho+o(1)$ and $\log H/n\le\eta+o(1)$, where
$\rho,\eta$ are finite nonnegative constants. If
\[
 \boxed{\eta+3(1+\rho)<\kappa,}
\]
then the bound in (RB) tends to zero exponentially, uniformly over
every coefficient vector in the specified integer box.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The denominator argument in Theorem~\ref{jr--reverse:raw-seed} applies
simultaneously to every index at most $M$.  The triangle inequality
and the geometric upper bound give
\[
 |F_c|
 \le D_MH\sum_{k=0}^r I_{n+k}
 <\frac{488}{945}D_MH\mathcal U_n
       \sum_{k=0}^\infty(256/729)^k
 =\frac{13176}{16555}D_MH\mathcal U_n.
\]
No cancellation hypothesis was used in this estimate.  Imposing
exact prime-log cancellation therefore changes the form of the
output without spending any extra budget, provided the coefficients
remain in the preassigned box.
Finally,
\[
 \log(D_MH\mathcal U_n)
 \le\{\eta+3(1+\rho)-\kappa+o(1)\}n.
\]
This proves the assertion.  In particular for $r=o(n)$ and $H=2^n$
the uniform bound is $\exp\{-\varepsilon_2n+o(n)\}$.
\end{proof}

\section{An exact residue bound and a constructive integer box}
\label{jr--reverse:counting-section}



The sharper residue-height input is
Lemma~\ref{s6--reverse:residue-height}, with $\beta=(16399/1296)^2$.
\begin{lemma}[Counting with separate row heights]
\label{jr--reverse:row-counting}
Let $A$ be an integer matrix with $s$ rows and $d$ columns, and
suppose that the entries of row $i$ have absolute value at most
$B_i\ge1$. If an integer $K\ge1$ satisfies
\[
 K^{d-s}>\prod_{i=1}^s(3dB_i),
\]
there exists a nonzero integer vector $c$ with $Ac=0$ and
$\|c\|_\infty\le K$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The $(K+1)^d$ vectors in $\{0,\ldots,K\}^d$ have at most
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^s(2dKB_i+1)
 \le K^s\prod_{i=1}^s(3dB_i)<K^d
\]
different images.  Two images coincide; their difference is the
required vector.  Enumeration of this finite input set gives a
deterministic construction whenever the displayed inequality holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cancellation inside a preassigned decay budget]
\label{jr--reverse:concrete-cancellation}
For $n\ge2$ put
\[
 r_n=\left\lceil\frac{25n}{\log n}\right\rceil,\qquad
 M_n=n+r_n,\qquad K_n=2^n.
\]
For every sufficiently large $n$, there exists a nonzero integer
vector $c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{r_n})$ with
\[
 \|c\|_\infty\le2^n,\qquad
 \sum_{k=0}^{r_n}c_kE_{n+k,\ell}=0
 \quad\text{for every prime }\ell.
\]
It produces an exactly log-free integer form
\[
 F_n=D_{M_n}\sum_{k=0}^{r_n}c_kI_{n+k}
       =Q_n\gamma-P_n,\qquad Q_n,P_n\in\mathbb Z,
\]
satisfying the unconditional bound
\[
 \boxed{|F_n|\le\exp\{-\varepsilon_2n+o(n)\}.}
\]
The construction uses no digits of $\gamma$. It does not assert
$F_n\ne0$ or $(Q_n,P_n)\ne(0,0)$.

In fact, the same block and the same height bound also contain,
for every sufficiently large $n$, a nonzero integer vector for
which all prime-log coefficients and both formal output
coordinates vanish. The corresponding rational kernel is nonzero
and changes sign on $(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $M=M_n$, $d=r_n+1$, and $s=\pi(3M)$.  The integer log matrix
$V=(2E_{n+k,\ell})_{\ell,k}$ has its entries bounded by
\[
 B_M=
 \left\lceil
 6(2M+1)\lceil\log_2(3M)\rceil\,\beta^M
 \right\rceil.
\]
This follows from Lemma~\ref{s6--reverse:residue-height}, summing the
$2m+1$ possible residues and using
$v_\ell(j)\le\log_2(3M)$.
The prime number theorem and the definition of the block give
\[
 M/n\to1,\qquad
 d=(25+o(1))\frac n{\log n},\qquad
 s=(3+o(1))\frac n{\log n},\qquad
 \log B_M=M\log\beta+O(\log M).
\]
For $K=2^n$, the two sides of the logarithmic counting inequality
have respective asymptotics
\begin{align*}
 (d-s)\log K
   &=(22\log2+o(1))\frac{n^2}{\log n},\\
 s\log(3dB_M)
   &=(3\log\beta+o(1))\frac{n^2}{\log n}.
\end{align*}
Lemma~\ref{s6--reverse:residue-height} gives the strict margin
$3\log\beta<22\log2$.  Thus the counting inequality holds for
every sufficiently large $n$, proving the required log-null vector.
Since $r_n=o(n)$, Theorem~\ref{jr--reverse:uniform-budget} proves the
claimed error bound uniformly for all such vectors.

For the formal-zero assertion, append the two integer rows
\[
 (16^k)_{k=0}^{r_n},\qquad
 (D_Mp_{n+k})_{k=0}^{r_n}.
\]
The first has row height $B_Q=16^{r_n}$. The second may be bounded by
\[
 B_P=
 \max\left(1,
 \left\lceil
 3D_M(2M+1)(3M+1)\beta^M
 \right\rceil\right).
\]
Indeed $|A_{m,j}|\le3\beta^M$ and
$H_j+1/(2j)\le3M+1$.  Therefore
$\log B_Q=O(r_n)$ and $\log B_P=O(n)$.
Use separate row heights in Lemma~\ref{jr--reverse:row-counting}.
Its logarithmic inequality now reads
\[
 (d-s-2)\log K>
 s\log(3dB_M)+\log(3dB_Q)+\log(3dB_P).
\]
Compared with the previous inequality, the changes on both sides
are $O(n)$, while its positive margin is of order $n^2/\log n$.
Hence it too holds for every sufficiently large $n$.
The first appended row kills the original gamma coefficient, since
$\sum c_k16^{n+k}=16^n\sum c_k16^k$; the second kills the constant
coefficient.  The resulting integral is exactly zero.

Let $m$ be the greatest index with nonzero coefficient in this
vector. The pole at $u=-(3m)^2$ occurs with nonzero residue only in
$R_m$ among the selected kernels. Thus the combined rational
function is not zero.  It is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, has zero
integral, and the integrating measure is positive with full support.
It must consequently take both signs.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{An integer-operation version.}
The width may instead be defined by
\[
 \widetilde r_n=
 \left\lceil\frac{37n}{\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor}\right\rceil
 \qquad(n\ge2).
\]
Its asymptotic constant is $37\log2>25$, so the same proof applies.
Here $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ is the binary length of $n$ minus one,
and all indices and coefficient-height bounds are computed by integer
operations. One may first check the exact counting inequality and
then enumerate inputs in lexicographic order until a repeated log
image appears. This yields a completely deterministic finite
selection procedure for every sufficiently large index, with no
evaluation of $\gamma$ or of the integrals.

\section{Which extension preserves the budget and guarantees nonvanishing?}
\label{jr--reverse:extension-section}

\begin{proposition}[The exact height window for independent outputs]
\label{jr--reverse:independent-window}
For a block $[n,n+r]$, put
\[
 S_r=\sum_{k=0}^r16^k,\qquad
 T_{n,r}=\sum_{k=0}^r\mathcal U_{n+k},\qquad M=n+r.
\]
If two integer log-null vectors $c^{(1)},c^{(2)}$ have independent
formal output pairs, then
\[
 \|c^{(1)}\|_\infty\|c^{(2)}\|_\infty
 \ge\frac1{2D_MS_rT_{n,r}}.
\]
For $r=o(n)$, a common height bound $H_n$ for such a pair therefore
necessarily satisfies
\[
 \liminf\frac{\log H_n}{n}\ge\frac{\delta}{2}.
\]
On the other hand, a common height exponent strictly below $\delta$
is sufficient to preserve denominator-cleared decay. In particular,
$H_n=2^n$ lies strictly between these two exponential thresholds.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Define integral normalized outputs
\[
 a(c)=\sum_{k=0}^r c_k16^k,\qquad
 P(c)=D_M\sum_{k=0}^r c_kp_{n+k}.
\]
The original first coordinate is $G_na(c)$, with
$G_n=D_M16^n$, so independence is unchanged.
For $\theta_n=G_n\gamma$ the error is
$e(c)=\theta_na(c)-P(c)=F_c$, and
\[
 |a(c)|\le S_r\|c\|_\infty,\qquad
 |e(c)|\le D_MT_{n,r}\|c\|_\infty.
\]
Cancellation of $\theta_n$ in the two-by-two determinant gives
\[
 1\le |a(c^{(1)})P(c^{(2)})-a(c^{(2)})P(c^{(1)})|
 \le2D_MS_rT_{n,r}\|c^{(1)}\|_\infty\|c^{(2)}\|_\infty.
\]
When $r=o(n)$, one has
$\log S_r=o(n)$,
$\log T_{n,r}=-\kappa n+o(n)$, and
$\log D_M=3n+o(n)$. This proves the lower threshold.
The upper threshold follows from Theorem~\ref{jr--reverse:uniform-budget}.
Finally $\delta/2<\log2<\delta$; the right inequality was checked
above, and the left follows, for example, from $e>5/2$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{A concrete remaining target.}
For the explicit width in Theorem~\ref{jr--reverse:concrete-cancellation},
prove that the integer box $\|c\|_\infty\le2^n$ contains two log-null
vectors with independent formal output pairs for infinitely many
$n$. This is a purely exact-arithmetic statement about specified
matrices and integer boxes. It has not been established here.
If it holds, choose such pairs and form
\[
 W_n(X)=(Q_{1,n}X-P_{1,n})^2+(Q_{2,n}X-P_{2,n})^2.
\]
Their nonzero determinant makes $W_n(X)>0$ for every real $X$,
while the already secured budget gives
$W_n(\gamma)\le\exp\{-2\varepsilon_2n+o(n)\}\to0$.
Under $\gamma=a/b$, the number $b^2W_n(\gamma)$ is then a positive
integer tending to zero, a contradiction.
This final paragraph is an implication from the stated independent-pair
target, not a claim that the target or irrationality has been proved.

\paragraph{Status of the five requirements in this construction.}
The concrete counting theorem supplies exact integer coefficients with
no remaining logarithms, a denominator-cleared bound tending to zero,
and a uniform existence proof for every sufficiently large index,
without an unproved arithmetic assumption. Its unresolved requirement
is a nonzero final value. The existence of formal-zero vectors in the
very same box proves why that requirement cannot be inferred merely
from nonzero input coefficients. The independent-pair target supplies
a specific route to nonvanishing while preserving the budget already
secured.


\clearpage
\part{Primitive quotient norms and exact transfer geometry}\label{part:quotients}


\section{Primitive quotient costs and exact finite certificates}
\label{s4--sec:quotient}

For $N\ge17$ and $v\in\mathbb R^2$, define
\begin{equation}
 C_N(c)=\sum_{n=1}^N\mathcal U_n|c_n|,\qquad
 F_N(v)=
 \min_{\substack{V_Nc=0\\\Psi_N(c)=v}}C_N(c),\qquad
 K_N=\{v:F_N(v)\le1\}.
 \label{s4--eq:quotient}
\end{equation}
Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:outputrank} guarantees feasibility for every real
target. A bounded-cost set of coefficients is compact, so the minimum
is attained. The norm $C_N$ and surjectivity of $\Psi_N$ on the kernel
show that $F_N$ is a norm. Its unit ball is a centrally symmetric
rational polygon: it is the image of a rational polytope obtained by
intersecting a weighted cross-polytope with $\ker V_N$.
For a rational target, an optimal rational lift exists by linear
programming over rational data.

\begin{lemma}[The quotient cost includes the whole output gcd]
\label{s4--lem:primitive}
Let $(q,p)\in\mathbb Z^2$ be primitive, and let $c\in\mathbb Q^N$ be
a log-null lift with $\Psi_N(c)=(q,p)$. If a positive integer $g$
clears every denominator of $c$, then
\[
 \Psi_N(gc)=(gq,gp),\qquad
 \gcd(|gq|,|gp|)=g.
\]
Consequently the upper cost after this entire gcd has been removed
is exactly $C_N(c)$, and
\[
 |q\gamma-p|\le F_N(q,p).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Linearity gives the output, primitiveness gives its gcd, and
$C_N(gc)=gC_N(c)$. The integral identity and the triangle inequality
give the bound for every lift; minimize over lifts.
\end{proof}

Define the first and second lattice minima by
\[
 \mu_1(N)=\min_{0\ne v\in\mathbb Z^2}F_N(v),\qquad
 \mu_2(N)=
 \min_{\substack{v,w\in\mathbb Z^2\\\det(v,w)\ne0}}
                 \max\{F_N(v),F_N(w)\}.
\]
Minimizers can be taken primitive. Both minima are nonincreasing in
$N$, because an old lift can be extended by zeros.
The independence condition in $\mu_2$ is what supplies nonvanishing
in Corollary~\ref{unified:independent-pair}.




\section{Certified finite minima and the area criterion}
\label{s3--sec:finite-quotient}
The notation $F_N$, its unit ball $K_N$, and the lattice
successive minima is fixed in the preceding section. The following
finite certificates use that same primitive quotient norm.
\begin{theorem}[Finite global optima for three proper-kernel blocks]
\label{s3--qopt:finite-theorem}
The first and second successive minima are attained, respectively,
at the following pairs; a change of sign has no effect:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\,,\,}r|r@{\,,\,}r}
N&\multicolumn{2}{c|}{v_1=(q_1,p_1)}&
  \multicolumn{2}{c}{v_2=(q_2,p_2)}\\ \hline
20&26685&15403&85313&49244\\
22&559595&323007&2739347&1581194\\
26&15700603&9062634&7040223&4063727
\end{array}
\]
The determinant of the two displayed targets has absolute value one
in every row. The following are strict rational inequalities:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
N&\text{bounds for }\mu_1(N)&\text{bounds for }\mu_2(N)\\ \hline
20&607002/10^{10}<\mu_1<607003/10^{10}
  &883918/10^{10}<\mu_2<883919/10^{10}\\
22&189360/10^{11}<\mu_1<189361/10^{11}
  &333400/10^{11}<\mu_2<333401/10^{11}\\
26&345529/10^{13}<\mu_1<345530/10^{13}
  &210024/10^{12}<\mu_2<210025/10^{12}
\end{array}
\]
In particular the two independent primitive forms at $N=26$ both
have certified absolute value less than $1/4700000$. At least one
is nonzero, solely by their independence. These are finite certificates;
no infinite decay conclusion is asserted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Exact finite verification and its completeness]
All the following operations are over the rational numbers. Row reduce
$V_N$ to obtain a basis of its rational kernel, of dimension $d$.
Identify this kernel with $\mathbb R^d$. Its input unit ball is the
section defined by $C_N(c)\le1$.

Every vertex of this section lies on at least $d-1$ independent
coordinate hyperplanes $c_i=0$. Indeed, if the vanishing coordinate
functionals had rank at most $d-2$, their common nullspace would
contain a nonzero direction also annihilating the active linear cost
functional. A sufficiently short segment in that direction would
preserve all other coordinate signs and the cost, contradicting
extremality. Thus all vertices are included by enumerating the
one-dimensional intersections of $d-1$ independent coordinate
hyperplanes with the kernel, and normalizing each of the two directions
to have cost one. Cofactor determinants generate these directions.

Project those normalized directions by $\Psi_N$ and take their exact
convex hull. The preceding argument proves that this gives the entire
polygon $K_N$, rather than an inner approximation. For $N=20,22,26$,
the kernel dimensions are $3,4,5$, and the hulls have $34,36,40$
vertices, respectively.

If $x,y$ are consecutive counterclockwise vertices, the corresponding
facet functional is
\[
 f_{x,y}(v)=\frac{\det(v,y-x)}{\det(x,y)},
 \qquad F_N(v)=\max_{(x,y)}f_{x,y}(v).
\]
Use the following unimodular bases $B_N=(b_1,b_2)$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\,,\,}r|r@{\,,\,}r|c}
N&\multicolumn{2}{c|}{b_1}&\multicolumn{2}{c|}{b_2}
 &\text{coordinate bounds}\\ \hline
20&-26685&-15403&58628&33841&(|m|,|n|)\le(1,1)\\
22&-559595&-323007&2179752&1258187&(|m|,|n|)\le(2,1)\\
26&15700603&9062634&-85543238&-49376897&(|m|,|n|)\le(7,1)
\end{array}
\]
Put $R_N=\max(F_N(b_1),F_N(b_2))$. For every lattice point
$v=mb_1+nb_2$ in $R_NK_N$,
\[
 |m|\le R_N\max_{x\in K_N}|\det(x,b_2)|,
 \qquad
 |n|\le R_N\max_{x\in K_N}|\det(b_1,x)|.
\]
The maxima occur at vertices. Exact evaluation and taking integer
parts give the displayed coordinate bounds. Enumerating the primitive
pairs in these finite rectangles, up to simultaneous change of sign,
proves the asserted global minima: $\mu_2\le R_N$ already follows
from the independent basis, so a point outside the rectangles cannot
improve either minimum. The first shortest vector and the first vector
not collinear with it give $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ in dimension two.
The rational interval comparisons in the theorem are then direct exact
comparisons of the facet values.

Attainment is verified on the input side as well. If a target $v$
attains its gauge on the edge $(x,y)$, then
\[
 v=\alpha x+\beta y,\quad
 \alpha=\frac{\det(v,y)}{\det(x,y)}\ge0,\quad
 \beta=\frac{\det(x,v)}{\det(x,y)}\ge0,\quad
 \alpha+\beta=F_N(v).
\]
The same combination of the normalized rational input lifts of $x,y$
is a rational optimizer for $v$. Clearing its denominators verifies
the exact output gcd identities stated above.

The complete verifier embedded in Appendix~\ref{unified:reproducibility}
implements precisely these finite rational operations using only the
Python standard library.
It constructs all residues, log matrices, kernel bases, polygons,
lattice rectangles, and optimizing lifts from their displayed formulas;
it reads no saved basis or external certificate. Decimal output is
informational only. No floating-point optimization or numerical value
of $\gamma$ enters any assertion.
\end{proof}

The old $N=20$ certificate already used $(26685,15403)$, with upper
bound approximately $6.42358\cdot10^{-5}$. The exact quotient minimum
is approximately $6.07002131\cdot10^{-5}$; the new result here is its
global optimality for this norm, the independent second direction, and
the improvements at larger blocks. The $N=26$ second minimum is about
$421$ times smaller than the $N=20$ second minimum. Finite improvement
does not establish a rate for an infinite sequence.

\begin{proposition}[A quantitative geometric condition for primitive decay]
\label{s3--qopt:minkowski}
Let $\mathcal A_N=\operatorname{area}(K_N)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{s3--qopt:area-minima}
 2\le\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)\mu_2(N)\le4,
 \qquad
 \frac{2}{\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)}\le\mu_2(N)
 \le\frac{4}{\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently $\mu_2(N)\to0$ is equivalent to
$\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)\to\infty$. For these cumulative blocks,
even unboundedness of $\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)$ suffices.
For example, bounds
\[
 \mathcal A_N\ge e^{\alpha N},\qquad
 \mu_1(N)\ge e^{-\beta N},\qquad \alpha>\beta,
\]
on an unbounded sequence of indices would prove primitive-error decay
for independent pairs, and hence irrationality of $\gamma$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first inequality is the two-dimensional case of Minkowski's second
theorem for the lattice $\mathbb Z^2$; see, for example,
\cite[Eq.~(1.4)]{minkowski-reference}.
Rearranging gives the other inequalities and the first equivalence.
Zero extension of an input lift shows $K_N\subseteq K_{N+1}$,
so $\mu_2(N)$ is nonincreasing. Unboundedness of
$\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)$ gives a subsequence with $\mu_2\to0$;
monotonicity gives the full limit. The final statement follows from
$|q\gamma-p|\le F_N(q,p)$ and the independent-pair criterion.
\end{proof}

The condition controls two quantities, not area alone. For example,
$K_T=[-T,T]\times[-1,1]$ has area $4T$, first minimum $1/T$, and
second minimum $1$. Moreover, the actual quotient polygons satisfy
$K_N\subseteq\{(q,p):|q\gamma-p|\le1\}$, so their ordinary Euclidean
inradii cannot tend to infinity. The relevant remaining task concerns
lattice directions and the product in \eqref{s3--qopt:area-minima}.
The computed values of $\mathcal A_N\mu_1(N)$ are approximately
$39167.12$, $952101.84$, and $16875495.18$ at $N=20,22,26$;
these three values are not a proof of unboundedness.

\begin{lemma}[Exact plateaus when a new prime occurs]
\label{s3--qopt:plateau}
If a prime $\ell$ satisfies $3N<\ell\le3(N+1)$, then
$F_{N+1}=F_N$ and $K_{N+1}=K_N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The $\ell$-log coefficient vanishes in every column indexed by
$n\le N$. In column $N+1$ it is $A_{N+1,\ell}\ne0$:
the interval ends below $2\ell$, so its only multiple of $\ell$ is
$\ell$ itself. Log cancellation therefore forces $c_{N+1}=0$.
The feasible quotient problem is exactly the preceding one.
\end{proof}

Thus the cumulative costs are monotone but need not improve at each
step; infinitely many exact plateaus occur because there are infinitely
many primes. The finite optimality theorem prevents arbitrary gcd
rescaling or further linear recombination within one of the fixed
blocks from beating its stated minima. It does not preclude better
analytic weights, correlated bounds, or improvement on unbounded
blocks. An infinite quantitative estimate sufficient for condition 3
remains unproved.


\section{Exact facet transfer and adaptive polygon certificates}
\label{s4--transfer:polygon-section}

Let $V$ have full row rank, let $\Psi(c)=(a^Tc,b^Tc)$ have rank two
on $\ker V$, and let $w_n>0$ be rational error weights. Put
\[
 K=\{\Psi(c):Vc=0,\ \sum_nw_n|c_n|\le1\}.
\]
This is the exact primitive quotient unit polygon: arbitrary rational
lifts, and hence arbitrary actual output gcds, are included.

\begin{lemma}[A finite primal--dual polygon certificate]
\label{s4--transfer:polygon-certificate}
Suppose a centrally symmetric polygon $P$ contains the origin in its
interior. For every vertex $v$ of $P$, suppose a rational vector $c_v$
satisfies $Vc_v=0$, $\Psi(c_v)=v$, and $\sum w_n|(c_v)_n|\le1$.
For every edge inequality $\ell\cdot v\le1$ of $P$, suppose a rational
vector $y$ satisfies
\[
 |\ell_1a_n+\ell_2b_n-(V^Ty)_n|\le w_n\qquad\text{for every }n.
\]
Then $P=K$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The vertex lifts and convexity give $P\subseteq K$. Conversely, for
$Vc=0$ the dual inequality gives
\[
 \ell\cdot\Psi(c)
 =\sum_n\bigl(\ell_1a_n+\ell_2b_n-(V^Ty)_n\bigr)c_n
 \le\sum_nw_n|c_n|.
\]
Every point of $K$ lies in every edge half-plane of $P$, so $K\subseteq P$.
\end{proof}

This lemma permits verification of the whole polygon without enumerating
all intersections of coordinate hyperplanes. A support oracle can locate
new vertices, while only the final rational lifts and edge inequalities
are needed for the proof. The computations here use an exact rational
simplex method even for the search; no floating-point optimization is
required.

\begin{theorem}[An exact one-column facet-survival rule]
\label{s4--transfer:facet-survival}
Assume that a new input column introduces no new prime-log row. Write
$v$ for its log column, $(a,b)$ for its output column, and $w>0$ for
its error weight. Let $\ell\cdot x\le1$ support an edge of the old
unit polygon. Define the nonempty rational polytope
\[
 Y(\ell)=\{y:|\ell_1a_n+\ell_2b_n-(V^Ty)_n|\le w_n
                    \text{ for all old columns }n\},
\]
and put
\[
 L=\min_{y\in Y(\ell)}v^Ty,\qquad
 H=\max_{y\in Y(\ell)}v^Ty.
\]
The old supporting line remains valid for the enlarged unit polygon
if and only if
\[
 \boxed{\ell_1a+\ell_2b\in[L-w,H+w].}
\]
If $Y(\ell)$ consists of a single vector $y$, this reduces to the
single exact residual test
$|\ell_1a+\ell_2b-v^Ty|\le w$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Finite-dimensional linear-programming duality gives the nonemptiness
of $Y(\ell)$, since the old support value equals one. Full row rank
of $V$ makes $Y(\ell)$ bounded: $V^Ty$ has bounded coordinates and
$V^T$ is injective. Thus $Y(\ell)$ is a compact rational polytope,
and the image of the linear functional $v^Ty$ is exactly $[L,H]$.
The new dual inequality is feasible precisely when this interval
meets $[\ell_1a+\ell_2b-w,\ell_1a+\ell_2b+w]$.
Strong duality gives equivalence with the new support value being at
most one. The old polygon is contained in the new one, so this value
is already at least one. This proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

At a prime-entry index, the new log row is zero on all old columns
and nonzero on the new column. Its free dual multiplier can absorb
the entire new residual. Every old edge survives, giving another proof
of the exact plateau. At the other indices, the theorem provides a
finite rational test for each old edge. It does not bound how often
edges change or the infinite rate of area growth.

\subsection{Further exact global minima}
Use the proper-kernel weights $w_n=\mathcal U_n$ on $1\le n\le N$.
The adaptive primal--dual certificate gives complete unit polygons with
$46,50,52$ vertices at $N=29,31,32$, respectively. The first and second
primitive successive minima are attained at
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
N&v_1=(q_1,p_1)&v_2=(q_2,p_2)\\\hline
29&(652385103,376566901)&(15700603,9062634)\\
31&(24091147002,13905787435)&(16278226369,9396047257)\\
32&(200542096649,115756039658)&(2181871916137,1259410648803).
\end{array}
\]
Every row has determinant of absolute value one. Exact rational bounds
are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
N&\text{bounds for }\mu_1&\text{bounds for }\mu_2\\\hline
29&861897/10^{15}<\mu_1<861898/10^{15}
  &495784/10^{14}<\mu_2<495785/10^{14}\\
31&898911/10^{16}<\mu_1<898912/10^{16}
  &143837/10^{15}<\mu_2<143838/10^{15}\\
32&188658/10^{17}<\mu_1<188659/10^{17}
  &640768/10^{17}<\mu_2<640769/10^{17}.
\end{array}
\]
In particular,
\[
 \boxed{\mu_2(32)<1/156000000000.}
\]
The two independent primitive integer forms therefore both have
certified absolute value below this bound, and at least one is nonzero.
The optimizing rational lifts at $N=32$ clear to integer relations
whose unscaled output gcds each have $770$ decimal digits. This
normalization-dependent size is reported only to make explicit that
large gcds were included; the invariant quantity is the quotient cost.

\paragraph{Completeness of the finite proof.}
The support search is a linear program in $x^+,x^-\ge0$ and a
nonnegative slack variable, with equalities
\[
 V(x^+-x^-)=0,\qquad
 \sum_n\mathcal U_n(x_n^++x_n^-)+s=1.
\]
Every vertex certificate specifies a feasible basis of this rational
system. Every edge certificate specifies a feasible basis with support
value one and nonpositive reduced costs. These are exact primal and
dual certificates for Lemma~\ref{s4--transfer:polygon-certificate}.
An independent verifier reconstructs all matrices and checks the
certificates by rational basis exchange; it does not rerun the support
search or trust its numerical summaries.

The integer-minimum check then uses exact facet gauges, as in the
preceding paper. Suitable unimodular bases are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
N&b_1&b_2&(|m|,|n|)\text{ bound}\\\hline
29&(-652385103,-376566901)&(-1972855912,-1138763337)&(8,1)\\
31&(-24091147002,-13905787435)&(-40369373371,-23301834692)&(2,1)\\
32&(200542096649,115756039658)&(1981329819488,1143654609145)&(4,1).
\end{array}
\]
Writing $R=\max(F_N(b_1),F_N(b_2))$, the bounds enclose every integer
point of $RK_N$, by the exact determinant coordinate bounds. Since
$\mu_2\le R$, exhaustive enumeration in these rectangles proves global
optimality for the specified weighted quotient norm. The verifier
checks the target determinants, all six rational intervals, all optimal
lifts, exact log cancellation, and the final output gcds.

The product $\operatorname{area}(K_N)\mu_1(N)$ is approximately
$5.5255322\cdot10^8$, $2.5505733\cdot10^{10}$, and
$4.6707794\cdot10^{11}$ on these three blocks. Its unboundedness has
not been proved. The finite second minimum at $32$ is roughly $32777$
times smaller than at $26$, but no infinite rate is inferred from these
values. The infinite rank law and recursive basis construction are
proved for all indices; primitive-error decay for two independent
integer outputs remains a separate, unproved quantitative assertion.

\begin{corollary}[Explicit bounds for the evaluated forms]
\label{s4--cor:finite-actual}
For the two primitive outputs in the $N=32$ row,
\[
 |q_1\gamma-p_1|<\frac1{1026000000000},\qquad
 |q_2\gamma-p_2|<\frac1{302000000000}.
\]
At least one of these values is nonzero.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{s4--dual:uniform-ratio} gives
$|q\gamma-p|<(488/945)F_N(q,p)$ for every nonzero target.
Use the exact bounds $\mu_1(32)<1/530000000000$ and
$\mu_2(32)<1/156000000000$ from the finite certificate.
The rational comparisons are
\[
 \frac{488}{945\cdot530000000000}
  <\frac1{1026000000000},\qquad
 \frac{488}{945\cdot156000000000}
  <\frac1{302000000000}.
\]
Independence supplies the nonzero member, as in
Corollary~\ref{unified:independent-pair}.
\end{proof}
\section{The limiting quotient seminorm and its exact infinite dual}
\label{s4--dual:geometry-section}

All coefficient vectors in this section have finite support unless
otherwise specified.  Write
\[
 (Ec)_\ell=\sum_n E_{n,\ell}c_n,\qquad
 \Psi(c)=\left(\sum_n16^nc_n,\sum_np_nc_n\right),\qquad
 C(c)=\sum_n\mathcal U_n|c_n|.
\]
Each column of $E$ has only finitely many prime coordinates.  The
identities defining the proper kernels give
\[
 Ec=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sum_nc_nI_n=\gamma\,\Psi(c)_1-\Psi(c)_2.
\]
The condition $Ec=0$ is the formal cancellation of every prime-log
coefficient; it is not replaced by a numerical smallness test on a sum
of logarithms.

For $N\ge17$, let $F_N$ be the quotient norm previously defined using
coefficients supported on $1,\ldots,N$.  Output rank two at $N=17$ is
provided by Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:outputrank}.  Put
\[
 L_\gamma(q,p)=\gamma q-p,\qquad
 F_\infty(v)=\inf_{N\ge17}F_N(v).
\]

\begin{theorem}[A continuous limit and an exact infinite multiplier test]
\label{s4--dual:infinite-dual}
The functions $F_N$ decrease to a finite continuous seminorm
$F_\infty$ and converge uniformly on every compact subset of
$\mathbb R^2$.  Moreover,
\[
 F_\infty(v)\ge\frac{|L_\gamma(v)|}{\rho_*},
\]
where $\rho_*<1$ is defined in
Corollary~\ref{s4--dual:ratio-scope}.  In particular $F_\infty$ is not
identically zero.

For a real pair $(\alpha,\beta)$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha q+\beta p\le F_\infty(q,p)$ for every real target $(q,p)$;
\item there are real numbers $y_\ell$, one for each prime, such that
\begin{equation}\label{s4--dual:global-multiplier}
 \left|\alpha16^n+\beta p_n+\sum_\ell y_\ell E_{n,\ell}\right|
 \le\mathcal U_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge1.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Every sum in \eqref{s4--dual:global-multiplier} is finite; no growth
restriction or convergence convention for the sequence $y_\ell$ is
being suppressed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Zero extension proves $F_{N+1}\le F_N$.  Homogeneity and the triangle
inequality pass to the decreasing limit.  Since $F_\infty\le F_{17}$,
\[
 |F_\infty(v)-F_\infty(w)|\le F_{17}(v-w),
\]
so the limit is continuous.  In fact the same modulus of continuity
works for every $F_N$.  Compactness and a finite net, or Dini's
monotone convergence theorem, then give uniform convergence on compact
sets.  Applying the estimate of Corollary~\ref{s4--dual:ratio-scope} to every
feasible lift proves the displayed lower bound.

Assume the first condition.  On the subspace
$M=\ker E$ of the normed space $c_{00}(\mathbb R)$ with norm $C$,
define
\[
 f(c)=\alpha\Psi(c)_1+\beta\Psi(c)_2.
\]
For $c\in M$, a finite block containing its support gives
$|f(c)|\le F_\infty(\Psi(c))\le C(c)$; symmetry was used for the
absolute value.  Hahn--Banach extends $f$ to a linear functional $r$
on all of $c_{00}$ satisfying $|r(c)|\le C(c)$.  If $e_n$ is the
$n$th coordinate vector, then $r_n=r(e_n)$ satisfies
$|r_n|\le\mathcal U_n$.

The linear functional
$c\mapsto\alpha\Psi(c)_1+\beta\Psi(c)_2-r(c)$ vanishes on $\ker E$.
It therefore factors through the algebraic image of $E$.  Extend that
factor linearly to the direct sum of all prime-coordinate spaces, and
write its value on the $\ell$th coordinate vector as $-y_\ell$.
Evaluation on $e_n$ gives precisely
\[
 r_n=\alpha16^n+\beta p_n+\sum_\ell y_\ell E_{n,\ell},
\]
and proves the second condition.  No continuity of $E$ or boundedness
of the multiplier sequence was used or needed.

Conversely, if \eqref{s4--dual:global-multiplier} holds and $Ec=0$, then
$|\alpha\Psi(c)_1+\beta\Psi(c)_2|\le C(c)$.
Take the infimum over every finite-block lift and then over $N$.
This gives the first condition.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact termwise integral weights have the same decay question]
\label{s4--dual:equivalent-weights}
Let $\widehat F_N$ be the quotient norm obtained by replacing the
cost $\sum_n\mathcal U_n|c_n|$ by
$\sum_n I_n|c_n|$, with precisely the same logarithm-cancellation
constraints and output map.  There is a constant $\rho_->0$,
independent of $N$, such that
\[
 \rho_- F_N(v)\le\widehat F_N(v)\le\rho_*F_N(v)
 \qquad(N\ge17,\ v\in\mathbb R^2).
\]
Consequently the second successive minima for these two weight
systems tend to zero simultaneously.  The same conclusion holds for
any intermediate positive weights $I_n\le W_n\le\mathcal U_n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $\rho_-=\inf_{n\ge1}I_n/\mathcal U_n$.  Each ratio is positive,
and Theorem~\ref{s4--dual:ratio-theorem} gives a positive limit, so
$\rho_->0$ by separating a finite prefix from a tail.  The two cost
inequalities hold for every feasible coefficient vector.  Taking
infima gives the norm inequalities, which pass to both successive
minima by their definitions.  Intermediate weights are sandwiched
between the two costs.
\end{proof}

This corollary concerns termwise positive bounds and the weighted
triangle inequality.  It says that replacing the current weights by
the exact positive values of all the integrals cannot by itself change
the answer to the uniform primitive-decay question.  It does not
exclude estimates that use cancellation between different integrals
before taking absolute values.

\begin{theorem}[Constructive infinite dual from bounded pivot residuals]
\label{s4--dual:pivot-residuals}
Use the pivot set $\mathcal P_\infty$ and the rational log-null basis
