$h^{(n)}$ of Theorem~\ref{s4--thm:kernelrecursion}.  Fix real
$\alpha,\beta$ and $B>0$.  A prime-multiplier sequence satisfying
\[
 \left|\alpha16^n+\beta p_n+\sum_\ell y_\ell E_{n,\ell}\right|
 \le B\mathcal U_n\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
exists if and only if one can choose numbers $r_b$, for
$b\in \mathcal P_\infty$, such that
\begin{align}
 |r_b|&\le B\mathcal U_b
       &&(b\in \mathcal P_\infty),\label{s4--dual:pivot-box}\\
 \left|\alpha\Psi(h^{(n)})_1+\beta\Psi(h^{(n)})_2
       -\sum_{b\in \mathcal P_{n-1}}h_b^{(n)}r_b\right|
       &\le B\mathcal U_n
       &&(n\ge10,\ n\notin \mathcal P_\infty).
       \label{s4--dual:pivot-slabs}
\end{align}
Each constraint involves only finitely many variables.  The infinite
system \eqref{s4--dual:pivot-box}--\eqref{s4--dual:pivot-slabs} is feasible
if and only if every finite prefix is feasible.

Given its pivot residuals, the multiplier sequence is unique and is
constructed by rational linear operations applied to the residuals,
$\alpha$, and $\beta$.  In particular, no compactness assumption on an
unbounded sequence of prime multipliers is required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $d_n=\alpha16^n+\beta p_n$.  Start by solving the invertible
nine-by-nine system
\[
 \sum_{\ell\le27}E_{b,\ell}y_\ell=r_b-d_b
 \qquad(1\le b\le9).
\]
At a later prime-entry index $b$, its unique new prime $\ell_b$
has $E_{b,\ell_b}=A_{b,\ell_b}\ne0$.  Define
\[
 y_{\ell_b}=
 \frac{r_b-d_b-\sum_{\ell<\ell_b}E_{b,\ell}y_\ell}
      {E_{b,\ell_b}}.
\]
Every prime eventually occurs, so this specifies all multipliers
uniquely.  Each step is finite, and the entries of the coefficient
matrices are rational.

At a nonpivot index $n$ define the resulting residual
$r_n=d_n+\sum_\ell E_{n,\ell}y_\ell$.
Since $Eh^{(n)}=0$ and $h_n^{(n)}=1$,
\[
 r_n+\sum_{b\in \mathcal P_{n-1}}h_b^{(n)}r_b
 =d_n+\sum_{b\in \mathcal P_{n-1}}h_b^{(n)}d_b
 =\alpha\Psi(h^{(n)})_1+\beta\Psi(h^{(n)})_2.
\]
Thus its required bound is exactly \eqref{s4--dual:pivot-slabs}.
Conversely any feasible multipliers supply pivot residuals satisfying
these equations, proving the first assertion.

The pivot residuals lie in the countable product of compact intervals
$\prod_{b\in \mathcal P_\infty}[-B\mathcal U_b,B\mathcal U_b]$.
Each slab is a closed cylinder set.  Feasibility of every prefix gives
the finite-intersection property, hence a common point.  Equivalently,
one may choose feasible solutions on increasing prefixes, extend their
unused coordinates by zero, and successively extract convergent
subsequences in each pivot coordinate; the diagonal limit satisfies
every fixed slab.  The converse is restriction to a prefix.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A rational finite test for each proposed extra-dual budget]
\label{s4--dual:pivot-finite-test}
For a fixed positive rational $B$, the extra-dual condition
\eqref{s4--dual:q-rigidity-target} with this budget is equivalent to
feasibility of every finite prefix of
\eqref{s4--dual:pivot-box}--\eqref{s4--dual:pivot-slabs} with
$(\alpha,\beta)=(1,0)$.
All coefficients of these finite linear inequality systems are
rational.  If no infinite solution with this budget exists, a finite
prefix already witnesses infeasibility.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{s4--dual:pivot-residuals}.
The numbers $\mathcal U_b$ and the coordinates of $h^{(n)}$ and
$\Psi(h^{(n)})$ are rational.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete geometric alternatives]
\label{s4--dual:alternatives}
Exactly one of the following occurs.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $F_\infty$ is a norm.  Both successive minima of $F_N$ converge
to the positive successive minima of $F_\infty$ on $\mathbb Z^2$.
In particular $\mu_2(N)$ does not tend to zero.
\item For a finite constant $\kappa\ge1/\rho_*$,
\[
 F_\infty(q,p)=\kappa|\gamma q-p|.
\]
The closure of $\bigcup_{N\ge17}K_N$ is exactly the strip
$|\gamma q-p|\le1/\kappa$.  Every compact subset of its strict
interior is contained in $K_N$ for all sufficiently large $N$.
\end{enumerate}
In the second case, if $\gamma=a/b$ is rational in lowest terms with
$b>0$, then
\[
 \mu_1(N)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \mu_2(N)\longrightarrow\kappa/b.
\]
If $\gamma$ is irrational, then both successive minima tend to zero.
These last two statements are alternatives, not assumptions about
which arithmetic case holds for Euler's constant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lower bound in Theorem~\ref{s4--dual:infinite-dual} puts the kernel of
$F_\infty$ inside the one-dimensional kernel of $L_\gamma$.
If that kernel is trivial, compactness of the Euclidean unit circle
gives $F_\infty(v)\ge a\|v\|$ for some $a>0$.  Since
$F_N\ge F_\infty$, all lattice vectors capable of improving the
fixed $F_{17}$ minima lie in one bounded Euclidean set.  Only finitely
many integer vectors occur there.  Pointwise convergence on that
finite set proves convergence of both successive minima to those
of the limiting norm.

If the kernel is nontrivial, it equals $\ker L_\gamma$.
Factoring the seminorm through the one-dimensional quotient gives
$F_\infty=\kappa|L_\gamma|$, with
$\kappa=F_\infty(0,-1)\ge1/\rho_*$.
If $F_\infty(v)<1$, then $F_N(v)<1$ eventually.
If $F_\infty(v)=1$, apply this observation to $(1-\varepsilon)v$
and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.  This proves the closure statement,
and uniform convergence on compact sets proves the interior statement.

In the rational case the primitive vector $v=(b,a)$ satisfies
$F_N(v)\to0$.  Every independent pair of integer vectors contains
a vector $w$ outside its line, for which
$|L_\gamma(w)|\ge1/b$.  Thus $\mu_2(N)\ge\kappa/b$.
Choose an integer $w$ with $|\det(v,w)|=1$ by Bezout's identity.
Then $|L_\gamma(w)|=1/b$ and
$F_N(w)\to\kappa/b$, proving the matching upper limit.

In the irrational case elementary rational approximation gives
infinitely many primitive integer vectors with
$|L_\gamma(v)|\to0$.  Distinct such vectors, up to sign, are not
collinear.  For each $\varepsilon>0$, choose two independent ones
whose limiting costs are less than $\varepsilon$.  Pointwise
convergence on these two fixed targets gives $\mu_2(N)<2\varepsilon$
eventually.  The first minimum is at most the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An additional dual functional is exactly the remaining geometry obstruction]
\label{s4--dual:extra-functional}
The limiting seminorm is a norm if and only if there exist a finite
constant $B>0$ and real prime multipliers $y_\ell$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{s4--dual:q-rigidity-target}
 \left|16^n+\sum_\ell y_\ell E_{n,\ell}\right|
 \le B\mathcal U_n\qquad(n\ge1).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the limiting polar contains a functional linearly
independent of $(q,p)\mapsto\gamma q-p$ if and only if
\eqref{s4--dual:q-rigidity-target} has such a solution.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $F_\infty$ is a norm, its unit ball is bounded, so
$|q|\le B F_\infty(q,p)$ for some $B>0$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{s4--dual:infinite-dual} to $(1/B,0)$ and rescale the
multipliers.  Conversely \eqref{s4--dual:q-rigidity-target} gives
$F_\infty(q,p)\ge|q|/B$.  Together with its lower bound by
$|L_\gamma|/\rho_*$, this makes its kernel trivial.
The limiting polar always contains the nontrivial segment of
evaluation functionals $\tau(\gamma,-1)$ for
$|\tau|\le1/\rho_*$.  An independent functional makes its support
seminorm a norm, while the strip case has only that one dual direction.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What these theorems leave undecided.}
The infinite dual can contain more than the evaluation direction:
excluding that possibility for these specific kernels requires ruling
out \eqref{s4--dual:q-rigidity-target}.  The finite polygons and the
asymptotic ratio theorem do not do so.  Conversely, proving strip
exhaustion would not establish $\mu_2(N)\to0$ without also excluding
the rational alternative in Theorem~\ref{s4--dual:alternatives}.
Thus the theorem separates a geometric limit question from the
arithmetic question; it does not count either unresolved assertion
as a proved irrationality result.

\paragraph{Connection to the five arithmetic requirements.}
The triangular basis and the rational quotient optimization enforce
exact cancellation of logarithms.  For an integer output $(q,p)$ the
remaining value is exactly $q\gamma-p$, so under
$\gamma=a/b$ the scaled value $b(q\gamma-p)$ is an integer.
Two independent integer outputs ensure that at least one such value
is nonzero, even under that rationality assumption.  A proof that
$\mu_2(N)\to0$ would supply, for every positive integer $k$, a finite
block and two independent integer outputs with rational log-null
lifts of cost less than $1/k$.  Rational lifts exist because the
finite optimization data are rational.  Their remainders are bounded
by $\rho_*/k$, and the scale $b$ is fixed under the rationality
assumption, so the nonzero integer would eventually have absolute
value less than one.

Conversely, that uniform supply of two small-cost integer outputs
is exactly the assertion $\mu_2(N)\to0$, by monotonicity of the
finite quotient norms.  The pivot recursion proves exact feasibility
and makes every finite budget test explicit; it does not supply the
required uniform decay.  No asymptotic arithmetic condition has been
replaced by finite numerical evidence in these statements.
\section{An exact dilation recursion and its primitive arithmetic cost}
\label{s4--sec:dilation-recursion}

This section tests a natural way to extend a finite logarithm-free
certificate to infinitely many larger supports. The recursion cancels
its new logarithms identically and makes the raw integrals geometrically
small. Nevertheless its actual primitive errors diverge. The result
applies to every fixed nonzero starting kernel, including a finite
prime-log-null combination of the proper kernels.

Let
\[
 d\mu(u)=\frac{du}{e^{2\pi\sqrt u}-1},\qquad
 h_m=H_m-\frac1{2m},\qquad
 F(u)=\sum_{m\in S}\frac{b_m}{u+m^2},
\]
where $S$ is a finite nonempty set of positive integers, every
$b_m\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}$, and
\[
 q_0=\sum_{m\in S}b_m\ne0,\qquad
 \sum_{m\in S}b_m v_\ell(m)=0\quad\hbox{for every prime }\ell.
\]
Thus Binet's formula gives $\int F\,d\mu=q_0\gamma-P_0$, where
$P_0=\sum_m b_mh_m$ is rational.
Fix an integer $a\ge2$, and define
\[
 (\mathscr D_aF)(u)=a^{-2}F(u/a^2),\qquad
 \mathscr T_a=2\mathscr D_a-\mathscr D_{a^2},\qquad
 F_n=\mathscr T_a^nF,\quad J_n=\int F_n\,d\mu.
\]
These identities define rational kernels without referring to $\gamma$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact preservation of the gamma and prime-log coordinates]
For every $n\ge0$,
\[
 F_n(u)=\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr2^{n-r}
                  \sum_{m\in S}\frac{b_m}{u+(ma^{n+r})^2},
\]
and
\[
 J_n=q_0\gamma-P_n,\qquad
 P_n=\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr2^{n-r}
                  \sum_{m\in S}b_mh_{ma^{n+r}}\in\mathbb Q.
\]
In particular every auxiliary logarithm vanishes exactly at every step.
The gamma coordinate $q_0$ is unchanged; the rational coordinate $P_n$
is generally changed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The dilation operators commute and
$\mathscr D_a^j=\mathscr D_{a^j}$, giving the binomial expansion.
Put $C(z)=2z-z^2$. Its coefficient vector at the $n$-th stage is
that of $C(z)^n$. Since $C(1)=1$ and $C'(1)=0$, the weights satisfy
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr2^{n-r}=1,\qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^n(n+r)(-1)^r\binom nr2^{n-r}=0.
\]
Applying Binet's identity to each pole, the old prime-log coordinates
are multiplied by the first sum, while the new $\log a$ coefficient
is $q_0$ times the second. Hence the displayed form is exact.
In fact the operator preserves every old prime-log coordinate, even
before the initial log-null hypothesis is imposed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Raw contraction for every nonzero finite starting kernel]
Write the Taylor expansion at zero as
\[
 F(u)=\sum_{j\ge0} f_j u^j,
 \qquad
 f_j=(-1)^j\sum_{m\in S}\frac{b_m}{m^{2j+2}},
\]
and let $\nu=\operatorname{ord}_{u=0}F<\infty$.
Define
\[
 \mu_j=\int_0^\infty u^j\,d\mu(u)
       =\frac{|B_{2j+2}|}{2j+2}>0,
 \qquad
 \beta_j=2a^{-2j-2}-a^{-4j-4}.
\]
There is a constant $0\le\eta<\beta_\nu<1$ such that
\[
 \boxed{J_n=f_\nu\mu_\nu\beta_\nu^n+O_F(\eta^n).}
\]
Thus $J_n$ has a fixed nonzero sign for every sufficiently large $n$.
The statement does not require pointwise positivity of $F_n$.
Here $B_j$ are Bernoulli numbers. This raw asymptotic applies to every
nonzero finite rational simple-pole kernel, even without a nonzero
gamma coordinate or a prime-log-null hypothesis.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For every integer $R\ge0$ and every $u\ge0$, the finite geometric
identity for each simple pole gives
\[
 \left|F(u)-\sum_{j=0}^R f_ju^j\right|
 \le C_Ru^{R+1},\qquad C_R=\sum_m\frac{|b_m|}{m^{2R+4}}.
\]
After dilation and the binomial expansion, integration yields the
entirely explicit bound
\[
 \left|J_n-\sum_{j=0}^R f_j\mu_j\beta_j^n\right|
 \le C_R\mu_{R+1}
          \left(2a^{-2R-4}+a^{-4R-8}\right)^n.
\]
The moment formula follows by $v=2\pi\sqrt u$, expansion of
$(e^v-1)^{-1}$, and the classical even-zeta evaluation.
Since $2t-t^2$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$,
$\beta_0>\beta_1>\cdots>0$ and $\beta_j\to0$.
Choose $R\ge\nu$ so large that
$2a^{-2R-4}+a^{-4R-8}<\beta_\nu$.
All terms below $\nu$ vanish, and all other bases are strictly smaller
than $\beta_\nu$. This proves the asymptotic and its nonvanishing assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The full primitive cost of the recursion diverges]
Let $Q_n=\operatorname{den}(P_n/q_0)$ be the actual reduced denominator,
and put $M_n=m_*a^{2n}$, where $m_*=\max S$.
If $S$ has more than one element let $m_{**}$ be its second largest;
otherwise put $m_{**}=0$. Set
\[
 \theta=\max\left\{\frac12,\frac1a,\frac{m_{**}}{m_*}\right\}<1.
\]
For every sufficiently large $n$,
\[
 \boxed{\prod_{\substack{\theta M_n<\ell\le M_n\\\ell\ {\rm prime}}}\ell
        \ \mid\ Q_n.}
\]
Consequently the prime number theorem gives
\[
 \log Q_n\ge(1-\theta+o(1))M_n,
 \qquad
 Q_n\left|\gamma-\frac{P_n}{q_0}\right|\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
This conclusion already incorporates every common factor removed
from the integrated output pair.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The largest pole parameter is $M_n$, arising only from $m=m_*$ and
$r=n$. Its residue is $(-1)^n b_{m_*}$.
Every other pole parameter is at most $\theta M_n$.
For sufficiently large $n$, primes in $(\theta M_n,M_n]$ divide
none of the fixed numerator or denominator factors of the $b_m$ or $q_0$.
Such a prime $\ell$ occurs exactly once in $H_{M_n}$ and does not
occur in any other harmonic number in $P_n$.
Also $\ell\nmid2M_n$: for $n\ge1$ the number $M_n$ is composite,
whereas a prime divisor exceeding $M_n/2$ would have to equal $M_n$.
Therefore
\[
 v_\ell(P_n)=-1,\qquad v_\ell(P_n/q_0)=-1.
\]
This proves the product divisibility for the reduced denominator.
The prime number theorem \cite{dlmf-primes} gives
$\sum_{\theta M_n<\ell\le M_n}\log\ell
=(1-\theta+o(1))M_n$.
Meanwhile the preceding theorem gives
$\log|J_n|=n\log\beta_\nu+O_F(1)$.
Since the primitive error equals $Q_n|J_n|/|q_0|$, its logarithm
tends to positive infinity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A finite independent pair cannot be bootstrapped this way]
Start from two finite prime-log-null kernels with nonzero gamma
coordinates and distinct rational targets. Apply the same fixed
operator $\mathscr T_a$ repeatedly to both.
Their targets remain distinct for every sufficiently large stage,
but both primitive errors tend to positive infinity.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the raw asymptotic to the nonzero difference of the two kernels
after dividing each by its gamma coordinate. Its evaluated integral
is the difference of the two rational targets, so that difference is
eventually nonzero. The primitive-cost theorem applies to each kernel.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{An elementary one-pole version requiring only Bertrand's theorem}

Take $F(u)=1/(u+1)$. Then $q_0=1$ and
\[
 \beta=\frac{2a^2-1}{a^4},\qquad
 \tau=\frac{2a^4+1}{a^8}<\beta.
\]
The explicit Taylor remainder at $R=0$ gives, for every $n\ge0$,
\[
 \frac{\beta^n}{12}-\frac{\tau^n}{120}
 \le J_n\le
 \frac{\beta^n}{12}+\frac{\tau^n}{120}.
\]
Thus $J_n\ge(3/40)\beta^n>0$.
For $n\ge1$, Bertrand's theorem \cite{erdos1932} gives a prime
$a^{2n}/2<\ell<a^{2n}$. It sees only the last harmonic pole and
has valuation $-1$ in the rational target. Hence the actual reduced
denominator exceeds $a^{2n}/2$, and
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal E_n=Q_nJ_n>
        \frac3{80}(2-a^{-2})^n\longrightarrow+\infty.}
\]
This exact log-free recursion satisfies integrality after reduction,
nonvanishing, and an infinite unconditional construction, but fails
primitive-error decay even under a lower bound using just one prime.

Pointwise positivity is not silently assumed. For example, at $a=2$,
\[
 (\mathscr T_2^4(1/(u+1)))\big|_{u=4^6}=-\frac7{348160}<0,
\]
while its integral is strictly positive by the displayed bound.

\paragraph{Scope and comparison with earlier constructions.}
The earlier corpus constructs positive multiscale kernels and proves
prime-survival bounds for particular schedules. The present result
concerns a fixed autonomous dilation operator applied to \emph{any}
finite starting log-null kernel; the raw asymptotic is determined by
its exact order of vanishing at zero. It therefore tests the proposed
bootstrap from a finite optimized proper-kernel certificate.
It does not exclude stage-dependent operators, growing cancellation
width, variable dilations, or other output-changing circuits.



\clearpage
\part{Positive and signed prefixes, output intervals, and repairs}\label{part:prefixes}


\section{Why coefficientwise positivity cannot supply nonvanishing}
\label{jc--sec:reverse-positive-cone}

An integer log-null vector whose cleared weighted error tends to zero
still needs a nonzero final value. One attractive sufficient condition
would be nonnegative combination coefficients, because every proper
kernel is strictly positive. The following exact separation theorem
excludes that particular completion of the construction.

\begin{theorem}[A separating functional for all proper-kernel log columns]
For $n\ge1$, put
\[
 R_n(u)=\frac{\prod_{k=0}^{2n-1}(4u+k^2)}
                  {\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(u+j^2)},\qquad q_n=16^n,
 \qquad
 L_n=\sum_{\ell\le3n}E_{n,\ell}\log\ell
     =\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}\log j.
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{L_n>16^n\log(3n)>0.}
\]
Consequently, on any finite nonempty set of indices, a nonzero real
vector cancelling every prime-log coordinate must have both a positive
and a negative coefficient. In particular no nonzero coefficientwise
nonnegative combination of these proper kernels is log-null.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The partial fractions and their leading coefficient give
\[
 R_n(u)=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac{A_{n,j}}{u+j^2},
 \qquad \sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}=q_n.
\]
Integrating each finite partial-fraction difference yields the
elementary identity
\[
 \int_0^\infty\left(\frac{q_n}{u+1}-R_n(u)\right)du
 =\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}
       \int_0^\infty\left(\frac1{u+1}-\frac1{u+j^2}\right)du
 =2L_n.
\]
Each difference is integrable; the cancellation of the $1/u$ terms
also makes the summed integrand $O(u^{-2})$ at infinity.
On the other hand, for every $u\ge0$,
\[
 \frac{R_n(u)}{q_n}
 =\frac1{u+9n^2}
   \prod_{k=0}^{2n-1}
     \frac{u+(k/2)^2}{u+(n+k)^2}
 <\frac1{u+9n^2},
\]
since $0\le k/2<n+k$. The inequality is strict throughout, including
at zero. Thus
\begin{align*}
 2L_n
 &>q_n\int_0^\infty
       \left(\frac1{u+1}-\frac1{u+9n^2}\right)du\\
 &=q_n\log(9n^2)=2q_n\log(3n).
\end{align*}
The strict comparison is legitimate because the difference between
the two integrands is positive and integrable.

If $c_n\ge0$ and at least one coefficient is positive, then
$\sum_n c_nL_n>0$. Exact cancellation of every prime-log coordinate
would instead give
\[
 \sum_n c_nL_n
 =\sum_\ell\left(\sum_n c_nE_{n,\ell}\right)\log\ell=0,
\]
a contradiction. Replacing a nonpositive vector by its negative proves
the full assertion.
\end{proof}

This theorem concerns the signs of the combination coefficients. It
does not exclude a signed combination whose resulting rational kernel
is nonnegative, and it does not exclude other positive integral
constructions. Its proof uses no arithmetic assumption about $\gamma$.



\section{Positive certificates and finite feasibility}
\label{s5--sec:positive-certificates}
The cumulative-positivity theorem proved with the common kernels
allows mixed coefficient signs; it controls the resulting kernel.
\subsection{An exact finite nonvanishing certificate at small primitive cost}

The first exact lift stored in
\path{primitive32_lift.json} has primitive output
\[
 (q,p)=(200542096649,115756039658).
\]
The rational coefficient vector and its weighted prefix sums have been
extracted to \path{cumulative_positive_kernel32.json}.
Regenerating the residues independently from their factorial formula
and using exact rational arithmetic verifies
\[
 V_{32}c=0,\qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^{32}16^jc_j=q,\qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^{32}p_jc_j=p,\qquad \gcd(q,p)=1,
\]
\[
 S_1=\cdots=S_6=0,\qquad S_7,\ldots,S_{32}>0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^{32}|c_j|\mathcal U_j<\frac1{530000000000}.
\]
Theorem~\ref{s6--thm:cumulative-cone} therefore gives the strict certified
inequality
\[
 \boxed{0<200542096649\gamma-115756039658
                <\frac1{530000000000}.}
\]
The sign certificate concerns the entire rational kernel and does not
use digits of $\gamma$. The standard-library verifier also clears every
coefficient denominator and checks that the complete gcd of the two
resulting integer output coordinates is exactly that clearing factor.
Thus the quoted cost is already the primitive cost.

This is one finite target. Repeating or scaling it does not establish
decay along an infinite sequence.



\subsection{The first canonical relation: positivity without small cost}

At $N=12$, the canonical log-null relation is unique up to scaling.
It is defined exactly by
\[
 h_{12}=1,\qquad
 (h_1,\ldots,h_{11})^T=-V_{11}^{-1}V_{12}[:,12].
\]
Clear denominators and remove the coefficient gcd to obtain the integer
vector in \texttt{cumulative\_positive\_kernel12.json}. If $Q$ denotes
its positive gamma coefficient, all twelve prefix sums satisfy
\[
 \frac{99}{100}Q<S_k<3Q,
 \qquad S_1>Q.
\]
This is an exact mixed-coefficient positive-kernel certificate. Its
primitive target, however, has denominator $q>10^{105}$ and primitive
error greater than $10^{98}$. Thus positivity by itself does not solve
the arithmetic-cost problem.

For the last lower bound, after normalization to the primitive target
the first Abel coefficient is $(q/Q)S_1>q$. On $1\le u\le2$,
\[
 f_1(u)=\frac{u(u+1/4)}{(u+1)(u+4)(u+9)}
       \ge\frac5{792}>\frac1{160},
 \qquad
 \frac{f_2(u)}{f_1(u)}
       \le\frac{153}{4\cdot17\cdot26\cdot37}<\frac12.
\]
Also $2\pi\sqrt2<9$ and $e<3$ give
$d\mu/du>1/20000$ there. Consequently
\[
 \int_1^2(f_1-f_2)\,d\mu
   >\frac1{320\cdot20000}>10^{-7}.
\]
All other Abel summands are nonnegative, so the primitive error exceeds
$q10^{-7}>10^{98}$. This check uses no numerical enclosure of $\gamma$.

\subsection{An exact feasibility alternative}

For a fixed window let $e_j=(E_{j,\ell}/16^j)_\ell$ be the rational
normalized log column. By Theorem~\ref{s6--thm:cumulative-cone}, a nonzero
log-null vector in the cumulative cone can be scaled to $S_M=1$.
It exists if and only if
\[
 -e_M\in\operatorname{cone}
       \{e_n-e_{n+1},\ldots,e_{M-1}-e_M\}.
\]
Equivalently, by the finite-dimensional Farkas alternative, it fails
to exist if and only if a real row vector $y$ satisfies
\[
 y\mathbin\cdot e_n\ge y\mathbin\cdot e_{n+1}\ge\cdots
       \ge y\mathbin\cdot e_M>0.
\]
All data in the feasibility problem are rational, so a feasible point
can be chosen rational and cleared to an integer certificate. The
functional $y_\ell=\log\ell$ that excluded nonnegative combination
coefficients does not satisfy this dual obstruction: it makes
$y\mathbin\cdot e_j=\rho_j$ strictly increasing.

For a prescribed integer target $(q,p)$, the whole finite intersection
is a rational linear program in the prefix variables. Put $S_{n-1}=0$,
$d_j=p_j/16^j$, and impose
\[
 S_k\ge0,\qquad S_M=q,
\]
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(e_k-e_{k+1})+q e_M=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(d_k-d_{k+1})+q d_M=p.
\]
The weighted primitive cost to minimize, for a primitive target, is
\[
 \sum_{j=n}^M\frac{\mathcal U_j}{16^j}|S_j-S_{j-1}|.
\]
Absolute values are linearized in the usual way. These constraints
simultaneously enforce exact log cancellation, the prescribed integer
target, strict final nonvanishing when feasible and nonzero, and the
actual weighted cost. The remaining infinite problem is to produce
primitive targets with such feasible lifts and costs tending to zero.

\subsection{Why ordinary pigeonhole collisions do not ensure comparability}

Define $x\preceq y$ when every weighted prefix sum of $y-x$ is
nonnegative. On any fixed log fiber, a nontrivial comparable pair must
have strictly different gamma coordinates, by
Theorem~\ref{s6--thm:cumulative-cone}. Consequently every joint fiber of
the log map and the gamma-coordinate map is an antichain. The same is
true, a fortiori, for fibers of the full formal coefficient map.

This gives a precise obstruction to simply adding an order condition
to the elementary collision count. For the reverse-budget window
$M-n=\lceil25n/\log n\rceil$ and grid height $H=2^n$, let
$\beta=(16399/1296)^2$. The row-specific bounds used in the
reverse-budget construction show that some full formal-coordinate
fiber of $\{0,\ldots,H\}^{M-n+1}$ contains at least
\[
 \exp\left((\eta+o(1))\frac{n^2}{\log n}\right)
 \quad\hbox{points},\qquad
 \eta=22\log2-3\log\beta>0.
\]
Indeed the grid logarithmic cardinality is
$(25\log2+o(1))n^2/\log n$; the prime-log image count contributes at
most $(3\log\beta+3\log2+o(1))n^2/\log n$; and the gamma and
denominator-cleared rational rows each contribute only $O(n)$.
All points in that large fiber form an antichain. Thus the already
proved small-input collision count does not supply the missing
comparable pair. A stronger order-sensitive estimate or a direct
construction would still be needed.


\section{A cost bound with no linear-horizon restriction}
\label{s6--sec:horizon-free-cost}

Retain the proper kernels, their rational bounds $\mathcal U_j$, and the
normalized logarithmic values $\rho_j$ defined above.
Write
\[
 r_j=\mathcal U_j/16^j,\qquad \alpha=16/729,\qquad
 T_j=2+\tfrac32H_{j-1},\qquad
 \Delta_j=\rho_{j+1}-\rho_j.
\]
The established estimates are $r_{j+1}\le\alpha r_j$,
$\Delta_j>1/(66j)$, and $0<\rho_j<T_j$.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted variation removes the horizon factor]
\label{s6--thm:horizon-free-cost}
Let a nonzero real vector $c$ on $[n,M]$ be exactly log-null and
have nonnegative weighted prefixes
$S_k=\sum_{j=n}^{k}16^jc_j$. Put $q=S_M>0$ and
$C(c)=\sum_{j=n}^{M}\mathcal U_j|c_j|$. Then
\[
 \boxed{\frac{C(c)}q<r_M+\frac{66\cdot745}{729}\,nT_Mr_n.}
\]
In particular, uniformly for all integers $M\ge n\ge2$ for which
such a vector exists,
\[
 C(c)=O\!\left(q\,729^{-n}\frac{\log(M+1)}{\sqrt n}\right),
\]
with an absolute implied constant.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $S_{n-1}=0$. The weighted total variation satisfies
\begin{align*}
 C(c)&=\sum_{j=n}^{M}r_j|S_j-S_{j-1}|\\
 &\le q r_M+\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(r_k+r_{k+1}).
\end{align*}
Moreover $kr_k$ is decreasing, since
$((k+1)/k)\alpha\le2\alpha<1$. Thus for $k\ge n$,
\[
 \frac{r_k+r_{k+1}}{\Delta_k}
 <66k(1+\alpha)r_k\le66n(1+\alpha)r_n.
\]
The exact summation-by-parts identity from logarithm cancellation is
$\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k\Delta_k=q\rho_M$.
Its right side is positive. Multiplying the last strict bound by
$S_k\Delta_k$ and summing therefore gives
\[
 C(c)<q r_M+66n(1+\alpha)r_nq\rho_M
 <q r_M+66n(1+\alpha)r_nqT_M.
\]
Finally $r_M\le r_n$,
$T_M=O(\log(M+1))$, and
$r_n\sim(\sqrt{2\pi}/12)n^{-3/2}729^{-n}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A larger admissible support horizon]
Suppose for unbounded $n$ there are rational vectors as above with
primitive integer outputs $(q_n,p_n)$ and
\[
 q_n\log(M_n+1)=o(729^n\sqrt n).
\]
Then $0<q_n\gamma-p_n<C(c^{(n)})\to0$, and hence $\gamma$ is
irrational. In particular, the conditions $q_n\le729^n$ and
$\log(M_n+1)=o(\sqrt n)$ suffice; the earlier restriction
$M_n\le An$ is not needed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{s6--thm:horizon-free-cost} and cumulative positivity.
If $\gamma=a/b$, the positive integers $a q_n-b p_n$ would tend to
zero. The complete denominator clearing and primitive gcd reduction
are exactly those described in Section~\ref{unified:scope}.
\end{proof}

This is a stronger conditional completion criterion. It does not
assert an infinite supply of the required primitive outputs.
For example, a horizon as large as
$M_n\le\exp(\sqrt n/\log n)$ is permitted with $q_n\le729^n$.

\begin{proposition}[The logarithmic horizon factor in a real relaxation]
Fix $n\ge1$ and relax separate prime-log cancellation to the single
real equation $\sum_jc_jL_j=0$, allowing real coefficients.
For every $M\ge n+2$ there is a cumulative-positive vector on
$[n,M]$ with $q=1$ and exact cost
\[
 C=r_M+\frac{\rho_M}{\Delta_n}(r_n+r_{n+1}).
\]
For fixed $n$ this cost is $\Theta_n(\log M)$ as $M\to\infty$.
Thus no bound independent of $M$ can hold on this relaxation.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Set $S_n=\rho_M/\Delta_n$, set all intervening prefixes to zero,
and set $S_M=1$. The only nonzero coefficients are
\[
 c_n=\frac{\rho_M}{16^n\Delta_n},\qquad
 c_{n+1}=-\frac{\rho_M}{16^{n+1}\Delta_n},\qquad
 c_M=16^{-M}.
\]
Their aggregate log sum equals
$\rho_M(\rho_n-\rho_{n+1})/\Delta_n+\rho_M=0$.
Their weighted total variation is the displayed cost, and the
kernel is $S_n(f_n-f_{n+1})+f_M>0$.

Pairing all numerator factors of $f_M$ with the first $2M$
denominator factors gives $f_M(u)<1/(u+9M^2)$. Hence Frullani's
identity gives
\[
 2\rho_M>
 \int_0^\infty\left(\frac1{u+1}-\frac1{u+9M^2}\right)du
 =\log(9M^2).
\]
Together with $\rho_M<T_M=O(\log M)$, this proves the two-sided
order statement for fixed $n$.
\end{proof}

The three displayed coefficients are real; they are not asserted
to be rational or to cancel the individual prime-log coordinates.
This proposition establishes sharpness only for the stated relaxed
problem. It does not exclude a stronger bound that uses the separate
prime rows or the arithmetic of rational coefficients.



\subsection{A signed prefix budget with no linear restriction on the window}
\label{s6--signed-prefix:section}

Write
\[
 r_j=\frac{\mathcal U_j}{16^j},\quad \alpha=\frac{16}{729},\quad
 \rho_j=\frac{\sum_\ell E_{j,\ell}\log\ell}{16^j},\quad
 \Delta_j=\rho_{j+1}-\rho_j,\quad
 \mathcal H_j=2+\frac32H_{j-1}.
\]
The established exact estimates are
\[
 r_{j+1}\le\alpha r_j,\qquad
 \Delta_j>\frac1{66j},\qquad 0<\rho_j<\mathcal H_j.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Uniform cost for bounded negative prefixes]
\label{s6--signed-prefix:cost}
Let rational coefficients $c_n,\ldots,c_M$ satisfy exact prime-log
cancellation. Assume explicitly that
\[
 q=\sum_{j=n}^M16^jc_j>0.
\]
Let $\lambda\ge0$ and suppose
\[
 S_k=\sum_{j=n}^k16^jc_j\ge-\lambda q\qquad(n\le k\le M).
\]
Then, with $C(c)=\sum_{j=n}^M \mathcal U_j|c_j|$,
\[
 \boxed{
 \frac{C(c)}q
 <\lambda r_n+(1+\lambda)r_M
 +66n(1+\alpha)(1+\lambda)\mathcal H_M r_n.}
\]
Uniformly over $M\ge n$, $\lambda\ge0$, and all such lifts,
\[
 \boxed{
 C(c)=O\!\left(
 (1+\lambda)q\,729^{-n}
 \frac{\log(M+1)}{\sqrt n}\right).}
\]
The implied constant is absolute. Strict positivity of the integral
is not asserted in this signed-prefix theorem.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $S_{n-1}=0$ and $T_k=S_k+\lambda q$ for $n-1\le k\le M$.
Then all $T_k\ge0$, $T_{n-1}=\lambda q$, and
$T_M=(1+\lambda)q$. Exact log cancellation and summation by parts give
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k\Delta_k=q\rho_M.
\]
Consequently
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}T_k\Delta_k
 &=q\rho_M+\lambda q(\rho_M-\rho_n)\\
 &=q\bigl((1+\lambda)\rho_M-\lambda\rho_n\bigr)
 <(1+\lambda)q\mathcal H_M.
\end{align*}
The additive offset does not change successive differences. Hence
\begin{align*}
 C(c)
 &=\sum_{j=n}^{M}r_j|T_j-T_{j-1}|\\
 &\le r_nT_{n-1}+r_MT_M
       +\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}(r_k+r_{k+1})T_k.
\end{align*}
For $k\ge n$,
\[
 \frac{r_k+r_{k+1}}{\Delta_k}
 <66k(1+\alpha)r_k\le66n(1+\alpha)r_n,
\]
because
$(k+1)r_{k+1}/(kr_k)\le(1+1/k)\alpha\le2\alpha<1$.
Multiplying the preceding log-budget identity by this uniform bound
proves the asserted cost inequality. If an empty sum occurs, the
same strict bound follows directly from the positive final added term.

Finally $r_M\le r_n$, $\mathcal H_M=O(\log(M+1))$, and
\[
 r_n\sim\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}n^{-3/2}729^{-n}.
\]
Since $\lambda\le1+\lambda$, these estimates prove the uniform
asymptotic bound. No comparison $M=O(n)$ was used.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Joining the signed budget to determinant nonvanishing]
\label{s6--signed-prefix:pair-closure}
Suppose that for unbounded integers $n$ there are two rational
log-null lifts $c^{(1,n)},c^{(2,n)}$ on a common window $[n,M_n]$.
Suppose their primitive integer outputs $(q_{i,n},p_{i,n})$ satisfy
\[
 q_{i,n}>0,\qquad
 \det\begin{pmatrix}q_{1,n}&q_{2,n}\\p_{1,n}&p_{2,n}\end{pmatrix}\ne0,
\]
and their prefixes satisfy
$S_k(c^{(i,n)})\ge-\lambda_{i,n}q_{i,n}$ with
$\lambda_{i,n}\ge0$. If
\[
 \max_{i=1,2}
 \frac{(1+\lambda_{i,n})q_{i,n}\log(M_n+1)}
      {729^n\sqrt n}\longrightarrow0,
\]
then $\gamma$ is irrational.
In particular it is sufficient that
\[
 (1+\lambda_{i,n})q_{i,n}\le729^n\quad(i=1,2),
 \qquad \log(M_n+1)=o(\sqrt n).
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The theorem gives costs $C_{i,n}\to0$, and hence errors
$|q_{i,n}\gamma-p_{i,n}|<C_{i,n}$.
The nonzero determinant implies that the two linear forms have no
common real zero, so
\[
 0<W_n(\gamma):=
 (q_{1,n}\gamma-p_{1,n})^2+
 (q_{2,n}\gamma-p_{2,n})^2
 <C_{1,n}^2+C_{2,n}^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
If $\gamma=a/b$ with integers $a,b$ and $b>0$, then
$b^2W_n(\gamma)$ is a positive integer tending to zero, a contradiction.
Clearing a common denominator of each rational lift and then removing
the complete output gcd returns exactly its primitive target and cost.
No separate assumption $q_{i,n}\to\infty$ is needed for this paired
argument.
\end{proof}

For example, the sufficient window condition allows every fixed
polynomial horizon $M_n\le n^A$ and also
$M_n\le\exp(n^{1/3})$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
The corollary is a conditional completion statement. The simultaneous
infinite supply of such integer outputs and bounded negative prefixes
is not established here. Its improvement is that strict kernel
positivity and linearly bounded windows are no longer requirements
for this cost-and-nonvanishing route.





% New synthesis proved during the 2 November 2026 consolidation.
% No preamble and no project-specific macros are required.
% Uses theorem, lemma, corollary, proposition and proof environments.

\section{A sharp budget for negative prefixes}
\label{new--new-prefix:section}

The nonnegative-prefix condition can be relaxed by an exact rational
budget. The budget is sharp for the class specified only by lower
bounds on its prefixes. Sharpness here is not a statement about the
smaller class satisfying prime-log cancellation. Its useful consequence
for that smaller class is unconditional positivity of every admitted
kernel, including the boundary of the budget.

For integers $j\ge1$ and $u>0$, set
\[
 R_j(u)=\frac{\prod_{h=0}^{2j-1}(4u+h^2)}
               {\prod_{h=j}^{3j}(u+h^2)},\qquad
 f_j(u)=16^{-j}R_j(u).
\]
Fix integers $1\le n<M$. Given real coefficients $c_n,\ldots,c_M$,
write
\[
 S_{n-1}=0,\qquad S_k=\sum_{j=n}^k16^jc_j,\qquad q=S_M,
 \qquad K_c(u)=\sum_{j=n}^Mc_jR_j(u).
\]
Summation by parts gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:abel}
 K_c(u)=\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k\bigl(f_k(u)-f_{k+1}(u)\bigr)+qf_M(u).
\end{equation}
Conversely, arbitrary values of the prefixes and of $q=S_M$ are
realized uniquely by $c_j=(S_j-S_{j-1})/16^j$.

\begin{lemma}[Initial slopes and monotone gap ratios]
\label{new--new-prefix:slopes}
The positive rational numbers
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:aj}
 a_j:=\lim_{u\downarrow0}\frac{f_j(u)}u
 =\frac{1}{16^j j^4\binom{3j}{j}^{\!2}}
\end{equation}
satisfy $0<a_{j+1}<a_j/729$. The functions
\[
 \vartheta_j(u):=\frac{f_{j+1}(u)}{f_j(u)}
 =\frac{(u+j^2)^2\bigl(u+(j+\tfrac12)^2\bigr)}
 {(u+(3j+1)^2)(u+(3j+2)^2)(u+(3j+3)^2)}
\]
are strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, have values in $(0,1)$,
and tend to $1$ at infinity. For $n\le k<M$, the functions
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:gk}
 g_{k,M}(u):=\frac{f_k(u)-f_{k+1}(u)}{f_M(u)}
 =\bigl(\vartheta_k(u)^{-1}-1\bigr)
    \prod_{\ell=k+1}^{M-1}\vartheta_\ell(u)^{-1}
\end{equation}
are strictly decreasing, with limits
\[
 g_{k,M}(0+)=\frac{a_k-a_{k+1}}{a_M},\qquad
 g_{k,M}(+\infty)=0.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The single zero factor $4u$ in the numerator of $R_j$ gives
\[
 a_j=\frac{4((2j-1)!)^2((j-1)!)^2}
 {16^j((3j)!)^2}
 =\frac{((2j)!)^2(j!)^2}{16^j j^4((3j)!)^2},
\]
which is \eqref{new--new-prefix:aj}. Cancellation of the common factors
of $R_{j+1}/R_j$ gives the displayed quotient $\vartheta_j$.
Pair its numerator factors with its denominator factors in the
displayed order. Each ratio has the form $(u+A)/(u+B)$ with
$0<A<B$, so it is positive, less than one, and strictly increasing.
Their product has the same properties and tends to one.
At zero,
\[
 \frac{a_{j+1}}{a_j}=\vartheta_j(0)
 =\frac1{729}
 \left(\frac{j}{j+\tfrac13}\right)^2
 \left(\frac{j}{j+\tfrac23}\right)^2
 \left(\frac{j+\tfrac12}{j+1}\right)^2
 <\frac1{729}.
\]
In \eqref{new--new-prefix:gk}, the first factor is positive and strictly
decreasing, and all remaining factors are positive and decreasing.
The product is therefore strictly decreasing. Its limits follow
from \eqref{new--new-prefix:aj} and $\vartheta_j(u)\to1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp nonuniform prefix budget]
\label{new--new-prefix:sharp}
Fix real numbers $\lambda_k\ge0$ for $n\le k<M$. The following
statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every real coefficient vector with $q>0$ and
$S_k\ge-q\lambda_k$ for $n\le k<M$ satisfies
$K_c(u)>0$ for every $u>0$.
\item The rationally weighted budget satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:budget}
 \boxed{\ \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}\lambda_k(a_k-a_{k+1})\le a_M.\ }
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
The equivalence remains true if ``every real coefficient vector''
is replaced by ``every rational coefficient vector''.

If the budget is exceeded, the extremal real prefix vector
$S_k=-q\lambda_k$ has a kernel that is negative near zero and
positive for sufficiently large $u$, with exactly one zero on
$(0,\infty)$. No prime-log cancellation is imposed in this
sharpness assertion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $T_k=S_k+q\lambda_k\ge0$. Equation~\eqref{new--new-prefix:abel}
becomes
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:baseline}
 K_c(u)=\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}T_k(f_k-f_{k+1})
 +qf_M(u)\left(1-\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}\lambda_k g_{k,M}(u)\right).
\end{equation}
Every term in the first sum is nonnegative. If some $\lambda_k$ is
positive, Lemma~\ref{new--new-prefix:slopes} gives, for every $u>0$,
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}\lambda_k g_{k,M}(u)
 <\frac{\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}\lambda_k(a_k-a_{k+1})}{a_M}\le1.
\]
If all $\lambda_k$ vanish, the same sum is zero. Thus the last
term in \eqref{new--new-prefix:baseline} is strictly positive even when
\eqref{new--new-prefix:budget} is an equality. This proves sufficiency.

If the budget is exceeded, take $T_k=0$ for every $k<M$.
Then the parenthesized sum in \eqref{new--new-prefix:baseline} is
$1-G(u)$, where $G$ is continuous and strictly decreasing from a
value greater than one to zero. There is exactly one point with
$G(u)=1$, and the claimed signs follow. These prefixes give a real
coefficient vector by the inverse formula preceding the lemma.
When the $\lambda_k$ are rational, choose $q=1$ to get a rational
counterexample directly. For arbitrary real $\lambda_k$, choose
rational numbers $0\le\lambda'_k\le\lambda_k$ sufficiently close
from below that their weighted budget still exceeds $a_M$.
The extremal prefixes $S_k=-\lambda'_k$, $q=1$, then give a rational
counterexample in the original prefix class. This proves necessity
also for that class.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact uniform tolerance]
\label{new--new-prefix:uniform}
Put
\[
 \kappa_{n,M}=\frac{a_M}{a_n}
 =16^{n-M}\left(\frac nM\right)^4
 \left(\frac{\binom{3n}{n}}{\binom{3M}{M}}\right)^2\in(0,1).
\]
For $\lambda\ge0$, every coefficient vector with $q>0$ and
$S_k\ge-\lambda q$ has a strictly positive kernel on $(0,\infty)$
if and only if
\[
 \boxed{\ 0\le\lambda\le
 \frac{\kappa_{n,M}}{1-\kappa_{n,M}}.\ }
\]
At equality positivity remains strict. The same statement holds
for real or rational coefficient vectors, without imposing
prime-log cancellation.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $\lambda_k=\lambda$ in Theorem~\ref{new--new-prefix:sharp} and use
$\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})=a_n-a_M$.
Equivalently, the extremal kernel is
$q((1+\lambda)f_M-\lambda f_n)$ and
$f_M(u)/f_n(u)>a_M/a_n$ for $u>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A certificate for an individual coefficient vector]
\label{new--new-prefix:negative-part}
Let $(x)_+=\max(x,0)$. If $q>0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:actual-budget}
 \boxed{\ \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})(-S_k)_+\le q a_M,\ }
\end{equation}
then $K_c(u)>0$ for all $u>0$. Every such vector also satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:universal-offset}
 S_k>-q/728\qquad(n\le k<M).
\end{equation}
Condition~\eqref{new--new-prefix:actual-budget} is sufficient for an
individual kernel; it is not asserted to be necessary for its
positivity.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{new--new-prefix:sharp} with
$\lambda_k=(-S_k)_+/q$. Moreover, each summand in the budget is
nonnegative, so
\[
 \frac{(-S_k)_+}{q}
 \le\frac{a_M}{a_k-a_{k+1}}
 \le\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k-a_{k+1}}
 <\frac{1/729}{1-1/729}=\frac1{728}.
\]
This proves \eqref{new--new-prefix:universal-offset}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The complete budget is a compact rational interval problem}

We now impose exact prime-log cancellation. Retain the established
linear forms
\[
 I_j=\int_0^\infty R_j(u)\,d\mu(u)
 =16^j\gamma-p_j+\sum_\ell E_{j,\ell}\log\ell,
 \qquad d\mu(u)=\frac{du}{e^{2\pi\sqrt u}-1},
\]
where $p_j,E_{j,\ell}$ are rational and only primes $\ell\le3M$
need be retained on this window. Define
\[
 e_j=(E_{j,\ell}/16^j)_\ell,\quad
 \bar p_j=p_j/16^j,\quad
 \rho_j=\sum_\ell e_{j,\ell}\log\ell,\quad
 \Delta_j=\rho_{j+1}-\rho_j>0.
\]
The strict positivity of $\Delta_j$ is the established logarithmic
ordering property of these kernels. For a normalized prefix vector
$S_M=1$, put
\[
 t(S)=\bar p_M+
       \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(\bar p_k-\bar p_{k+1}).
\]

\begin{theorem}[A rational interval for all admissible negative budgets]
\label{new--new-prefix:polytope}
The set
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal B_{n,M}=\biggl\{(S,\lambda):\;&
 \lambda_k\ge0,\quad S_k+\lambda_k\ge0\quad(n\le k<M),\\
 &\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})\lambda_k\le a_M,\\
 &\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(e_k-e_{k+1})=-e_M\biggr\}
\end{align*}
is either empty or a compact rational polytope. Its projection onto
the $S$ coordinates is exactly the set of normalized log-null
prefix vectors satisfying \eqref{new--new-prefix:actual-budget} with
$q=1$. If it is nonempty, its output image under $t(S)$ is a closed
rational interval $[A_{n,M},B_{n,M}]$, possibly a singleton, and
\[
 B_{n,M}<\gamma.
\]
Every rational point of this interval has a rational feasible lift.
Consequently, for relatively prime integers $q>0,p$, a rational
log-null lift with output $(q,p)$ satisfying
\eqref{new--new-prefix:actual-budget} exists if and only if
$p/q\in[A_{n,M},B_{n,M}]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All defining equations and inequalities have rational coefficients.
The existence of nonnegative $\lambda_k$ with
$\lambda_k\ge(-S_k)_+$ and the displayed budget is equivalent to
the negative-part budget itself; for the reverse direction choose
$\lambda_k=(-S_k)_+$. This proves the projection statement.

Because $a_k-a_{k+1}>0$, the budget bounds each $\lambda_k$.
Taking the scalar product of the prime-row equation with
$(\log\ell)_\ell$ gives
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k\Delta_k=\rho_M.
\]
For $T_k=S_k+\lambda_k\ge0$ this becomes
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}T_k\Delta_k
 =\rho_M+\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}\lambda_k\Delta_k.
\]
The right side is bounded on the already bounded set of possible
$\lambda$, and every $\Delta_k$ is strictly positive. Thus each
$T_k$, and hence each $S_k$, is bounded. Closedness proves
compactness.

A nonempty bounded rational polyhedron has rational vertices.
Linear projection onto one coordinate is a compact interval with
rational endpoints, attained at rational feasible points.
For every feasible point, Corollary~\ref{new--new-prefix:negative-part}
gives
\[
 \gamma-t(S)=\int_0^\infty K_c(u)\,d\mu(u)>0.
\]
The upper endpoint is attained, so its inequality is strict as well.
For any rational point of a nonsingleton image interval, rational
convex interpolation of rational endpoint lifts gives a rational
lift. A singleton already has a rational attaining lift.

Finally, multiply a normalized rational lift of $p/q$ by $q$ to
obtain the integer output $(q,p)$. Conversely, divide a lift of
$(q,p)$ by $q>0$ to obtain a normalized feasible point. Both the
prime-row equations and the negative-part budget are homogeneous
under this positive scaling.
\end{proof}

This polytope contains the nonnegative-prefix polytope, by taking
$\lambda=0$. It also contains every uniform-offset polytope whose
offset is at most the sharp value in
Corollary~\ref{new--new-prefix:uniform}. The usual exact
minimum-denominator calculation for a closed rational interval
therefore applies to this entire budget at once. When the old
nonnegative-prefix output interval is nondegenerate, its enlargement
can be made explicit without another linear optimization.

\begin{corollary}[Constructive strict enlargement of an output interval]
\label{new--new-prefix:strict-enlargement}
Suppose that the normalized nonnegative-prefix polytope on $[n,M]$
has a nondegenerate output interval $[A,B]$. Choose rational
nonnegative endpoint lifts $S^-,S^+$, with outputs $A,B$, and set
\[
 D_k=S_k^+-S_k^-,\qquad
 Z_+=\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})(D_k)_+,\qquad
 Z_-=\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})(-D_k)_+.
\]
Then $Z_+,Z_->0$, and the new weighted-budget output interval
contains the strictly larger rational interval
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:enlarged-interval}
 \boxed{\left[
 A-\frac{a_M}{Z_+}(B-A),\quad
 B+\frac{a_M}{Z_-}(B-A)
 \right].}
\end{equation}
Both displayed endpoints have explicit rational log-null lifts and
are strictly below $\gamma$. The least primitive denominator in
the new interval cannot exceed its value in the old interval.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Subtracting the prime-row equations for $S^+$ and $S^-$ gives a
homogeneous prime-row equation for $D$. In particular,
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}D_k\Delta_k=0.
\]
The difference of the outputs is $B-A>0$, so $D\ne0$.
As every $\Delta_k>0$, the vector $D$ has both positive and
negative coordinates. Hence $Z_+,Z_->0$.

Set $\varepsilon_+=a_M/Z_+$ and
$\varepsilon_-=a_M/Z_-$. The extrapolated prefixes
\[
 \widetilde S^-=S^- -\varepsilon_+D,\qquad
 \widetilde S^+=S^+ +\varepsilon_-D
\]
still satisfy the normalized prime-row equation. Nonnegativity of
$S^-$ and $S^+$ gives the componentwise bounds
\[
 (-\widetilde S_k^-)_+\le\varepsilon_+(D_k)_+,\qquad
 (-\widetilde S_k^+)_+\le\varepsilon_-(-D_k)_+.
\]
Their weighted negative masses are at most $a_M$, so both are
feasible for the new polytope. Linearity of the output map gives
the endpoints in \eqref{new--new-prefix:enlarged-interval}; positivity
and the strict inequalities below $\gamma$ follow from
Theorem~\ref{new--new-prefix:polytope}. Convexity supplies every point
between them. The denominator assertion follows from containment;
strict enlargement alone does not imply a strict decrease in the
minimum denominator.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A conditional completion using one output at each index}

Write $\mathcal U_j$ for the established rational bounds $0<I_j<\mathcal U_j$ and
$C(c)=\sum_{j=n}^M \mathcal U_j|c_j|$. The signed-prefix estimate gives
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:cost-input}
 C(c)=O\!\left((1+\lambda)q\,729^{-n}
       \frac{\log(M+1)}{\sqrt n}\right)
\end{equation}
for every rational log-null vector with $q>0$ and
$S_k\ge-\lambda q$, uniformly in $M\ge n$, $\lambda\ge0$, and
the chosen lift. This is the earlier signed cost estimate, with
an absolute implied constant.

\begin{corollary}[Single-output completion under the sharp budget]
\label{new--new-prefix:single-output}
Suppose that for unbounded integers $n$ there are integers $M_n>n$
and rational log-null lifts $c^{(n)}$ on $[n,M_n]$ with integer
outputs
\[
 q_n=\sum_{j=n}^{M_n}16^jc_j^{(n)}>0,\qquad
 p_n=\sum_{j=n}^{M_n}p_jc_j^{(n)}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Suppose their prefixes satisfy
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M_n-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})(-S_k^{(n)})_+
 \le q_n a_{M_n},
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{new--new-prefix:height-condition}
 \frac{q_n\log(M_n+1)}{729^n\sqrt n}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Then $\gamma$ is irrational. It is sufficient, for example, to have
$q_n\le729^n$ and $\log(M_n+1)=o(\sqrt n)$.
No second output, determinant condition, or separate assumption
$q_n\to\infty$ is needed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{new--new-prefix:negative-part} gives a strictly positive
kernel and $S_k^{(n)}>-q_n/728$. Apply
\eqref{new--new-prefix:cost-input} with the fixed value $\lambda=1/728$.
Exact prime-log cancellation and the strict integral bound give
\[
 0<q_n\gamma-p_n<C(c^{(n)})
 =O\!\left(q_n729^{-n}\frac{\log(M_n+1)}{\sqrt n}\right)
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
If $\gamma=a/b$ with integers $a,b$ and $b>0$, then
$b(q_n\gamma-p_n)=aq_n-bp_n$ would be a positive integer tending
to zero, which is impossible.
\end{proof}

For primitive targets the rational-input formulation already accounts
for clearing denominators and removing the complete output gcd:
if $D$ clears a rational lift of a coprime pair $(q,p)$, its output
is $(Dq,Dp)$ and the complete gcd is $D$. Dividing the form and its
cost by $D$ restores exactly the target and cost used above.

\paragraph{Scope and provenance.}
The ratio calculations, the exact negative-prefix budget, its sharp
endpoint, and its use with the signed cost bound are proved here.
Summation by parts, monotonicity of products of positive functions,
and rational-polytope projection are classical ingredients.
No claim of historical priority for a general principle is made.
Theorem~\ref{new--new-prefix:sharp} settles positivity for its specified
prefix class; it does not produce log-null vectors in that class.
Corollary~\ref{new--new-prefix:single-output} leaves explicit the
unproved existence of integer outputs obeying its conditions at
unbounded indices. It is not a proof of the irrationality of
$\gamma$.


% Independently derived exact sanity example for new-prefix:sharp.
\begin{example}[The first nontrivial window and its sharp boundary]
For $n=1$, $M=2$, the initial slopes are
\[
 a_1=\frac1{144},\qquad a_2=\frac1{921600},\qquad
 \kappa_{1,2}=\frac1{6400}.
\]
Thus the exact uniform tolerance is $\lambda_*=1/6399$.
At its boundary, take $q=1$, $S_1=-1/6399$, $S_2=1$.
The unique coefficients are
\[
 c_1=-\frac1{102384},\qquad c_2=\frac{25}{6399}.
\]
Direct simplification gives
\[
 K_c(u)=\frac{6400f_2(u)-f_1(u)}{6399}
 =\frac{u^2(4u+1)(6399u^2+27123u+33324)}
 {25596\prod_{r=1}^{6}(u+r^2)}>0\qquad(u>0).
\]
The leading order at zero has changed from $u$ to $u^2$, with
\[
 \lim_{u\downarrow0}\frac{K_c(u)}{u^2}
 =\frac{2777}{1105747200}>0.
\]
For a general uniform offset $\lambda$, the extremal kernel is
$(1+\lambda)f_2-\lambda f_1$ and
\[
 \lim_{u\downarrow0}\frac{(1+\lambda)f_2(u)-\lambda f_1(u)}u
 =\frac{1-6399\lambda}{921600}.
\]
It is therefore negative near zero whenever $\lambda>1/6399$.
This example checks strict positivity at the budget boundary and the
sharp failure immediately beyond it. It does not satisfy prime-log
cancellation: $E_{1,5}=0$, $E_{2,5}=-2600$, so its coefficient of
$\log5$ is $-65000/6399\ne0$.
\end{example}


\section{An exact affine correction joins primitive arithmetic and nonvanishing}
\label{s5--join:affine-section}

For a finite rational coefficient vector $c$ define
\[
 Ec=\left(\sum_jc_jE_{j,\ell}\right)_\ell,\qquad
 \Psi(c)=\left(\sum_j16^jc_j,\sum_jp_jc_j\right),\qquad
 C(c)=\sum_j\mathcal U_j|c_j|.
\]
If $Ec=0$ and $\Psi(c)=(q,p)$, then
\[
 \sum_jc_jI_j=q\gamma-p,\qquad
 |q\gamma-p|\le C(c).
\]
All vectors below may be padded with zeros, so their sums and common
supports are unambiguous.

\begin{lemma}[A fixed exact correction of cost less than four]
\label{s5--join:fixed-correction}
There is a rational vector $d_0$ supported on $1,\ldots,17$ with
\[
 Ed_0=0,\qquad \Psi(d_0)=(0,1),\qquad B_0:=C(d_0)<4.
\]
The vector is uniquely specified by
\[
 d_0=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  V_{17}\\(16^j)_{j=1}^{17}\\(p_j)_{j=1}^{17}
 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\\vdots\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The displayed matrix is the nonsingular rational $17$-by-$17$
augmented matrix whose nonsingularity is certified by the exact elimination below. Thus the vector
is defined and has the required formal output.
The standard-library verifier
\texttt{verify\_affine\_completion.py} regenerates every matrix entry
from the residue and harmonic-number formulas, solves the displayed
system by exact rational elimination, checks all seventeen equations,
and checks the strict rational bounds
\[
 \frac{3775898}{10^6}<C(d_0)<\frac{3775899}{10^6}<4.
\]
No numerical value of $\gamma$ or of a logarithm is used. The
qualitative correction theorem below only needs the finite constant
$B_0$; the additional inequality $B_0<4$ is this explicit finite
arithmetic certificate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Primitive completion with exact cost and error bounds]
\label{s5--join:primitive-completion}
Suppose $c$ is rational, $Ec=0$, and
\[
 \Psi(c)=(q,p)\in\mathbb Z^2,\qquad q>0,\qquad \gcd(q,p)=1.
\]
Put $\varepsilon=C(c)$ and $e=q\gamma-p$.
Choose integers $r,s$ satisfying
\[
 qs-pr=1,\qquad |r|\le q/2.
\]
Such a choice exists by Bezout's identity and reduction modulo $q$.
The explicit rational vector
\[
 \boxed{c'=\frac rq\,c+\frac1q\,d_0}
\]
has
\[
 Ec'=0,\qquad \Psi(c')=(r,s),\qquad
 \det\begin{pmatrix}q&r\\p&s\end{pmatrix}=1.
\]
Its weighted cost and its evaluated error satisfy the distinct bounds
\[
 \boxed{C(c')\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{B_0}{q}
                <\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac4q,}
\]
\[
 \boxed{e':=r\gamma-s=\frac rq\,e-\frac1q,\qquad
        |e'|\le\frac{|e|}{2}+\frac1q.}
\]
The correction has support contained in the support of $c$ together
with $1,\ldots,17$. Both output pairs are primitive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $q>1$, take the centered representative
$r\equiv-p^{-1}\pmod q$, and set $s=(1+pr)/q$.
For $q=1$, take $(r,s)=(0,1)$.
Linearity gives
\[
 \Psi(c')=\frac rq(q,p)+\frac1q(0,1)
          =\left(r,\frac{rp+1}{q}\right)=(r,s),
\]
and $Ec'=0$.  The cost bound is the weighted triangle inequality.
Evaluation at $\gamma$ gives the displayed identity for $e'$,
because the evaluated value of $d_0$ is $-1$.
The determinant is one, which also proves primitiveness of $(r,s)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Clearing coefficients introduces no hidden primitive cost]
\label{s5--join:primitive-clearing}
If a rational log-null lift $h$ has primitive integer output
$(a,b)$, and a positive integer $g$ clears its coefficient
denominators, then $u=gh$ is integral,
\[
 \Psi(u)=g(a,b),\qquad
 \gcd(|\Psi(u)_1|,|\Psi(u)_2|)=g,\qquad C(u)/g=C(h).
\]
Thus Theorem~\ref{s5--join:primitive-completion} bounds the actual cost
after the complete output gcd has been removed. It does not assume
that the rational coefficient denominators may be ignored.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Linearity gives the output identity, and $\gcd(a,b)=1$ gives the
exact gcd. Positive homogeneity gives the cost identity.
If a further common normalization makes the entire output map
integral, it multiplies both the cost and the exact output gcd by
the same factor and cancels in the same way.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A general transverse-anchor correction]
\label{s5--join:transverse-anchor}
In place of $d_0$, let $d$ be any rational log-null vector with
output $w$ and cost $B$.  Let $c$ have primitive integer output $u$,
and assume $\Delta=\det(u,w)\ne0$.
There is an explicit rational log-null lift $h$ of an integer vector
$v$ with
\[
 \det(u,v)=1,\qquad
 C(h)\le\frac{C(c)}2+\frac{B}{|\Delta|}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose any integer $v_0$ with $\det(u,v_0)=1$.
Since $\det(u,w/\Delta)=1$, there is a rational $t$ with
$w/\Delta=v_0+tu$. Choose an integer $k$ with $|k-t|\le1/2$.
Then
\[
 h=d/\Delta+(k-t)c,\qquad
 v=v_0+ku
\]
have the claimed output, determinant, and cost.
\end{proof}

\section{One compatible primitive family is enough}
\label{s5--join:family-section}

\begin{theorem}[All five conditions from one primitive family]
\label{s5--join:family-gluing}
Suppose a sequence of rational log-null lifts $c_m$ has primitive
integer outputs $(q_m,p_m)$ with
\[
 q_m>0,\qquad q_m\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 \varepsilon_m:=C(c_m)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{s5--join:primitive-completion} separately at every
index and write the complementary output as $(r_m,s_m)$.
The resulting integer polynomials
\[
 W_m(X)=(q_mX-p_m)^2+(r_mX-s_m)^2
\]
have discriminant exactly $-4$ and satisfy
\[
 W_m(X)>0\quad\text{for every real }X,
\]
\[
 0<W_m(\gamma)\le
 \varepsilon_m^2+
 \left(\frac{\varepsilon_m}{2}+\frac1{q_m}\right)^2
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
All logarithms cancel exactly, both linear outputs have primitive
integer coefficients, and the polynomial degree is the fixed number
two. If $\gamma=a/b$ were rational, the numbers
$b^2W_m(\gamma)$ would be positive integers tending to zero.
Thus the stated hypotheses imply irrationality.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The determinant of the two output columns is one. They therefore
cannot vanish at the same real argument, proving the strict
positivity of the sum of squares. Equivalently, its discriminant is
$-4(q_ms_m-p_mr_m)^2=-4$, and its minimum on the real line is
$1/(q_m^2+r_m^2)>0$. The error estimate follows from
the separate evaluation bounds in
Theorem~\ref{s5--join:primitive-completion}. Under a rationality
assumption the common integerizing factor is the fixed number $b^2$.
The preceding lemma verifies that coefficient clearing and removal
of the complete output gcd cause no unrecorded loss in the cost.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A positive primitive family makes denominator growth automatic]
\label{s5--join:positive-family}
Suppose the $c_m$ in Theorem~\ref{s5--join:family-gluing} instead satisfy
\[
 q_m>0,\qquad C(c_m)\to0,\qquad
 \sum_jc_{m,j}I_j>0,
\]
where the last inequality is proved by an exact kernel certificate.
Then $q_m\to\infty$, so the same conclusion follows.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $q_m\le H$ on infinitely many indices, then
$0<q_m\gamma-p_m<1$ eventually on those indices.
Only finitely many integer pairs $(q_m,p_m)$ are possible.
Their strictly positive errors form a finite set and hence have a
positive minimum, contradicting convergence of those errors to zero.
This holds for every fixed $H$, proving $q_m\to\infty$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A divisibility escape is an alternative joining condition]
\label{s5--join:valuation-escape}
Suppose rational log-null lifts $h_m$ have integer outputs
$(Q_m,P_m)$, satisfy $C(h_m)\to0$, and obey
\[
 2^{t_m}\mid Q_m,\qquad
 P_m\ne0,\qquad v_2(P_m)\le t_m-a_m,\qquad a_m\to\infty.
\]
Here $0\le a_m\le t_m$ are integers and the valuation inequality is an exact
arithmetic condition, not a sign or size test on $\gamma$.
For all sufficiently large $m$, $Q_m\ne0$, and the primitive output
denominator satisfies
\[
 q_m=\frac{|Q_m|}{\gcd(|Q_m|,|P_m|)}\ge2^{a_m}.
\]
After primitive normalization and orientation, the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{s5--join:family-gluing} hold.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $Q_m=0$, then the evaluated error is the nonzero integer $-P_m$,
whose absolute value is at least one. This contradicts
$|Q_m\gamma-P_m|\le C(h_m)\to0$ for large $m$.
For nonzero $Q_m$, the two-adic valuation of the primitive denominator
is
\[
 v_2(q_m)=
 \max\{v_2(Q_m)-v_2(P_m),0\}\ge a_m.
\]
Dividing the input by the complete output gcd and changing its sign
if necessary cannot increase its cost. The preceding theorem applies.
\end{proof}


For a concrete reverse-design box, put
\[
 M_n=n+\left\lceil\frac{25n}{\log n}\right\rceil,\qquad
 |c_k|\le2^n\quad(0\le k\le M_n-n),\qquad c_k\in\Z.
\]
For every vector in this box the fully cleared cost satisfies
\[
 D_{M_n}\sum_k \mathcal U_{n+k}|c_k|
 \le\frac{729}{473}D_{M_n}2^n\mathcal U_n
 =\exp\{-\varepsilon n+o(n)\}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad \varepsilon=\log(729/32)-3>0.
\]
Indeed $M_n=n+o(n)$ and the prime number theorem
\cite{dlmf-primes} gives $\log D_{M_n}=3n+o(n)$, while the
factorial expression for $\mathcal U_n$ gives
$\log \mathcal U_n=-\log(729/16)n+O(\log n)$.
If the input is log-null, its integer gamma coordinate is
$Q_n=D_{M_n}16^n\sum_k16^kc_k$.
Thus one may take $t_n=4n+v_2(D_{M_n})$ in the preceding
corollary. Finding an exactly log-null vector in this box with
\[
 P_n\not\equiv0\pmod {2^{\,t_n-a_n+1}},
 \qquad a_n\to\infty,
\]
would supply the divisibility escape without changing the secured
denominator-cleared decay. No such infinite surviving family is
established here. This box estimate does not identify which inputs
have exact log cancellation, nonzero outputs, or positive kernels.

The cumulative-prefix criterion
\[
 \sum_{j\le k}16^jc_{m,j}\ge0\quad\text{for every prefix }k,
 \qquad c_m\ne0,
\]
together with exact log cancellation, supplies the strict positivity
and $q_m>0$ in Corollary~\ref{s5--join:positive-family} by the cumulative
cone theorem. The latter strict inequality uses more than prefix
nonnegativity: the normalized log values
$\rho_j=L_j/16^j$ increase strictly, and summation by parts gives
$0=\sum_{k<M}S_k(\rho_k-\rho_{k+1})+S_M\rho_M$.
If $S_M=q_m=0$ and the input is nonzero, this sum would be negative.
Thus the criterion can be checked using rational arithmetic, with
its implication justified by that structural theorem.
What remains to be proved is an infinite
supply of primitive integer targets with such lifts and costs tending
to zero. The existence of one finite certificate does not supply
that infinite family.

\paragraph{Compatibility and the scope of the correction.}
The matrices
$B_m=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}q_m&r_m\\p_m&s_m\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
lie in $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. Hence consecutive stages are
automatically related by the exact nonautonomous integral transfer
$B_{m+1}=B_m(B_m^{-1}B_{m+1})$, with
$B_m^{-1}B_{m+1}\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
This is compatibility of already constructed stages, not a uniform
bound on those transfer matrices or an algorithm for finding the next
cheap positive lift.

The correction uses rational coefficients and the fixed old block
$1,\ldots,17$, followed by exact primitive normalization.
It therefore does not assert the existence of two small-height
integer input vectors supported in the same thin moving block.
The previously proved raw-height obstruction for such pairs is
unaffected.

\section{Finite brackets and the fixed-output trap}
\label{s5--join:brackets-section}

\begin{proposition}[An exact adjacent rational bracket]
\label{s5--join:farey-bracket}
Suppose $q>1$, $\gcd(q,p)=1$, and an exact certificate gives
$0<e=q\gamma-p<1/q$.
Choose the uncentered solution $0<r<q$ of
$pr\equiv-1\pmod q$, and put $s=(1+pr)/q$.
Then
\[
 \frac pq<\gamma<\frac sr,\qquad
 \frac sr-\frac pq=\frac1{qr}.
\]
The corresponding proper-kernel lift is
$c'=(r/q)c+d_0/q$ and has cost at most
$C(c)+B_0/q$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The lower inequality is the assumed positive error. The exact
complementary error is $(re-1)/q<0$, since $r<q$ and $qe<1$.
Dividing by positive $r$ gives the upper inequality. The determinant
identity gives the interval width, and the triangle inequality gives
the cost.
\end{proof}

For the certified positive primitive target at $N=32$,
\[
 (q,p)=(200542096649,115756039658),\qquad
 C(c)<\frac1{530000000000},
\]
one has $qC(c)<1$. The uncentered complement is exactly
\[
 (r,s)=(176450949647,101850252223),
\]
while the centered complement is
$(-24091147002,-13905787435)$.
The standalone verifier checks both the determinant arithmetic and
the complete output-gcd normalization of the centered proper-kernel
lift. These are finite certificates; no infinite assertion follows
from their repetition or scaling.

\begin{proposition}[Why contraction in a fixed output fiber is insufficient]
\label{s5--join:fixed-fiber-trap}
If rational log-null lifts $h_m$ all have the same integer output
$v=(q,p)$ and $C(h_m)\to0$, then $q\gamma-p=0$.
Two independent fixed integer outputs cannot both have such lifts.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The same evaluated value satisfies
$|q\gamma-p|\le C(h_m)$ for every $m$ and hence is zero.
The kernel of the nonzero linear functional
$(q,p)\mapsto q\gamma-p$ is one-dimensional, so it cannot contain
two independent outputs.
\end{proof}

Thus a nested-fiber or compactness construction cannot obtain the
desired certificate merely by preserving one fixed formal output
while shrinking its cost. The primitive outputs must move, or strict
nonvanishing must be supplied by another condition. The affine
correction theorem makes that movement compatible with exact
integrality and determinant-one independence; it does not supply
the unresolved infinite cost decay in the positive cone.



\section{The entire finite output problem is a rational interval problem}
\label{s6--sec:cone-interval}

For fixed integers $1\le n<M$ put
$e_j=(E_{j,\ell}/16^j)_\ell$ and $\bar p_j=p_j/16^j$.
Let $\mathcal P_{n,M}$ be the normalized prefix polytope
\[
 \left\{(S_n,\ldots,S_{M-1}):\ S_k\ge0,\quad
 \sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(e_k-e_{k+1})=-e_M\right\},
 \qquad S_M=1.
\]
Define its output coordinate
\[
 t(S)=\bar p_M+\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}S_k(\bar p_k-\bar p_{k+1}).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Exact interval reduction, including boundary points]
\label{s6--thm:interval-reduction}
Either $\mathcal P_{n,M}$ is empty or it is a compact rational
polytope. In the latter case its output image is a closed rational
interval $[a_{n,M},b_{n,M}]$, possibly a singleton, and
$b_{n,M}<\gamma$. For relatively prime integers $q>0,p$, the
following assertions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is a rational log-null lift on $[n,M]$ with all prefixes
nonnegative and output $(q,p)$.
\item $p/q\in[a_{n,M},b_{n,M}]$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the least possible primitive denominator is exactly the
least denominator of a rational in this closed interval.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The prefix bound already proved gives
$0\le S_k<66MT_M$ throughout this rational polyhedron; it is
therefore bounded and closed, hence compact. Linear projection to
one real coordinate gives a compact interval. A bounded nonempty
rational polyhedron has rational vertices, so both extrema are
rational and have rational attaining prefix vectors $S^-,S^+$.

Every normalized feasible vector has nonzero cumulative-positive
kernel and hence evaluated error $\gamma-t(S)>0$. The maximum is
attained, so $b_{n,M}<\gamma$, including the endpoint.

Normalize a lift of $(q,p)$ by $q$ to prove the first implication.
Conversely, for a rational $t=p/q$ in a nonsingleton interval, put
\[
 \lambda=\frac{t-a_{n,M}}{b_{n,M}-a_{n,M}},\qquad
 S=(1-\lambda)S^-+\lambda S^+.
\]
This is a rational feasible prefix vector. Multiplying its associated
coefficients $(S_j-S_{j-1})/16^j$ by $q$ gives the required lift.
For a singleton, use either rational attaining vector. No strict
interior assumption is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A short certificate of denominator minimality]
Suppose $[a,b]$ is contained strictly between Farey neighbors
$L=u/v<R=w/z$, where $v,z>0$ and $wv-uz=1$. If their mediant
\[
 t_*=(u+w)/(v+z)
\]
belongs to $[a,b]$, then $v+z$ is the least denominator of a
rational in $[a,b]$. The mediant is the unique such rational of
that denominator. Integer translations preserve this assertion.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a reduced rational $p/q$ strictly between $L$ and $R$, the
integers $r=wq-zp$ and $s=vp-uq$ are both positive. The determinant
identity gives $q=rv+sz\ge v+z$. Equality forces $r=s=1$,
giving the mediant. The general integer and singleton cases are
handled separately.
\end{proof}

Subtract $\lfloor a\rfloor$ first. If the interval contains an
integer, its minimum denominator is one. Otherwise the translated
interval lies strictly between zero and one. The accelerated
Stern--Brocot algorithm starts from $0/1,1/0$ and moves the left or right endpoint
by the largest integer multiple of the other that keeps the
bracket strictly outside the closed target interval. It stops at
the first mediant in the interval. Equivalently the jump on the
left is
\[
 k=\left\lceil\frac{av-u}{w-az}\right\rceil-1,
 \qquad (u,v)\leftarrow(u+kw,v+kz),
\]
and the right jump is the analogous formula with $b$.
The strict-bracket condition treats rational endpoints correctly.
A rational singleton is returned directly; an interval containing
an integer has least denominator one. Standard Stern--Brocot
termination also follows by retaining any fixed rational in the
interval: every skipped node is strictly outside, and a finite
path reaches that rational unless an earlier mediant already lies
inside. The final neighboring pair is a four-integer exact
minimality witness; no numerical gamma approximation is needed.

For a one-dimensional affine prefix fiber, two endpoint linear
programs are unnecessary. Exact elimination writes every solution
as $S=x+t z$. Nonnegativity gives the closed parameter interval
\[
 \max_{z_i>0}(-x_i/z_i)\le t\le
 \min_{z_i<0}(-x_i/z_i),
\]
provided every fixed coordinate with $z_i=0$ is nonnegative.
Projection of its two endpoints yields $[a,b]$ exactly. This is the
case in the finite moving-window certificates accompanying this note.

\paragraph{Scope and provenance.}
Compact-polytope projection and Farey denominator minimality are
classical. The point here is their exact use for this gamma-kernel
cone: a fixed-window mixed-integer search becomes two rational
linear optimizations and one rational-interval calculation. Neither
the reduction nor a finite list of successful intervals proves
that the required height inequality holds at unbounded indices.

\begin{proposition}[The signed-prefix interval is also compact]\label{s6--prop:offset-interval}
Fix rational $\lambda\ge0$ and replace $S_k\ge0$ in
$\mathcal P_{n,M}$ by $S_k\ge-\lambda$. The resulting rational
polyhedron is either empty or compact, and its output is a closed
rational interval with rational lifts of every rational point.
The inequality $b_{n,M}<\gamma$ is not asserted for this offset case.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $T_k=S_k+\lambda$. The exact identity used in
Theorem~\ref{s6--signed-prefix:cost} gives
$\sum_{k=n}^{M-1}T_k\Delta_k=(1+\lambda)\rho_M-\lambda\rho_n$.
Its summands are nonnegative and $\Delta_k>0$, so every $T_k$,
and hence every $S_k$, is bounded. Closedness and rationality give
compactness and rational endpoint lifts. Convex interpolation
proves the assertion for all intermediate rational outputs.
\end{proof}


\subsection{A determinant-one pair costs no extra denominator height in an interval}
\label{s6--sec:minimum-height-pairs}

\begin{theorem}[The two smallest denominator levels in a rational interval]
\label{s6--thm:second-denominator}
Let $I=[a,b]$ be a nondegenerate closed rational interval containing
no integer. Let $F=P/Q$ be its least-denominator rational, and let
$L=u/v<R=w/z$ be its final enclosing Farey neighbors, translated
back if necessary, so that
\[
 L<a\le F\le b<R,\qquad wv-uz=1,\qquad
 (P,Q)=(u+w,v+z),\qquad v,z>0.
\]
If $a<F$, define
\[
 k_- =\left\lceil\frac{av-u}{P-aQ}\right\rceil,
 \qquad F_- =\frac{u+k_-P}{v+k_-Q}.
\]
If $F<b$, define
\[
 k_+ =\left\lceil\frac{w-bz}{bQ-P}\right\rceil,
 \qquad F_+ =\frac{w+k_+P}{z+k_+Q}.
\]
At least one candidate is defined. Each defined candidate belongs
to $I$, is distinct from $F$, and has determinant of absolute value
one with $F$. The candidate of smaller denominator has the least
possible denominator among all rationals in $I\setminus\{F\}$.
Consequently the pair formed by $F$ and that candidate minimizes
the maximum denominator among all pairs of distinct rationals in $I$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The defining thresholds are strictly positive, so every $k_\pm\ge1$.
The left candidate lies strictly below $F$ and at least $a$ by the
ceiling inequality; the right one lies strictly above $F$ and at
most $b$. Closed endpoints are therefore included correctly.

Every reduced rational $p/q$ in $[a,F)$ lies strictly between the
Farey neighbors $L$ and $F$. It has the unique representation
\[
 (p,q)=r(u,v)+s(P,Q),\qquad r,s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]
The inequality $p/q\ge a$ implies
$s/r\ge(av-u)/(P-aQ)$. Hence $s\ge k_-$ and
$q=rv+sQ\ge v+k_-Q$, with equality attained by $r=1,s=k_-$.
The corresponding right-side argument uses the Farey neighbors
$F,R$ and gives $q\ge z+k_+Q$.
The determinants with $F$ are $\pm1$ because adding an integer
multiple of $F$ to either neighbor preserves that determinant.
This also proves that the candidate fractions are already reduced.

Any pair of distinct fractions in $I$ must contain a fraction other
than the unique minimum-denominator fraction $F$. Thus its largest
denominator is at least the smaller candidate denominator, and the
displayed pair attains this bound.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Integer and singleton cases.}
A singleton interval contains no pair of distinct fractions.
If an interval contains two integers, it contains two consecutive
integers; these give a determinant-one pair of maximum denominator one.
If it contains exactly one integer $m$, the candidates distinct from
$m$ of least denominator on its two sides are
\[
 m-\frac1{\lceil1/(m-a)\rceil}\quad(a<m),\qquad
 m+\frac1{\lceil1/(b-m)\rceil}\quad(m<b).
\]
For example, every reduced $p/q<m$ in $I$ has
$1/q\le m-p/q\le m-a$, proving the left denominator bound;
the other case is identical. Each candidate is adjacent to $m$.
Thus every nondegenerate rational interval admits an explicitly
computable determinant-one pair that minimizes the largest denominator
among all distinct rational pairs in that interval.

\begin{corollary}[No extra height cost for determinant nonvanishing]
Suppose a normalized rational prefix polytope has output interval $I$.
For an integer $B\ge1$, it has two primitive integer outputs of
positive denominators at most $B$ and nonzero determinant if and
only if it has such a pair with determinant of absolute value one.
The minimum possible value of the largest denominator is given by
the preceding interval algorithm.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Distinct rational output slopes are equivalent to nonzero output
determinant. Every rational point of the interval has a rational
lift by convex interpolation of rational endpoint lifts. Apply the
theorem and the explicitly handled integer cases, then scale each
normalized lift to its reduced integer target. Interchanging the
pair gives determinant positive one if desired.
\end{proof}

The corollary applies to the nonnegative-prefix polytope. It also
applies to its rational offset variant $S_k\ge-\lambda$ for any
rational $\lambda\ge0$, by Proposition~\ref{s6--prop:offset-interval}. It is a finite exact height statement and
does not itself bound the resulting height as the window moves.






\section{Extension schedules, failed shifts, and exact finite repairs}
\label{s5--sec:extension-chronology}
The prime-entry rank theorem in Part~\ref{part:kernels} supplies
the rank input for this schedule.
\subsection{A guaranteed schedule of genuine extension indices}
\label{s5--shift:schedule-section}

If $(3N-3,3N]$ contains a new prime, its row forces $c_N=0$ in every
log-null vector supported on $1,\ldots,N$.
Thus both the full quotient norm and the cumulative-positive feasible
cone are exactly unchanged at that step.

There are nevertheless unconditional free extension indices with
bounded gaps. For $N\ge12$, every $N\equiv2$ or $9\pmod {10}$ has no
new prime: the sole possible odd prime candidate is respectively
$3N-1$ or $3N-2$, and it is a multiple of five greater than five.
The other candidate is even, and $3N$ is composite.
The gaps between these guaranteed indices alternate between seven and
three. The exact kernel dimension therefore increases on an infinite
explicit schedule with gaps at most seven.

In particular the six indices $33,\ldots,38$ introduce respectively
$97,101,103,107,109,113$ and are exact plateaus.
Index $39$ is the first genuine new direction after $32$.
The next proposition tests that direction using a particular canonical
repair. It does not exclude a different, cost-controlled repair or
an optimized primitive lift at the same index. Kernel dimension growth
by itself gives no bound on primitive cost.

\section{A canonical shift preserves positivity but destroys the arithmetic budget}
\label{s5--shift:canonical-section}

Let $V_N$ be the integer prime-log matrix, and let $\mathcal P_N$
be its canonical pivot set: the first nine indices, followed by every
new-prime index. Write
$B_N=V_N[:,\mathcal P_N]$. The exact rank theorem makes $B_N$
invertible. If $\iota_N$ inserts pivot coordinates into the full
coefficient vector, define the rational projection
\[
 \mathcal R_N(z)=z-\iota_N B_N^{-1}V_Nz.
\]
It cancels every prime-log coefficient, fixes every vector already in
$\ker V_N$, and leaves all nonpivot coordinates of $z$ unchanged.
This gives one fully specified log-repair rule.

\begin{proposition}[Exact failure of the first available shifted repair]
\label{s5--shift:failure}
Let $c$ be the certified first primitive lift at $N=32$,
with output
$(200542096649,115756039658)$ and cost below
$1/530000000000$.
Shift its coefficients by seven indices:
$z_{j+7}=c_j$, with its first seven entries zero.
Form $\widetilde c=\mathcal R_{39}(z)$ and normalize its rational
output to a primitive integer output with positive first coordinate.
Call the resulting rational lift $c^*$.
Exact arithmetic gives
\[
 C(z)<10^{-23},\qquad C(\widetilde c)>10^{73},
 \qquad C(c^*)>10^{1088}.
\]
Every weighted prefix
$S_k^*=\sum_{j=1}^k16^jc_j^*$ is strictly positive, and
\[
 S_1^*>10^{1091}.
\]
In particular the repaired lift has a positive final kernel, but its
actual primitive evaluated error satisfies
\[
 \boxed{\sum_jc_j^*I_j>10^{1084}.}
\]
The failure is therefore present in the evaluated arithmetic form,
not only in the chosen weighted upper bound.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The script \texttt{shift\_repair.py} regenerates $V_{39}$, its
canonical pivots, and all rational weights. It solves the repair
equations by reverse substitution on new-prime pivots and exact
elimination on the initial nine-by-nine block. It checks
$V_{39}\widetilde c=0$, computes the rational output and its complete
primitive normalization, and verifies all displayed rational
inequalities and all thirty-nine prefix signs. The exact data are in
\texttt{shift32\_to39\_certificate.json}. Neither the computation nor
the following lower bound evaluates $\gamma$ or a prime logarithm.

Put $f_j=16^{-j}R_j$. Finite summation by parts gives
\[
 \sum_jc_j^*R_j
 =\sum_{j=1}^{38}S_j^*(f_j-f_{j+1})+S_{39}^*f_{39}.
\]
Every term is positive. On $1\le u\le2$ one has
\[
 f_1(u)\ge\frac5{792}>\frac1{160},\qquad
 \frac{f_2(u)}{f_1(u)}
 \le\frac{153}{4\cdot17\cdot26\cdot37}<\frac12.
\]
Also $2\pi\sqrt2<9$ and $e<3$ imply
$d\mu/du>1/20000$ there. Hence
\[
 \int_1^2(f_1-f_2)\,d\mu
 >\frac1{320\cdot20000}>10^{-7}.
\]
The first Abel coefficient alone therefore gives a strict lower
