bound $S_1^*10^{-7}>10^{1084}$.
\end{proof}


\section{A certified arithmetic extension at dimension 39}
\label{s5--sec:pair39}
The failure of the canonical repair is specific to that repair rule.
At the same dimension, rational quotient optimization produces a much
smaller compatible pair. The following finite theorem needs only the
displayed witnesses and their exact checks, not a claim of global
optimality of the search procedure.

\begin{proposition}[An exact one-direction update]
Let $N\ge9$, let $M>N$ introduce no new prime, and suppose every
intervening index $N+1,\ldots,M-1$ introduces one. Let $h^{(M)}$
be the canonical log-null vector whose last coordinate is one and
whose other nonpivot coordinates are zero. Then
\[
 \ker_{\Q}V_M=(\ker_{\Q}V_N)\oplus\Q h^{(M)},
\]
where old vectors are padded with zeros. Every new lift has the unique
form $c=u+t h^{(M)}$ and exact cost
\[
 C_M(c)=\sum_{j=1}^N\mathcal U_j|u_j+t h_j^{(M)}|
       +|t|\sum_{j=N+1}^M\mathcal U_j|h_j^{(M)}|.
\]
The output coordinates and cumulative prefixes are affine functions
of $(u,t)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The invertible pivot submatrix defines $h^{(M)}$. Subtract
$c_Mh^{(M)}$ from any $c\in\ker V_M$. The result has last coordinate
zero; the intervening fresh-prime rows successively force its last
remaining coordinates to zero until its support is contained in
$1,\ldots,N$. Uniqueness follows from $h^{(M)}_M=1$.
The cost formula is its definition applied to that decomposition.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[An exact finite contraction]
There are rational log-null lifts $c^{(1)},c^{(2)}$ supported on
$1,\ldots,39$ with primitive integer outputs
\[
 (q_1,p_1)=(18585954467984,10728104066067),
\]
\[
 (q_2,p_2)=(3361033349029,1940041099316)
\]
such that
\[
 q_1p_2-q_2p_1=1,\qquad
 C(c^{(1)})<\frac1{7000000000000},\qquad
 C(c^{(2)})<\frac1{5600000000000}.
\]
Writing $e_i=q_i\gamma-p_i$, the polynomial
\[
 W_{39}(X)=(q_1X-p_1)^2+(q_2X-p_2)^2
\]
has integer coefficients and discriminant exactly $-4$. In particular
\[
 0<W_{39}(\gamma)
 <\frac1{7000000000000^2}+\frac1{5600000000000^2}.
\]
Both costs are less than one tenth of the cost of the positive
$N=32$ lift, and their maximum is less than one thirty-sixth of the
cost of the second primitive certificate previously constructed at $N=32$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The supplement supplies the exact rational vectors in
\path{pair39_witness.json} and a standalone checker
\path{verify_pair39.py}. The checker regenerates each residue from
its factorial formula, verifies every prime-log coordinate, both
outputs, primitiveness, the full output gcd after coefficient
clearing, and the displayed strict rational cost inequalities.
The rational comparisons with the prior $N=32$ data are also checked.
No value of $\gamma$ or of a prime logarithm is evaluated.

For any determinant-one pair the coefficients of $W$ are
$A=q_1^2+q_2^2$, $-2B=-2(q_1p_1+q_2p_2)$ and
$C=p_1^2+p_2^2$. The identity
\[
 AC-B^2=(q_1p_2-q_2p_1)^2=1
\]
gives discriminant $-4$ and the positive real minimum $1/A$.
The individual integral bounds give the estimate at $\gamma$.
\end{proof}

The exact costs are approximately $1.4211968134\cdot10^{-13}$ and
$1.7713337217\cdot10^{-13}$; these decimals are explanatory only.
The two particular optimized lifts have mixed prefix signs and do
not supply cumulative-prefix positivity certificates. Their
nonvanishing certificate is the determinant-one sum of squares.

This is one successful arithmetic extension after six exact
plateaus. Neither the decrease factor nor the existence of another
such decrease at every future extension index is inferred from it.
\section{An exact obstruction for the two new targets at index 39}
\label{s5--sec:cone39-exclusion}

The two unconstrained primitive quotient targets at $N=39$ are
\[
\begin{gathered}
 u_1=(q_1,p_1)=(18585954467984,10728104066067),
\\
 u_2=(q_2,p_2)=(3361033349029,1940041099316).
\end{gathered}
\]
They satisfy $q_1p_2-p_1q_2=1$. The first target has an exact log-null
lift with weighted cost less than $1/(7\cdot10^{12})$.
Neither target has a cumulative-positive lift on $[1,39]$.
The proof does not infer infeasibility merely from the signs of the
previously optimized lifts.

\begin{proposition}[A rational dual certificate for the first target]
There is no rational or real vector $c\in\mathbb R^{39}$ satisfying
\[
 V_{39}c=0,\qquad \Psi_{39}c=u_1,\qquad
 S_k(c)=\sum_{j=1}^k16^jc_j\ge0\quad(1\le k\le39).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The accompanying file \texttt{cone39\_exclusion\_certificate.json}
specifies primitive integer vectors $y\in\mathbb Z^{30}$ and
$w\in\mathbb Z^{39}$ and integers $\alpha>0$, $\beta<0$ such that
\[
 w_k\ge0,\qquad
 \{k:w_k>0\}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,10\},
\]
and the following is an identity of rational-linear forms in every
$c\in\mathbb R^{39}$:
\[
 \boxed{
 \sum_{k=1}^{39}w_kS_k(c)
   = y^T V_{39}c+\alpha Q(c)+\beta P(c).}
\]
It also certifies the strict integer inequality
$\alpha q_1+\beta p_1<0$.
The standalone standard-library verifier regenerates all residues from
their factorial formula and checks the displayed identity in all
39 coordinate columns, the nonnegative integer weights, the primitive
gcd, and the negative right side. Thus this is an exact rational Farkas
certificate. On a putative feasible lift the left side would be
nonnegative and the right side strictly negative, a contradiction.

For a direct reproducible definition of the certificate, put
$W=[V_{39};(16^j);(p_j)]$ and $B=W[:,8{:}39]$. Exact elimination
shows that this $32$ by $32$ matrix is invertible. Let $h_j=16^j$
for $8\le j\le10$ and $h_j=0$ for $11\le j\le39$; solve
$B^Tz=h$. If $r=z^TW$ and $r_{40}=0$, set
$\widetilde w_j=r_j/16^j-r_{j+1}/16^{j+1}$.
Clearing the common denominators of $(z,\widetilde w)$ and removing
their total gcd gives exactly $(y,\alpha,\beta,w)$ in the certificate.
The verifier checks the resulting identity directly and does not need
to trust the elimination that discovered it.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The second target has negative value]
The exact value $q_2\gamma-p_2$ is strictly negative. Consequently it
has no cumulative-positive lift at any index.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $e_i=q_i\gamma-p_i$. The determinant identity gives
\[
 q_2e_1-q_1e_2=1.
\]
The independently verified first lift proves
$|e_1|<1/(7\cdot10^{12})$. If $e_2\ge0$, then
\[
 1=q_2e_1-q_1e_2
 \le q_2|e_1|
 <\frac{3361033349029}{7000000000000}<1,
\]
a contradiction. Every nonzero cumulative-positive log-null lift has
strictly positive evaluated value, so none can represent $u_2$.
\end{proof}

The first obstruction concerns the specified cumulative-prefix cone
through index $39$; it does not exclude a different positivity
certificate for a resulting kernel, or a cumulative-positive lift of
$u_1$ after adding later indices. The second obstruction is an exact
sign statement for its oriented target. Neither result is inferred
from a numerical approximation to $\gamma$.

\section{Exact target transfer and rational repair}
\subsection{Separating integral target transfer from formal-zero repair}
\label{s6--transfer:normal-form-section}

Retain the proper-kernel maps $E,\Psi$ and weighted cost
$C(c)=\sum_j\mathcal U_j|c_j|$. All spaces and lifts below are over $\mathbb Q$.
Put
\[
 K_N=\ker E_N,\qquad Z_N=K_N\cap\ker\Psi_N.
\]
Here $K_N$ denotes a coefficient space, not the image of a cost ball.
Old coefficient vectors are padded with zeros when the index increases.

\begin{theorem}[An exact normal form for a one-direction extension]
\label{s6--transfer:normal-form}
Suppose $K_M=K_N\oplus\mathbb Qh$ and rational lifts $c_1,c_2\in K_N$
have output matrix
\[
 B=[\Psi(c_1)\ \Psi(c_2)]\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z).
\]
Set $\eta=B^{-1}\Psi(h)$ and
\[
 g=h-\eta_1c_1-\eta_2c_2.
\]
Then $Z_M=Z_N\oplus\mathbb Qg$. A pair $d_1,d_2\in K_M$ has
integer outputs of determinant one if and only if it has the form
\[
 \boxed{
 d_i=\sum_{j=1}^2c_jT_{ji}+z_i+t_i g\quad(i=1,2),
 \quad T\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z),\quad
 z_i\in Z_N,\quad t_i\in\mathbb Q.}
\]
For a given pair the matrix $T$, the two scalars $t_i$, and the two
vectors $z_i$ are unique.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The vector $g$ has zero formal output and the same nonzero class as
$h$ modulo $K_N$. For a vector $z\in Z_M$, write $z=x+th$ with
$x\in K_N$; then $z-tg\in K_N$ and has zero output, proving the
direct-sum identity. For a determinant-one integer output matrix $D$,
the matrix $T=B^{-1}D$ lies in $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
Subtracting the corresponding combinations of $c_1,c_2$ leaves two
vectors in $Z_M$, which have unique decompositions in its displayed
direct sum. The converse follows by applying $\Psi$.
\end{proof}

The theorem puts integrality entirely into $T$. The repair parameters
$t_i$ are rational and need not be integral because the repairs have
zero formal output. In particular, requiring every intermediate
output-changing correction to be integral is an additional restriction;
it is not a consequence of integrality of the final pair.

\begin{lemma}[Exact one-variable repair by a weighted median]
\label{s6--transfer:weighted-median}
Let $h\ne0$ be a rational vector and let all $\mathcal U_j>0$ be rational.
For fixed rational $c$, the minimum of $C(c+th)$ over real $t$ is
attained at a rational weighted median of
\[
 r_j=-c_j/h_j,\qquad w_j=\mathcal U_j|h_j|\quad(h_j\ne0).
\]
Define
\[
 A=\sum_{c_j\ne0}\mathcal U_jh_j\operatorname{sgn}(c_j),\qquad
 Z=\sum_{c_j=0}\mathcal U_j|h_j|.
\]
There is a strict cost decrease from $t=0$ if and only if $|A|>Z$.
When this holds, put $\sigma=-\operatorname{sgn}(A)$,
$\Delta=|A|-Z$, and
\[
 \tau=\min_{c_j\sigma h_j<0}|c_j/h_j|.
\]
Then $\tau$ exists, is positive and rational, and
\[
 \boxed{C(c+\sigma\tau h)=C(c)-\Delta\tau.}
\]
If $Eh=0$ and $\Psi(h)=0$, every such repair preserves all log
cancellations and the exact primitive target of $c$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The coordinates with $h_j=0$ contribute a constant, while the others
give $\sum_jw_j|t-r_j|$. Its minimizers are exactly its weighted
medians. A median can be chosen among the rational knots.
The left and right derivatives at zero are $A-Z$ and $A+Z$.
Convexity therefore gives strict improvement exactly when $|A|>Z$.
In the indicated direction the derivative is $-\Delta$ until the
first nonzero coordinate crosses zero. Such a crossing must exist:
otherwise every nonzero coordinate would have nonnegative derivative
in that direction, contradicting the strict negative total derivative.
Integrating the constant derivative through the first knot proves the
exact gain formula. The last assertion follows from linearity.
\end{proof}

This lemma supplies an exact finite descent step. For a fixed target
whose evaluated value $q\gamma-p$ is nonzero, the inequality
$C(c)\ge|q\gamma-p|$ prevents its cost from tending to zero.
For an arbitrary fixed target, such decay would force
$q\gamma-p=0$ and would not furnish a nonzero irrationality
certificate. Integral target transfer and the choice of repair
directions must be controlled together in an infinite argument.

\subsection{An arithmetic obstruction to a restricted shared-direction update}
\label{s6--transfer:shear-section}

\begin{theorem}[Classification and cost of integral shared-direction updates]
\label{s6--transfer:shear-classification}
Let $c_1,c_2$ have an integer determinant-one output matrix $B$ and
support in $1,\ldots,N$. Let $h$ be rational and log-null, with
primitive integer output $u=\Psi(h)$. Write
\[
 (a,b)^T=B^{-1}u\in\mathbb Z^2,
 \qquad \gcd(a,b)=1.
\]
The two lifts $c_i+t_ih$ have integer outputs of determinant one
if and only if, for an integer $k$,
\[
 (t_1,t_2)=k(b,-a).
\]
The resulting output transfer matrix is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}1+kab&-ka^2\\kb^2&1-kab\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If
\[
 T_{\mathrm{new}}(h)=\sum_{j>N}\mathcal U_j|h_j|,
\]
then every nonzero such update satisfies
\[
 \boxed{
 \max_i C(c_i+t_ih)
 \ge |k|\max(|a|,|b|)T_{\mathrm{new}}(h).}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $t_iu$ is integral and $u$ is primitive, Bezout's identity forces
$t_i$ to be an integer. Expansion of the output determinant gives
$1+at_1+bt_2$. Since $(a,b)$ is primitive, the integer solutions of
$at_1+bt_2=0$ are precisely $(t_1,t_2)=k(b,-a)$.
Multiplication by $B$ gives the displayed transfer matrix, whose
determinant is one. On coordinates beyond $N$, the old lifts vanish,
so their new cost contributions are exactly
$|t_i|T_{\mathrm{new}}(h)$. Dropping the remaining nonnegative terms
proves the lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A certified obstruction at the next extension]
\label{s6--transfer:shear40}
Use the determinant-one pair at $N=39$ and the canonical log-null
direction at $N=40$: its last coordinate is one, its earlier nonpivot
coordinates vanish, and its pivot coordinates are determined by
the prime-log equations. Normalize its output to a primitive integer
pair. Then every nonzero integral shared-direction update from
Theorem~\ref{s6--transfer:shear-classification} has
\[
 \max_i C(c_i+t_ih)>10^{595}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The file \path{rank_one_shear40_certificate.json} specifies the
direction and all rational quantities in the lower bound. The
standard-library script \path{verify_rank_one_shear.py} regenerates
the residues and canonical pivot solution, performs the exact primitive
normalization, and checks
\[
 \max(|a|,|b|)\mathcal U_{40}|h_{40}|>10^{595}.
\]
The preceding theorem applies to every nonzero integer $k$.
\end{proof}

This is a lower bound on the specified weighted cost, not a lower
bound on the actual absolute error. It excludes this restricted
primitive-direction update rule. It does not exclude rational
formal-zero repairs or the full normal form of
Theorem~\ref{s6--transfer:normal-form}.

\subsection{A new determinant-one pair at index 40}
\label{s6--transfer:pair40-section}

Write the preceding pair as
\[
 u_1=(18585954467984,10728104066067),\qquad
 u_2=(3361033349029,1940041099316),
\]
with $\det(u_1,u_2)=1$.

\begin{theorem}[An exact finite transfer with strict contraction]
\label{s6--transfer:pair40}
There are rational log-null lifts at index $40$ of the primitive
integer vectors
\[
 w=(1072041369684608,618799072004451),\qquad
 v=(21946987817013,12668145165383)
\]
whose costs satisfy
\[
 C_w<\frac1{289000000000000},\qquad
 C_v<\frac1{332000000000000}.
\]
Their exact transfer is
\[
 \boxed{[w\ v]=[u_1\ u_2]
 \begin{pmatrix}49&1\\48&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det(w,v)=1.}
\]
The maximum new cost is less than one fifty-first of the maximum
cost of the preceding supplied pair. In particular, if
$w=(q_w,p_w)$ and $v=(q_v,p_v)$, then
\[
 0<(q_w\gamma-p_w)^2+(q_v\gamma-p_v)^2
 <\frac1{289000000000000^2}+\frac1{332000000000000^2}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The exact vectors in \path{pair40_witness.json} are checked by
\path{verify_pair40.py}. The checker regenerates all residues and
weights, verifies every prime-log equation, both output coordinates,
and all strict rational cost bounds. It clears every input denominator
and verifies that the complete output gcd returns the displayed
primitive pair and the same cost. The previous reference lift is
also rechecked for the strict factor-$51$ comparison.
The transfer matrix has determinant one, so the sum-of-squares
polynomial has discriminant $-4$ and is strictly positive on
$\mathbb R$. Its upper bound follows from the integral estimates.
No value of $\gamma$ or of a logarithm is evaluated.
\end{proof}

The costs are approximately $3.4509735587\cdot10^{-15}$ and
$3.0083861504\cdot10^{-15}$; these decimals are not proof inputs.
The finite theorem uses the supplied witnesses and does not require
any global optimality assertion for the unrestricted cost problem.

\begin{corollary}[An exact sign transfer and an adjacent rational bracket]
\label{s6--transfer:sign-bracket}
The new second form is negative, and the previous first form is
positive:
\[
 q_v\gamma-p_v<0,
 \qquad18585954467984\gamma-10728104066067>0.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \boxed{
 \frac{10728104066067}{18585954467984}
 <\gamma<
 \frac{12668145165383}{21946987817013}.}
\]
The exact bracket width is
\[
 \frac1{407905716276403181959011792}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Put $e_w=q_w\gamma-p_w$, $e_v=q_v\gamma-p_v$, and
$e_1=q_1\gamma-p_1$ for the first preceding output.
The determinant identity gives $q_ve_w-q_we_v=1$.
If $e_v\ge0$, it would imply
$1\le q_v|e_w|<q_v/(289000000000000)<1$.
Thus $e_v<0$. Since $v=u_1+u_2$ and $\det(u_1,v)=1$,
\[
 q_ve_1-q_1e_v=1,
 \qquad
 e_1>\frac{1-q_1/(332000000000000)}{q_v}>0.
\]
The signs prove the bracket. Its cross determinant is one, so its
width is $1/(q_1q_v)$, equal to the displayed fraction.
\end{proof}

The previous first target therefore has positive actual value despite
its proved exclusion from the cumulative-prefix cone through index
$39$. This distinguishes scalar sign from that particular sufficient
kernel certificate. The transfer matrix and its cost decrease are
proved for this step only. No iteration with uniformly shrinking
cost is inferred, and the infinite-family requirement remains open.
\begin{proposition}[The new finite pair lies in this enlarged region]
\label{s6--signed-prefix:finite40}
The supplied index-$40$ pair $(w,v)$ has a common starting index $8$.

 S_k\ge-\frac{q_v}{800}\qquad(1\le k\le40).
\]

 q_w\le729^8,\qquad \frac{801}{800}q_v\le729^8.

\begin{proof}
The exact weighted prefixes and inequalities are checked from the

\end{proof}




\clearpage
\part{Columnwise budgets, binary arithmetic, and output classes}\label{part:columns}


\section{Clearing each column separately removes the terminal-index penalty}
\label{s6--sec:columnwise-budget}

The common denominator of an entire window need not be imposed on
every column before searching for integer coefficients. Put
\[
 d_j=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3j),\qquad
 J_j=d_jI_j,\qquad v_j=d_j\mathcal U_j,
 \qquad \delta=\log(729/16)-3>0.
\]
The factor-two denominator theorem (Section~\ref{s6--adic:section}) gives the exact integer expansion
\[
 J_j=a_j\gamma-b_j+\sum_\ell F_{j,\ell}\log\ell,
 \qquad
 a_j=d_j16^j,\quad b_j=d_jp_j,\quad
 F_{j,\ell}=d_jE_{j,\ell}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
For an integer vector $c$ of finite support define
\[
 \mathcal B(c)=\sum_jv_j|c_j|.
\]
This is the cost after these individual denominator clearings;
it is not an unnormalized integral estimate.

\begin{theorem}[A terminal-index-independent integer budget]
\label{s6--thm:columnwise-tail}
Fix $0\le\eta<\delta$. Uniformly over all finite terminal indices
$M\ge n$ and all integer vectors satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{supp}(c)\subseteq[n,M],\qquad
 |c_j|\le e^{\eta j},
\]
one has
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal B(c)\le
 \exp\{-(\delta-\eta)n+o(n)\}\longrightarrow0.}
\]
If $Fc=0$, the resulting form is exactly
$Q\gamma-P$ with $Q,P\in\mathbb Z$, and the same bound holds.
No claim that this form is nonzero is part of the theorem.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The prime number theorem \cite{dlmf-primes} gives $\log d_j=3j+o(j)$, and Stirling's
formula \cite{dlmf-stirling} gives $\log \mathcal U_j=-\log(729/16)j+O(\log j)$.
Thus $\log v_j=-\delta j+o(j)$. Define
\[
 \epsilon_n=\sup_{j\ge n}
 \frac{|\log v_j+\delta j|}{j},
\]
so $\epsilon_n\to0$. For large $n$, the ratio
$\exp(-\delta+\eta+\epsilon_n)$ is less than one. Hence
\[
 \mathcal B(c)\le
 \sum_{j=n}^\infty e^{-(\delta-\eta-\epsilon_n)j}
 =\frac{e^{-(\delta-\eta-\epsilon_n)n}}
 {1-e^{-(\delta-\eta-\epsilon_n)}}
 =e^{-(\delta-\eta)n+o(n)}.
\]
Every coefficient in the displayed expansion of $J_j$ is integral.
Exact prime-row cancellation therefore leaves $Q\gamma-P$, and
the triangle inequality gives its absolute-value bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Short exact cancellations on a doubling window]
\label{s6--thm:columnwise-counting}
For $n\ge2$ put
\[
 \mathfrak h_n=\left\lceil\exp\left(\frac{128n}{\log n}\right)\right\rceil.
\]
For every sufficiently large $n$ the individually cleared log matrix
on $[n,2n-1]$ has a nonzero integer kernel vector with
$\|c\|_\infty\le \mathfrak h_n$. Every such vector satisfies
\[
 \left|\sum_{j=n}^{2n-1}c_jJ_j\right|
 \le\mathcal B(c)\le e^{-\delta n+o(n)}.
\]
The same box also contains a nonzero vector for which both output
coordinates $Q$ and $P$ vanish exactly.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use Lemma~\ref{s6--reverse:residue-height}
\[
 2|A_{j,k}|\le6\beta^j,\qquad
 \beta=(16399/1296)^2,\qquad \beta^3<2^{22}.
\]
The matrix has $n$ columns and
$s_n=\pi(6n-3)=(6+o(1))n/\log n$ rows. Its entries have a common
integer bound $B_n$ satisfying
\[
 \log B_n\le2(3+\log\beta)n+o(n).
\]
Indeed the log coefficient is a sum of at most $2j+1$ residues
times valuations bounded by $\log_2(3j)$, followed by multiplication
by $d_j$. All polynomial factors contribute only $O(\log n)$.

For completeness, an integer matrix with $d$ columns, $s$ rows,
and row bounds $B_i\ge1$ has a nonzero integer kernel vector
of height at most $H$ whenever
\[
 H^{d-s}>\prod_{i=1}^s(3dB_i).
\]
The $(H+1)^d$ vectors in $\{0,\ldots,H\}^d$ have fewer than
$H^d$ possible images under this inequality; subtract two with
the same image.

For the present matrix the logarithms of the two sides have leading
coefficients $128$ and $12(3+\log\beta)$, respectively, on the scale
$n^2/\log n$. The second is strictly smaller, since
\[
 12(3+\log\beta)<36+88\log2<124<128.
\]
The counting condition therefore holds eventually.
Furthermore $\log \mathfrak h_n=o(n)$, so
\[
 \mathcal B(c)\le \mathfrak h_n\sum_{j=n}^{2n-1}v_j
 \le e^{-\delta n+o(n)}
\]
by the same tail argument as in Theorem~\ref{s6--thm:columnwise-tail}.

Append the two integer rows $(a_j)$ and $(b_j)$. Their entry
logarithms are $O(n)$ on this window. The two extra row factors
and the change from $d-s$ to $d-s-2$ alter the logarithmic counting
inequality by only $O(n)$, whereas its positive margin has order
$n^2/\log n$. Thus the same box contains a nonzero formal-zero vector.
\end{proof}

An integer-operation alternative is
\[
 \widehat{\mathfrak h}_n=2^{\left\lceil
 288n/\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor\right\rceil}.
\]
Its logarithm is asymptotic to
$288(\log2)^2 n/\log n$, whose coefficient exceeds $128$
because $\log2>2/3$. The same argument applies.

\begin{proposition}[What the change of normalization does and does not do]
\label{s6--prop:columnwise-normalization}
Let $D=d_M$, and suppose $z_n,\ldots,z_M$ are integers. Then
\[
 c_j=(D/d_j)z_j\in\mathbb Z
\]
represents the same form in the individually cleared system:
\[
 \sum_jc_jJ_j=D\sum_jz_jI_j,
 \qquad
 \mathcal B(c)=D\sum_j|z_j|\mathcal U_j.
\]
Thus changing the notation for a fixed form does not lower its cost.
It changes the admissible search space: individually cleared columns
permit integer coefficients without paying $D$ on every column.
In particular, an attainable odd constant output in the common-$D$
system remains attainable in the columnwise system, but its new input
height may be large.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $j\le M$ the least common multiple defining $d_j$ divides the
one defining $D$. Substitute the displayed integer $c_j$ and take
absolute values to obtain both identities.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A concrete parity-coset completion target]
\label{s6--cor:columnwise-odd-completion}
Suppose that for unbounded integers $n$ there are exactly log-null
integer inputs on $[n,2n-1]$ with height at most $\mathfrak h_n$ as above and
\[
 P_n=\sum_jd_jp_jc_j\quad\hbox{odd}.
\]
Then $\gamma$ is irrational. More generally it suffices that
$P_n\ne0$ and $4n-v_2(P_n)\to\infty$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The cost tends to zero, and $2^{4n}\mid Q_n$.
If $Q_n=0$, the error is the nonzero integer $-P_n$, which is
impossible for large $n$. Write $g_n=\gcd(|Q_n|,|P_n|)$.
The primitive positive denominator satisfies
\[
 v_2(|Q_n|/g_n)
 =\max\{v_2(Q_n)-v_2(P_n),0\}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
If $\gamma=a/b$ were rational, the integers
$aQ_n-bP_n$ would tend to zero and hence would vanish eventually.
The reduced denominator of $P_n/Q_n=\gamma$ would then be the
fixed denominator $b$, contradicting the proved unbounded binary
order. This argument also covers the odd-output special case.
\end{proof}

The short log-null vectors and the attainability of a particular
output congruence class are separate statements. The missing step is
a short representative of that class at unbounded starting indices.
The formal-zero vectors in the same height box make this compatibility
issue explicit.




\section{Binary arithmetic foundations and supercongruences}
\label{s6--app:binary-background}\label{s6--adic:section}

This section consolidates the binary arithmetic results proved in the
preceding research note \cite{previous}. They are included
with their proofs so that the present dyadic reflection and output
obstructions have no unproved internal arithmetic dependencies.
They are background results, not additional new claims of this paper.

Write $v=v_2$, with $v(2)=1$ and $v(0)=+\infty$.
For a rational number, membership in $\mathbb Z_2$ means that its
reduced denominator is odd. Polynomial congruences are coefficientwise.
Retain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R_n(u)&=\frac{\prod_{h=0}^{2n-1}(4u+h^2)}
 {\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(u+j^2)},\\
 p_n&=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}\left(H_j-\frac1{2j}\right),
 &E_{n,\ell}&=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}v_\ell(j).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $H_j=\sum_{k=1}^j1/k$ and $v_\ell(j)$ is the exponent of
$\ell$ in $j$.

\begin{lemma}[Residue formula, half-integrality, and total mass]
\label{s6--binary-bg:integrality}
The proper partial fractions of $R_n$ are
\[
 R_n(u)=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac{A_{n,j}}{u+j^2},
\]
\[
 A_{n,j}=(-1)^{j-n}
 \frac{4j^2(2j+2n-1)!(n+j-1)!}
 {(2j-2n)!(j-n)!(3n-j)!(3n+j)!}.
\]
Moreover $B_{n,j}:=2A_{n,j}$ is integral and
$\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}=16^n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The poles are distinct and the numerator degree is one less than the
denominator degree. Taking residues gives
\[
 A_{n,j}=\frac{\prod_{h=0}^{2n-1}(h^2-4j^2)}
 {\prod_{n\le k\le3n,\ k\ne j}(k^2-j^2)},
\]
and factoring each difference of squares gives the displayed
factorial formula. Put $a=j+n$, $b=j-n$, and
\[
 U=\binom{2a}{b},\quad V=\binom a{2b},\quad
 U'=\binom{2a-1}{b-1},\quad V'=\binom{a-1}{2b-1},
\]
with $U'=V'=0$ when $b=0$. Direct cancellation gives
\[
 B_{n,j}=(-1)^b\bigl(UV+4U'V+U'V'\bigr)
 =(-1)^bUV\left(\frac{2j}{a}\right)^2.
\]
The first expression proves integrality. Finally comparison of the
$u^{-1}$ coefficients at infinity, where
$R_n(u)=16^nu^{-1}+O(u^{-2})$, gives the total mass.
\end{proof}

We use the elementary factorial valuation identity
$v(m!)=\sum_{a\ge1}\lfloor m/2^a\rfloor=m-s_2(m)$,
where $s_2(m)$ is the number of ones in the binary expansion of $m$.
The first equality counts powers of two in each factorial factor;
the second follows by writing $m$ in binary. In particular the
valuation of a binomial coefficient is unchanged when both of its
arguments are multiplied by the same power of two.

\subsection{The exact common denominator and dyadic constant coefficient}

Put $L_m=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3m)$.
\begin{lemma}[Parity of the residue coefficients]
\label{s6--adic:residue-parity}
For $n\le j\le3n$, set $a=j+n$ and $b=j-n$. Then
\[
 B_{n,j}=(-1)^b
 \binom{2a}{b}\binom a{2b}\left(\frac{2j}{a}\right)^2.
\]
If $v_2(j)\ne v_2(n)$, then $4\mid B_{n,j}$. More precisely, if
$v_2(j)>v_2(n)$, then
\[
 v_2(B_{n,j})\ge2+2\bigl(v_2(j)-v_2(n)\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The displayed identity follows by cancellation of factorials in the
residue formula. The two binomial coefficients are integers. For
unequal valuations one has
$v_2(j+n)=\min(v_2(j),v_2(n))$. Hence the valuation of the squared
rational factor is
$2+2v_2(j)-2\min(v_2(j),v_2(n))$, which gives both claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A factor-two improvement in the common denominator]
\label{s6--adic:half-denominator}
For every $n\ge1$,
\[
 \boxed{2L_n p_n\in\mathbb Z.}
\]
Consequently $\widetilde D_M=2L_M$ simultaneously clears all
coefficients of $1$, $\gamma$, and the prime logarithms in $I_n$ for
$1\le n\le M$. 
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The defining expression gives
\[
 2L_np_n=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}L_nB_{n,j}H_j
             -\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac{L_nB_{n,j}}{2j}.
\]
Every term in the first sum is integral. Put
$a=\lfloor\log_2(3n)\rfloor=v_2(L_n)$. The integer $L_n/j$ is even
unless $v_2(j)=a$, in which case $j=2^a$ is the unique possibility.
Since $v_2(n)\le a-1$, Lemma~\ref{s6--adic:residue-parity} makes
$B_{n,2^a}$ even. Thus each term in the second sum is also integral.
For $n\le M$, $L_n$ divides $L_M$. Finally $2E_{n,\ell}$ is integral,
so $\widetilde D_ME_{n,\ell}$ is integral as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact constant-coefficient valuation at dyadic indices]
\label{s6--adic:dyadic-p}
For every integer $s\ge0$,
\[
 \boxed{v_2(p_{2^s})=-s-2.}
\]
In particular $\widetilde D_{2^s}p_{2^s}$ is odd. More generally, if
$n=2^s$ and $n\le M<4n/3$, then
$\widetilde D_Mp_n$ is odd, whereas
$v_2(\widetilde D_M16^n)=s+2+4n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $n=2^s$. The only $j\in[n,3n]$ with $v_2(j)=s$ are $j=n,3n$.
All other residue coefficients are even by
Lemma~\ref{s6--adic:residue-parity}. Moreover
\[
 B_{n,n}=1,\qquad B_{n,3n}=\frac94\binom{8n}{2n}
\]
are both odd. Indeed the elementary factorial identity
$v_2(k!)=k-s_2(k)$ gives
$v_2\binom{8n}{2n}=1+2-1=2$.

For $n\le j\le3n$, the $2$-adic integer $2^{s+1}H_j$ is even when
$j<2n$ and odd when $j\ge2n$: only the summand $1/(2n)$ can have
denominator with $2$-adic valuation $s+1$. Therefore
\[
 2^{s+1}\sum_{j=n}^{3n}B_{n,j}H_j\equiv1\pmod2.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 2^s\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac{B_{n,j}}j\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
To verify this, the endpoint terms are $B_{n,n}$ and $B_{n,3n}/3$,
both odd, so their sum is even. If $v_2(j)<s$, the remaining term
has valuation at least $s-v_2(j)+2>0$. The only $j$ with valuation
greater than $s$ is $j=2n$; there $16\mid B_{n,2n}$ and the term
has valuation at least three. Combining these two congruences in
\[
 2^{s+2}p_n
 =2^{s+1}\sum_jB_{n,j}H_j-2^s\sum_j\frac{B_{n,j}}j
\]
proves that the left side is odd. Finally $v_2(\widetilde D_M)=s+2$
when $n\le M<4n/3$, proving the remaining statements.
\end{proof}


\subsection{Residue valuations and binary dilation}

\begin{lemma}[A lower-order residue bound]
\label{s6--bin:low-order}
Put $t=v(n)$ and $u=v(j)$. If $u<t$, then
\[
 v(A_{n,j})\ge t-u+2.
\]
If $u>t$, then $v(A_{n,j})\ge1+2(u-t)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use
\[
 2A_{n,j}=(-1)^{j-n}
 \binom{2a}{b}\binom a{2b}\left(\frac{2j}{a}\right)^2,
 \qquad a=j+n,\quad b=j-n.
\]
The second assertion follows at once from $v(a)=t$ and integrality
of the binomial product. For the first assertion, divide $n,j,a,b$
by $2^u$. The valuations of both binomial coefficients are unchanged,
as follows from the factorial valuation formula. Thus assume that
$j$ is odd and $v(n)=h=t-u\ge1$. Then $a,b$ are odd and
$a\equiv b\pmod{2^{h+1}}$.

For $q=2^k$, $1\le k\le h+1$, write $a=Aq+r$, $b=Bq+r$, with
$0<r<q$. Direct substitution gives
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{2a}{q}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac a q\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac b q\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac{2a-b}{q}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac{2b}{q}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac{a-2b}{q}\right\rfloor=1.
\]
This is the contribution of level $k$ to the valuation of the
binomial product. Contributions at all other levels are nonnegative,
being the sum of two binomial carry counts. Hence that product has
valuation at least $h+1$. The squared factor has valuation two,
giving $v(2A_{n,j})\ge h+3$, as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The exact signed doubling identity]
\label{s6--bin:residue-doubling}
For $0\le k\le m$ put
\[
 T(m,k)=\frac{\binom{2m}{2k}}{\binom m k}
 =(-1)^k\prod_{r=1}^k\left(1-\frac{2m}{2r-1}\right).
\]
For $n\le j\le3n$, $a=j+n$, and $b=j-n$, one has
\[
 \frac{A_{2n,2j}}{A_{n,j}}=(-1)^bT(2a,b)T(a,2b).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Separating the odd and even factors in the factorial expressions
for the binomial ratio gives the displayed product for $T$.
In the binomial formula of Lemma~\ref{s6--adic:residue-parity},
simultaneous doubling of $n,j$ leaves $(2j/a)^2$ unchanged and
changes the sign by $(-1)^b$. The two remaining binomial ratios
are precisely $T(2a,b)$ and $T(a,2b)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Residues at a higher binary order]
\label{s6--parity:high-order}
If $v_2(j)>v_2(n)$, then
\[
 v_2(A_{n,j})\ge2+2\bigl(v_2(j)-v_2(n)\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the exact binomial formula for $2A_{n,j}$, divide $n,j$ by
$2^{v_2(n)}$. The binomial valuations are unchanged under this
simultaneous scaling. Now $n$ is odd and $j$ is even, so
$a=j+n$ and $b=j-n$ are odd. The binomial coefficient
$\binom{2a}{b}$ is even: this follows from
$\binom{2a}{b}=(2a/b)\binom{2a-1}{b-1}$.
The squared rational factor has valuation
$2+2(v_2(j)-v_2(n))$. Subtracting one for $A$ instead of $2A$
and adding the extra even binomial factor proves the claim.
\end{proof}


\subsection{A coefficientwise product congruence}

\begin{lemma}[A balanced odd-product polynomial]
\label{s6--super:polynomial}
For an integer $b\ge1$ define
\[
 \mathcal R_b(X)=
 \prod_{r=1}^{b}\left(1-\frac{4X}{2r-1}\right)
 \prod_{r=1}^{2b}\left(1-\frac{2X}{2r-1}\right).
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal R_b(X)-1
 \in2^{v_2(b)+2}X(X-b)\mathbb Z_2[X].}
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pair the consecutive factors in the second product. With $t=2r-1$,
the resulting factor is
\[
 F_r(X)=\left(1-\frac{4X}{t}\right)
 \left(1+\frac{4X(X-2t)}{4t^2-1}\right),
 \qquad \mathcal R_b=\prod_{r=1}^{b}F_r.
\]
Every denominator is odd, and $F_r\in1+4\mathbb Z_2[X]$.
More generally, if $t,t'$ are odd and $t\equiv t'\pmod{2^h}$,
the coefficients after dividing $F(X,t)-F(X,t')$ by four are
congruent to zero modulo $2^h$. Indeed those coefficients are rational
functions of $t$ with integral coefficients and denominators that are
units at odd $t$; subtracting two such values preserves the indicated
congruence. Thus for $h\ge1$,
\[
 F_{r+2^{h-1}}\equiv F_r\pmod{2^{h+2}}.
\]

Put $Q_h=\prod_{r=1}^{2^h}F_r$. The last congruence gives
\[
 Q_h\equiv Q_{h-1}^2\pmod{2^{h+2}}\qquad(h\ge1).
\]
Starting from $Q_0=F_1\equiv1\pmod4$, induction yields
$Q_h\equiv1\pmod{2^{h+2}}$. If $b=2^hm$ with $m$ odd, split
the product into $m$ consecutive blocks of length $2^h$.
The same coefficientwise periodicity makes every block congruent to
$Q_h$ modulo $2^{h+2}$. Hence
\[
 \mathcal R_b(X)-1\in2^{h+2}\mathbb Z_2[X].
\]

Finally $\mathcal R_b(0)=1$ and $\mathcal R_b(b)=1$ exactly.
For the second identity put $O_m=\prod_{r=1}^{m}(2r-1)$.
At $X=b$ the two products have values
$(-1)^bO_{2b}/O_b^2$ and $(-1)^bO_b^2/O_{2b}$, respectively.
The polynomial $(\mathcal R_b-1)/2^{h+2}$ therefore vanishes at
both $0$ and $b$. Division by the monic factors $X$ and $X-b$
preserves $\mathbb Z_2[X]$, proving the assertion. In the second
division the first quotient vanishes at $b$ because $b\ne0$ in
$\mathbb Q_2$; no assumption that $b$ is a unit is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A stronger residue supercongruence]
\label{s6--super:residues}
For every $n\ge1$ and $n\le j\le3n$,
\[
 \boxed{A_{2n,2j}-A_{n,j}
       \in2^{2v_2(n)+5}\mathbb Z_2.}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At $j=n$ the difference is zero. Otherwise put $a=j+n$, $b=j-n>0$.
The exact signed doubling identity gives
\[
 \frac{A_{2n,2j}}{A_{n,j}}=\mathcal R_b(a).
\]
The polynomial lemma therefore gives
\[
 v_2(A_{2n,2j}-A_{n,j})
 \ge v_2(A_{n,j})+v_2(a)+v_2(b)+v_2(n)+3.             \tag{S}
\]
Write $t=v_2(n)$ and $u=v_2(j)$. If $u<t$, then
$v_2(a)=v_2(b)=u$ and Lemma~\ref{s6--bin:low-order} gives
$v_2(A_{n,j})\ge t-u+2$. The right side of (S) is therefore at
least $2t+u+5\ge2t+5$.
If $u>t$, it is at least
$1+2(u-t)+2t+t+3=3t+4+2(u-t)\ge2t+5$.
If $u=t$, the sum and difference of the two odd integers
$j/2^t,n/2^t$ have valuations at least one and two in some order.
Thus $v_2(a)+v_2(b)\ge2t+3$. Since $v_2(A_{n,j})\ge-1$,
(S) is at least $3t+5\ge2t+5$.
\end{proof}



\begin{corollary}[Sharper log-coordinate congruences]
\label{s5--super:log-coordinates}
For every odd prime $\ell$ and every $n\ge1$,
\[
 E_{2n,\ell}-E_{n,\ell}\in2^{v_2(n)+3}\mathbb Z_2.
\]
For $n\ge2$,
\[
 E_{2n,2}-E_{n,2}\in2^{2v_2(n)+5}\mathbb Z_2.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \boxed{E_{2^s,2}\equiv-32\pmod{128}\qquad(s\ge1).}
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For odd $\ell$, the even new indices are controlled by the residue
theorem, while each odd new index has residue valuation at least
$v_2(n)+3$ by Lemma~\ref{s6--bin:low-order}.
For $\ell=2$, use the exact identity
\[
 E_{2n,2}-E_{n,2}
 =16^n+\sum_{j=n}^{3n}(A_{2n,2j}-A_{n,j})(v_2(j)+1).
\]
When $n\ge2$, one has $4n\ge2v_2(n)+5$, so every term has the
required valuation. Finally direct computation gives
$E_{2,2}=3808\equiv-32\pmod{128}$, and the proved difference is
divisible by $128$ at every subsequent dyadic step.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Scope.}
The congruences concern individual residue and prime-log columns.
They neither provide exact log cancellation nor an integer input in
a prescribed small box with a surviving constant coefficient.
The full parity distinction between powers of two and nonpowers is
proved separately in Theorem~\ref{s6--parity:complete-pattern}. Its
necessary integer-kernel congruence also does not supply a short
surviving affine representative.


\subsection{Exact moments and the complete log-two parity law}

\begin{lemma}[Exact even-moment denominators]
\label{s6--parity:moments}
For every integer $r\ge0$,
\[
 M_r(n):=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}j^{2r}
       \in16^n4^{-r}\mathbb Z.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At infinity the proper partial-fraction identity gives
\[
 R_n(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}(-1)^rM_r(n)u^{-r-1}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 R_n(u)=\frac{16^n}{u}
 \frac{\prod_{k=0}^{2n-1}(1+k^2/(4u))}
      {\prod_{j=n}^{3n}(1+j^2/u)}.
\]
The coefficient of $u^{-r}$ in the last quotient belongs to
$4^{-r}\mathbb Z$: numerator coefficients have those denominators,
and denominator reciprocals have integral coefficients. Comparison
proves the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The two base parity classes]
\label{s6--parity:base-classes}
If $n\ge3$ is odd, or if $n\ge6$ and $v_2(n)=1$, then
\[
 E_{n,2}\in64\mathbb Z_2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First let $n\ge3$ be odd and set
$f(X)=(X-1)(X-9)$. For odd $j$, one has
$v_2(f(j^2))\ge7$: both factors are divisible by eight, and their
difference is eight, so at least one is divisible by sixteen.
Since $v_2(A_{n,j})\ge-1$, the product vanishes modulo $64$.
For $v_2(j)=1$, one has $j^2\equiv4\pmod{16}$ and
$f(j^2)\equiv1\pmod{16}$, while
Lemma~\ref{s6--parity:high-order} gives $v_2(A_{n,j})\ge4$.
For $v_2(j)\ge2$, that lemma gives $v_2(A_{n,j})\ge6$.
These cases prove, term by term,
\[
 E_{n,2}\equiv\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}f(j^2)\pmod{64}.
\]
The polynomial has degree two with integer coefficients, so
Lemma~\ref{s6--parity:moments} makes the right side divisible by
$2^{4n-4}$, which is divisible by $64$ for $n\ge3$.

Now assume $v_2(n)=1$ and $n\ge6$. Put
\[
 g(X)=(X-4)(X-36),\qquad
 F(X)=-g(X)+\frac{(X-1)(X-9)g(X)}{16}.
\]
We verify
\[
 \sum_jA_{n,j}(v_2(j)-1)
 \equiv\sum_jA_{n,j}F(j^2)\pmod{64}                 \tag{P}
\]
term by term. If $j$ is odd, then $g(j^2)\equiv1\pmod8$ and
$v_2((j^2-1)(j^2-9))\ge7$, hence
$F(j^2)\equiv-1\pmod8$.
Lemma~\ref{s6--bin:low-order} gives $v_2(A_{n,j})\ge3$, as required.
If $v_2(j)=1$, write $j=2k$ with $k$ odd. Then
\[
 g(j^2)=16(k^2-1)(k^2-9),\qquad v_2(g(j^2))\ge11.
\]
It follows that $v_2(F(j^2))\ge7$, which is sufficient even when
$v_2(A_{n,j})=-1$.
If $v_2(j)=2$, write $j=4k$. Then
\[
 \frac{g(j^2)}{16}=(4k^2-1)(4k^2-9)\equiv1\pmod4,
 \qquad (j^2-1)(j^2-9)\equiv1\pmod4.
\]
Thus $F(j^2)\equiv1\pmod4$, and
$v_2(A_{n,j})\ge4$ proves the needed congruence.
Finally, if $v_2(j)\ge3$, then $v_2(A_{n,j})\ge6$ and
$F(j^2)\in\mathbb Z_2$, since $16\mid g(j^2)$ for even $j$.
This proves (P).

The difference between $E_{n,2}$ and the left side of (P) is
$\sum_jA_{n,j}=16^n$. The polynomial $F$ has degree four and its
coefficients belong to $\frac1{16}\mathbb Z$, so its moment sum
has valuation at least $4n-12\ge12$. Hence $E_{n,2}$ is divisible
by $64$, completing both cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The complete log-two parity pattern]
\label{s6--parity:complete-pattern}
The exact congruences are
\[
 E_{1,2}=-16,\qquad
 \boxed{
 E_{n,2}\equiv
 \begin{cases}
 32\pmod{64},&n=2^s,\ s\ge1,\\
 0\pmod{64},&n\ge2\text{ is not a power of two}.
 \end{cases}}
\]
In particular $E_{n,2}/32$ is an integer for every $n\ge2$, and
it is odd exactly at the powers of two.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The factorial residue formula gives $A_{1,2}=-16$, hence
$E_{1,2}=-16$. The dyadic assertion was proved in
Corollary~\ref{s5--super:log-coordinates}. For a nonpower, write
$n=2^tm$ with $m\ge3$ odd. If $t=0$, use the first base class.
If $t\ge1$, the second base class gives $E_{2m,2}\equiv0\pmod{64}$.
At each further doubling the previous index has valuation at least
one, so the proved difference has valuation at least
$2v_2(\text{previous index})+5\ge7$.
Induction proves the result. Each $E_{n,2}$ is already a half-integer
by its residue formula; the asserted $2$-adic divisibility therefore
gives ordinary integral divisibility by $32$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary congruence in the actual integer log kernel]
\label{s6--parity:integer-kernel}
Let $(c_n)$ be a finitely supported integer log-null vector with
support in $n\ge2$. Then
\[
 \boxed{\sum_{s\ge1}c_{2^s}\equiv0\pmod2.}
\]
Consequently, if its support is contained in $[2^s,M]$ with
$s\ge1$ and $M<2^{s+1}$, then $c_{2^s}$ is even. In this moving
block the normalized gamma coordinate
$\sum_{j=2^s}^{M}16^{j-2^s}c_j$ is also even.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The exact log-two equation is $\sum_nc_nE_{n,2}=0$.
Divide its integer row by $32$ and reduce modulo two using the
theorem. This is a necessary condition for every actual integer
kernel vector; it does not assume that every modular kernel vector
lifts to an integer one. The indicated interval contains exactly one
power of two. All later terms in its normalized gamma coordinate
are divisible by sixteen.
\end{proof}


\paragraph{Use in the present paper.}
The factor-two denominator theorem, the dyadic valuation of $p_n$,
and the complete log-two parity theorem above are the reproduced
inputs for Section~\ref{s6--nextadic:section}. That section adds the
thin-block reflection and constant-row parity results. Neither these
background statements nor their modular consequences supply a short
representative of a prescribed coset in the actual integer log kernel.





\section{A lacunary support cannot cancel the new prime rows}
\label{s5--sec:lacunary-support}
\begin{proposition}[A lacunary obstruction to exact cancellation]
Let $n_1<\cdots<n_r$ be positive integers with
$n_{i+1}\ge2n_i$. The corresponding prime-log columns are linearly
independent over $\Q$. In particular no nonzero finite exactly log-null
relation is supported entirely on powers of two.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $M=n_r$. For $M\ge2$, Bertrand's postulate \cite{erdos1932} applied to
$\lfloor3M/2\rfloor$ supplies a prime
$3M/2<\ell<3M$. Every previous pole index is at most
$3n_{r-1}\le3M/2$, so the earlier $\ell$-rows vanish.
In the last column the only pole index divisible by $\ell$ is
$j=\ell$, and its coefficient is $A_{M,\ell}\ne0$.
The last coefficient of an exactly log-null relation must therefore
vanish. Descending induction proves the claim, with the possible
singleton $M=1$ checked using $E_{1,2}=-16$.
\end{proof}

The distinction between congruence and exact cancellation can thus be
seen on a two-column example. Put $n=2^s$ with $s\ge1$. By the sharper
log-coordinate congruences,
\[
 V_{2n}(e_{2n}-e_n)\equiv0\pmod{2^{s+4}},
\]
where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard coordinate vector. Its input height
is one, and the modulus tends to infinity. Nevertheless the exact
prime-log kernel on these two columns is zero. Increasing congruence
precision alone cannot produce the exact log-null inputs required
in the irrationality construction.



\section{A dyadic reflection law and an obstruction to odd constant output}
\label{s6--nextadic:section}

Retain the proper-kernel residues $A_{n,j}$, put $B_{n,j}=2A_{n,j}$,
and write
\[
 p_n=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}\left(H_j-\frac1{2j}\right),
 \qquad E_{n,2}=\sum_{j=n}^{3n}A_{n,j}v_2(j).
\]
All congruences involving rational numbers below are in $\mathbb Z_2$.
The already proved residue identity is
\[
 B_{n,j}=(-1)^b\left\{
 \binom{2a}{b}\binom a{2b}
 +4\binom{2a-1}{b-1}\binom a{2b}
 +\binom{2a-1}{b-1}\binom{a-1}{2b-1}
 \right\}.
\]
Here $a=j+n$ and $b=j-n$.
Binomial coefficients with negative lower argument are zero.

\begin{lemma}[Two copies of a smaller residue row modulo two]
\label{s6--nextadic:reflection}
Let $N=2^s$ and $1\le k<N/3$. For $N+k\le j\le3(N+k)$,
\[
 B_{N+k,j}\equiv
 \begin{cases}
 B_{k,r}\pmod2,&j=N+r,\quad k\le r\le3k,\\
 B_{k,r}\pmod2,&j=3N-r,\quad k\le r\le3k,\\
 0\pmod2,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The two indicated ranges are disjoint and lie on opposite sides of $2N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We use two consequences of Lucas's theorem. For a power of two $L$,
\[
 \binom{qL+a}{b}\equiv\binom ab\pmod2
 \quad(0\le a,b<L),
\]
and
\[
 \binom{L-a}{L-b}\equiv\binom{b-1}{a-1}\pmod2
 \quad(1\le a,b\le L).
\]
For the second identity, both sides are zero if $a>b$; otherwise
replace the lower argument by $b-a$ and compare coefficients below
degree $L$ in $(1+X)^{L-a}\equiv(1+X)^{-a}\pmod{2,X^L}$.
The middle term with coefficient four in the residue identity can
be discarded throughout this proof.

First write $j=N+r<2N$, so $k\le r<N$.
Put $d=r+k$ and $h=r-k$. Then $a=2N+d$, $b=h$.
Removing the high binary digits in the four binomial factors gives,
in order,
\[
 \binom{2d}{h},\qquad \binom d{2h},\qquad
 \binom{2d-1}{h-1},\qquad \binom{d-1}{2h-1}.
\]
These are precisely the four factors for $B_{k,r}$.
If $r>3k$, both factors with lower argument $2h$ or $2h-1$ vanish,
so the residue is even.

Next write $j=3N-r$ with $1\le r\le N$.
If $r>k$, put again $d=r+k$, $h=r-k$; now
$a=4N-h$, $b=2N-d$. Digit removal followed by the complement identity
transforms the same four factors into
\[
 \binom{d-1}{2h-1},\qquad \binom{2d-1}{h-1},\qquad
 \binom d{2h},\qquad \binom{2d}{h}.
\]
Their two products give the same parity as $B_{k,r}$.
Again it is zero for $r>3k$. If $r=k$, the first two original
factors are even and the last two are odd, giving $B_{k,k}=1$.
If $r<k$, both factors with upper arguments $2a$ and $2a-1$ are
even: after removal of the $8N$ digit their upper arguments are
$2(k-r)$ and $2(k-r)-1$, smaller than the respective lower arguments
$2N-r-k$ and $2N-r-k-1$.

Finally write $j=3N+r$ with $0\le r\le3k$.
Here $a=4N+k+r$ and $b=2N+r-k$.
After removing the $8N$ digit from $2a$ and $2a-1$, both resulting
upper arguments are smaller than the respective lower arguments,
since $2N-3k-r\ge2N-6k>0$. Both products are even.
These cases cover the full pole interval. The separation follows from
$N+3k<2N<3N-3k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The constant row has the same thin-block parity as the log-two row]
\label{s6--nextadic:constant-parity}
Let $N=2^s$, and let $N\le n<4N/3$. Then
\[
 \boxed{
 2^{s+2}p_n\equiv
 \begin{cases}1\pmod2,&n=N,\\0\pmod2,&N<n<4N/3.
 \end{cases}}
\]
For $s\ge1$, this is equivalently
\[
 2^{s+2}p_n\equiv E_{n,2}/32\pmod2.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The half-denominator theorem ensures $2^{s+2}p_n\in\mathbb Z_2$.
For $j<4N$, the value $2^{s+1}H_j$ is congruent to zero when
$j<2N$ and to one when $j\ge2N$: among the harmonic denominators
only $2N$ has binary order $s+1$.
Moreover
\[
 2^s\sum_{j=n}^{3n}\frac{B_{n,j}}j\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
Indeed terms with $v_2(j)<s$ are even. At $j=2N$ the residue is
divisible by at least four, so division by two still leaves an even
term. The only other possible denominators of order at least $s$
are $j=N,3N$. If $n>N$, only $3N$ lies in the pole interval and its
residue is even because $v_2(n)<s=v_2(3N)$. If $n=N$, both endpoint
residues are odd and their two contributions cancel modulo two.
Thus
\[
 2^{s+2}p_n
 =2^{s+1}\sum_jB_{n,j}H_j-2^s\sum_jB_{n,j}/j
 \equiv\sum_{j\ge2N}B_{n,j}\pmod2.
\]
For $n=N$, the only odd residue in this tail is $B_{N,3N}$.
For $n=N+k$, $1\le k<N/3$, Lemma~\ref{s6--nextadic:reflection} gives
\[
 \sum_{j\ge2N}B_{N+k,j}
 \equiv\sum_{r=k}^{3k}B_{k,r}
 =2\cdot16^k\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
This proves the first assertion. The second follows from the complete
log-two parity theorem, since $N$ is the only power of two in this block.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Odd cleared constant output is impossible in the thin dyadic block]
\label{s6--nextadic:odd-output-obstruction}
Let $N=2^s$ with $s\ge1$, let $N\le M<4N/3$, and let integers
$c_N,\ldots,c_M$ cancel every prime-log coordinate exactly. Put
\[
 D=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3M),\qquad
 Q=D\sum_{n=N}^{M}16^nc_n,\qquad
 P=D\sum_{n=N}^{M}p_nc_n.
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{2\mid c_N,\qquad 2\mid P,\qquad 2^{s+3+4N}\mid Q.}
\]
Consequently the two raw integer outputs have a common factor two.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The exact log-two relation and its complete parity law give $c_N$ even.
Since $v_2(D)=s+2$, the quotient $D/2^{s+2}$ is odd.
Theorem~\ref{s6--nextadic:constant-parity} therefore gives
$P\equiv c_N\equiv0\pmod2$.
Finally
\[
 Q=D16^N\left(c_N+\sum_{n>N}16^{n-N}c_n\right)
\]
has the claimed divisibility.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The obstruction persists under individual column clearing]
In the same thin block, put $d_n=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3n)$.
Suppose integers $h_n$ cancel the individually cleared log rows,
$\sum_nh_nd_nE_{n,\ell}=0$ for every prime $\ell$.
For $Q=\sum_nh_nd_n16^n$ and $P=\sum_nh_nd_np_n$, one still has
\[
 2\mid h_N,\qquad 2\mid P,\qquad 2^{s+3+4N}\mid Q.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every $d_n$ in this block has binary order $s+2$; write
$d_n=2^{s+2}\eta_n$ with $\eta_n$ odd.
Divide the exact log-two equation by $2^{s+7}$.
Its coefficient $\eta_n E_{n,2}/32$ is odd exactly at $n=N$,
so $h_N$ is even. By the constant-row parity theorem,
$P\equiv\eta_Nh_N\equiv0\pmod2$.
Finally $Q/(2^{s+2}16^N)=\eta_Nh_N+
\sum_{n>N}16^{n-N}\eta_nh_n$ is even.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Scope.}
This is an all-index restriction on the actual integer log kernel;
it does not replace exact cancellation by congruence cancellation.
It excludes the previously tempting choice of an odd cleared constant
output in these blocks. It does not bound $v_2(P)$ from above, does not
exclude outputs with $v_2(P)=1$, and does not determine the complete
output gcd. In particular it does not provide a bounded-height surviving
family or an irrationality proof.


\section{An exact image invariant of an actual integer log kernel}
\label{s6--nextadic:true-image}

\begin{lemma}[Determinantal divisors measure the output image]
Let $A\in\mathbb Z^{r\times d}$ have row rank $r$, let
$T\in\mathbb Z^{k\times d}$, and suppose $[A;T]$ has row rank
$r+k$. Write $\delta_j(B)$ for the positive gcd of all $j$ by $j$
minors of $B$. Then the full-rank output lattice
\[
 \Lambda=T(\ker_{\mathbb Z}A)\subseteq\mathbb Z^k
\]
has index
\[
 \boxed{[\mathbb Z^k:\Lambda]=
 \frac{\delta_{r+k}([A;T])}{\delta_r(A)}.}
\]
For $k=1$ this index is the positive generator of the image ideal.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $A$ in integer Smith normal form using unimodular row and
column operations. Its nonzero diagonal entries are $a_1,\ldots,a_r$.
Apply the same column operations to $T$, and let $T_0$ denote its
last $d-r$ columns. Those columns generate the output lattice.
A nonzero $(r+k)$-minor of the augmented matrix must contain all
first $r$ columns, and equals $\pm(a_1\cdots a_r)$ times a
$k$-minor of $T_0$. Thus
$\delta_{r+k}([A;T])=\delta_r(A)\delta_k(T_0)$.
The last determinantal divisor is the index of its column lattice,
again by Smith normal form.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Finite simultaneous binary survival on a wider dyadic block]
Let the pole-index block be $256\le n\le511$, put
\[
 D=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,1533),\qquad
 \mathcal L=\left\{c\in\mathbb Z^{256}:
 \sum_{n=256}^{511}c_nE_{n,\ell}=0\text{ for every prime }\ell\right\},
\]
and define integer output maps
\[
 P(c)=D\sum_{n=256}^{511}p_nc_n,\qquad
 G(c)=\sum_{n=256}^{511}16^{n-256}c_n.
\]
The lattice $\mathcal L$ has rank $14$. Its two-coordinate image
has rank two and satisfies
\[
 \min_{P(c)\ne0}v_2(P(c))=0,
 \qquad
 \min_{G(c)\ne0}v_2(G(c))=4,
\]
and
\[
 v_2\bigl([\mathbb Z^2:(P,G)(\mathcal L)]\bigr)=4.
\]
In particular an actual integer log-null vector exists with
$P$ odd and $G\equiv16\pmod{32}$ simultaneously.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take $A=(2E_{n,\ell})$ with rows the $242$ primes at most $1533$.
The attached exact verifier regenerates the matrix from the factorial
residue formula and performs invertible Smith operations modulo
$2^{64}$. The following table records the ranks and the sums of the
binary orders of the nonzero Smith entries:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{rows}&\text{rank}&\sum v_2(\text{Smith entry})\\\hline
A&242&288\\
{[A;P]}&243&288\\
{[A;G]}&243&292\\
{[A;P;G]}&244&292.
\end{array}
\]
Every nonzero Smith entry in all four calculations has binary order
at most $11$, strictly below the modulus precision $64$; hence the
displayed ranks and valuations are exact, not lower bounds from a
truncated computation. To justify this precision claim explicitly,
lift the performed invertible modular operations to $\mathbb Z_2$.
Their resulting matrix is $[\operatorname{diag}(2^{e_i})\mid0]$
modulo $2^{64}$. Factor $2^{e_i}$ from row $i$. The remaining first
square block is the identity modulo two, since $e_i<64$, and is
therefore invertible over $\mathbb Z_2$; all remaining columns are
integral. This gives precisely the same local Smith invariants as
the displayed diagonal matrix.
In regenerating the $P$ row, the verifier uses
$2^{11}p_n$ instead of $Dp_n$. Since $D/2^{11}$ is odd, this is
an invertible row scaling over $\mathbb Z_2$ and does not alter any
binary determinantal-divisor valuation.

The lemma gives the three asserted image invariants by subtraction.
Let $\Lambda=(P,G)(\mathcal L)$. The second invariant implies
$\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z\times16\mathbb Z$, and the third
implies that its index in this latter lattice is odd. Therefore its
reduction modulo $2(\mathbb Z\times16\mathbb Z)$ is surjective.
In particular it contains a vector with $P$ odd and $G/16$ odd.
This concerns the image of the actual integer kernel, not a kernel
computed merely modulo a power of two.
\end{proof}

For the vector in the proposition, the unnormalized gamma coordinate
is $Q=D16^{256}G$. Thus $v_2(Q)=11+4\cdot256+4=1039$,
while $P$ is odd; primitive reduction leaves the binary order of
the gamma denominator equal to $1039$.
No bound on the height of a representative $c$ is obtained.

\paragraph{Per-column normalization.}
Let $d_n=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3n)$.
Since $d_n\mid D$, the integer vector
$c'_n=(D/d_n)c_n$ gives the same exactly log-free form through
$\sum c'_nd_nI_n$. Consequently the proven finite odd-constant
attainability also holds in the basis with individually cleared
columns. The preceding proposition does not control the height
of $c'$ or its weighted error.

\paragraph{Scope.}
The block $[256,511]$ is outside the thin-block reflection theorem,
so odd constant output does not contradict that obstruction.
It is also outside the former common-denominator decay budget;
individual column clearing removes that particular analytic restriction.
The surviving difficulty is a small representative in the correct
integer-kernel congruence class, uniformly along unbounded blocks.
The classical determinantal-divisor lemma and this finite image
certificate do not prove that height bound or an irrationality result.


\section{Two precise infinite completion targets}
\label{s6--sec:remaining}
The new reductions expose two different compatibility assertions.
They must not be replaced by a count of successful finite examples.

\subsection{Heights in moving output intervals}
For a nonempty normalized offset-prefix interval on $[n,M]$, let
$h_2(n,M,\lambda)$ be the minimum possible largest primitive
denominator of two distinct rational points. Set it to infinity
when the interval is empty or a singleton. The interval theorem
computes this quantity exactly in every finite instance.
The sufficient infinite target is
\begin{equation}\label{s6--eq:height-target}
 \frac{(1+\lambda_n)h_2(n,M_n,\lambda_n)\log(M_n+1)}
 {729^n\sqrt n}\longrightarrow0
\end{equation}
along unbounded $n$, with rational $\lambda_n\ge0$.
The minimum-height pair theorem and the signed-prefix estimate
would then give a positive integer-under-rationality sum of squares
that tends to zero. A particularly concrete sufficient special case is
\[
 (1+\lambda_n)h_2(n,M_n,\lambda_n)\le729^n,\qquad
 \log(M_n+1)=o(\sqrt n).
\]
The eighteen exact positive windows satisfy the displayed height
inequality at their own indices. They do not establish it along an
unbounded sequence. Extending an old lift by zeros preserves its
starting index and error, so it does not solve this target.

\subsection{Short representatives of an attainable output class}
For the individually cleared columns on $[n,2n-1]$, the target is
\begin{equation}\label{s6--eq:coset-target}
 Fc=0,\qquad c\in\Z^n,\qquad
 \|c\|_\infty\le\left\lceil e^{128n/\log n}\right\rceil,\qquad
 \sum_{j=n}^{2n-1}d_jp_jc_j\ \text{odd},
\end{equation}
again for unbounded $n$.
The counting theorem supplies a nonzero vector satisfying the first
three conditions eventually. The image calculation proves that the
odd-output class is attainable at one larger block, without a height
bound. These are different existential statements; they do not
give a vector satisfying all four conditions.

The weaker survival requirement
$P_n\ne0$ and $4n-v_2(P_n)\to\infty$ would also suffice. The thin-block
obstruction rules out odd $P$ on those thin blocks, but it does not
rule out every weaker valuation escape.

\subsection{The logical status of the five requirements}
For the certified positive finite windows, exact arithmetic,
nonvanishing, and the stated small fully normalized errors are proved
without extra assumptions. No theorem here supplies infinitely many
such windows with vanishing costs. Conversely the columnwise counting
theorem is an unconditional infinite statement about small log-null
inputs, but it does not exclude formal-zero outputs. Therefore the
five requirements have not yet been met by one infinite family.

The reductions do remove some previous restrictions. Signed prefixes
can be used with a determinant pair; the terminal index need not be
linear in the starting index; determinant one does not impose extra
maximum denominator height in a finite output interval; and an
individual denominator budget permits doubling windows. None of these
facts supplies the missing infinite height or coset representative
bound by itself.




\clearpage
\section{The consolidated outcome and the exact remaining junction}
\label{unified:outcome}

The earlier stages now fit into one arithmetic picture. Positive
target realization and sharp degree bounds settle existence and
analytic complexity inside specified classes. Exact prime valuations
show that several natural realizations pay too much in primitive
denominators. Output quotient norms remove irrelevant coefficient
denominators, while cumulative-prefix geometry makes positivity and
cost simultaneously tractable. The new nonuniform theorem enlarges
the certified positive class by a precisely weighted allowance for
negative prefixes. Columnwise integerization secures smallness on
long windows before a useful output class is selected.

\subsection{Which directions are closed, and which are conditional?}
\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.25\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.66\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule Direction & Current conclusion\\\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule Direction & Current conclusion\\\midrule
\endhead
Canonical dyadic targets and interpolation
& Exact kernels, brackets, valuations, and full-class obstructions
are proved. Failure for dyadic interpolation does not exclude
arbitrary rational interpolation.\\
Repaired rational localization
& The exact threshold is $q_M=o(M)$, and the two-adic argument
excludes it for every parameter of the repaired $k=1$ family.
The threshold is a failed route for that family, not an outstanding
existence problem within it.\\
Bessel mirror and acceleration
& Large harmonic-core costs and the displayed mirror/accelerated
obstructions are proved. The accelerated core-cancelled family $X_j$ has exact two-adic
cancellation and odd-prime survival criteria; the latter are not a
universal denominator estimate for every possible subsequence.\\
Autonomous dilation of a fixed admissible kernel
& Raw error decays, but the actual primitive error diverges under
the stated fixed-kernel and nonzero-output hypotheses.\\
Finite quotient optimization
& Exact finite minima and transfer certificates are proved. The
infinite seminorm and its dual have precise alternatives; the
favorable alternative is not established.\\
Nonuniform negative-prefix positivity
& The universal prefix threshold, including its boundary, is
settled. The individual-vector sufficient test and compact rational
output interval are unconditional. Infinite cheap output existence
is not supplied by those geometric facts.\\
Columnwise small vectors
& Short exact log-null integer inputs exist eventually, and their
fully cleared cost tends to zero. Equally short formal-zero vectors
also exist. A useful bounded-height output class is still needed.\\
Wide-block binary output class
& The desired simultaneous congruence class exists in the actual
integer kernel on the stated finite window. No height bound or
unbounded sequence follows from that image computation.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\normalsize

\subsection{Two explicit ways to complete the same-family argument}
The positive route can now be stated without a determinant partner.
For unbounded $n$, find a rational log-null lift on $[n,M_n]$ with
integer output $(q_n,p_n)$, $q_n>0$, such that
\[
 \sum_{k=n}^{M_n-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})(-S_k)_+\le q_n a_{M_n},
 \qquad
 \frac{q_n\log(M_n+1)}{729^n\sqrt n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The new positivity theorem and the signed cost estimate would then
give $0<q_n\gamma-p_n\to0$. This is a concrete sufficient theorem,
not a claim that the required lifts have been found infinitely often.

The integer-column route starts with
$d_j=2\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,3j)$ and $J_j=d_j I_j$.
The uniform budget and counting arguments already provide short
log-null inputs. It remains to choose such inputs with output
$(Q_n,P_n)$ satisfying, for example,
\[
 P_n\ne0,\qquad 4n-v_2(P_n)\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
Small cost and $P_n\ne0$ force $Q_n\ne0$ eventually.
The gamma coordinate is divisible by $2^{4n}$; the displayed
valuation gap forces the primitive denominator to diverge. The
affine-completion theorem then produces a determinant-one companion
and a positive quadratic form tending to zero. A finite surviving
class and an unrelated short input do not establish their intersection.

\subsection{Five-condition audit}
\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.06\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.28\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.57\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule & Requirement & What has and has not been established\\\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule & Requirement & What has and has not been established\\\midrule
\endhead
1 & Integer coefficients, no residual logs
& Established exactly for the stated finite lifts and the infinite
log-cancellation constructions.\\
2 & Nonzero evaluated value
& Established for the positive-prefix and new budget-certified
kernels, and for independent-output sums of squares. It is not
established for the short vectors supplied by counting alone.\\
3 & Decay after arithmetic normalization
& Uniform sufficient bounds and short-vector budgets are proved;
many concrete finite costs are certified. Their compatibility with
the required output/sign class at unbounded indices is unresolved.\\
4 & Infinitely many useful indices
& Infinite log-null inputs and free extension indices are proved.
Infinite useful outputs obeying all the same cost and nonvanishing
conditions are not.\\
5 & No unproved premise in the final contradiction
& The general theorems and exact finite certificates keep their
hypotheses explicit. The proposed irrationality conclusions remain
conditional on the missing simultaneous existence assertion.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\normalsize

Thus it is not accurate to say that only requirement 3 remains
independently of the others. The unresolved statement joins a cost
bound to a useful output class for infinitely many indices. The
new sharp theorem improves that joining problem by providing an
exact, larger positive class. It does not by itself resolve the
infinite arithmetic selection problem.

\section{Exact starting certificates for the infinite rank theorems}
\label{s4--app:rankcert}
The two finite calculations below close the base cases of
Theorems~\ref{s4--thm:rank} and \ref{s4--thm:outputrank}. They take place in
finite fields and do not require numerical integration.
The residue entries $2A_{n,j}$ are computed by the integral binomial
identity from Section 2, and independently checked against their
factorial expression. The row $p_n$ is computed using modular
inverses of the harmonic denominators. The moduli exceed $6N$,
so all factorial and harmonic denominators appearing in these
checks are units.

The following complete Python program uses only the standard library.
Its determinant outputs are
\[
 \det V_9=97\pmod{101},\qquad
 \det W_{17}=65\pmod{211}.
\]
They are nonzero, which is all the infinite induction needs.

\begin{lstlisting}
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Standard-library modular certificates for the infinite rank induction."""
from math import comb,factorial,isqrt
from pathlib import Path
import json

def primes(n):return [p for p in range(2,n+1) if all(p%d for d in range(2,isqrt(p)+1))]
def valuation(n,p):
    v=0
    while n%p==0:n//=p;v+=1
    return v

def matrix(N,mod,augmented):
    assert mod>6*N and mod in primes(mod)
    rows=[];constants=[]
    for n in range(1,N+1):
        residues={};h=0;pn=0
        for j in range(1,3*n+1):
            h=(h+pow(j,-1,mod))%mod
            if j<n:continue
            a=j+n;b=j-n
            B=comb(2*a,b);C=comb(a,2*b)
            Bp=comb(2*a-1,b-1) if b else 0
            Cp=comb(a-1,2*b-1) if b else 0
            w=(-1)**b*(B*C+4*Bp*C+Bp*Cp)%mod
            numerator=(-1)**b*8*j*j*factorial(2*j+2*n-1)*factorial(n+j-1)
            denominator=factorial(2*j-2*n)*factorial(j-n)*factorial(3*n-j)*factorial(3*n+j)
            assert w==numerator*pow(denominator,-1,mod)%mod
            residues[j]=w
            pn=(pn+w*pow(2,-1,mod)*(h-pow(2*j,-1,mod)))%mod
        assert sum(residues.values())%mod==2*pow(16,n,mod)%mod
        rows.append(residues);constants.append(pn)
    ps=primes(3*N)
    V=[[sum(w*valuation(j,p) for j,w in row.items())%mod for row in rows]for p in ps]
    if augmented:V+=[[pow(16,n,mod) for n in range(1,N+1)],constants]
    return V,ps

def determinant(A,mod):
    A=[row[:] for row in A];n=len(A);assert all(len(row)==n for row in A)
    product=1;pivots=[];swaps=[]
    for j in range(n):
        k=next((k for k in range(j,n) if A[k][j]),None)
        assert k is not None
        if k!=j:A[j],A[k]=A[k],A[j];product=-product;swaps.append((j,k))
        p=A[j][j];pivots.append(p);product=product*p%mod;inv=pow(p,-1,mod)
        for k in range(j+1,n):
            f=A[k][j]*inv%mod
            for l in range(j,n):A[k][l]=(A[k][l]-f*A[j][l])%mod
    return product%mod,pivots,swaps

def verify():
    out=[]
    for N,mod,augmented,expected in [(9,101,False,97),(17,211,True,65)]:
        A,ps=matrix(N,mod,augmented);det,piv,swaps=determinant(A,mod)
        assert det==expected
        out.append({'N':N,'modulus':mod,'augmented':augmented,'primes':ps,'matrix':A,'determinant':det,'pivots':piv,'swaps':swaps})
        print('N',N,'modulus',mod,'determinant',det,'pivots',piv,'swaps',swaps)
    assert all(len(primes(3*n))>n for n in range(1,9))
    assert all(n-len(primes(3*n))<2 for n in range(9,17))

if __name__=='__main__':verify()
\end{lstlisting}

The historical ten-result-group list in S1 comprised: least-denominator
selection; exact primitive-error optimization; positive target
realization; the polynomial-square image; Laguerre integerization;
primitive-cost obstructions; support compression; localization;
adverse-prime removal; and integerized signed cancellation. Every
group is included above. The original rank numbers are not reused
as a ranking of the substantially enlarged manuscript.

\paragraph{Editorial and mathematical corrections.}
An imprecise sentence in S1 asserted rationality of all displayed
kernel masses, although one display contained $\gamma-1/2$.
The corrected assertion concerns only the rational masses of $K_a$.
No argument depends on rationality of $\gamma-1/2$.
Meyer's rational-isotropy theorem is explicitly attributed to its
classical literature~\cite{meyer-davenport}. The exact factorial
moment is
\[
 \int_0^\infty t^s(t-1)\log t\,e^{-t}\,dt
 =s!\bigl(1+sH_s-s\gamma\bigr).
\]
The earlier redundant display with an extra $s$ is not retained.
Historical ``remaining target'' statements are superseded where
later proofs settle the corresponding family, particularly the
repaired localization obstruction. The proper-kernel majorant is
renamed $\mathcal U_j$ to separate it from the core-cancelled
approximant $U_j$.

\paragraph{Proof status.}
The numbered statements are proved deductions, explicitly conditional
completion results, or exact finite certificates as identified in
their statements. Standard external inputs are cited where used.
Computer-assisted finite statements are defined by exact rational
equations or inequalities and accompanied by reproducible verifiers.
The compilation and checks do not constitute independent peer review,
a formal proof-assistant development, or a historical novelty search.

\subsection{An exact finite test of the new interval enlargement}
\label{unified:extension-assessment}

The strict-enlargement formula can be applied directly to an existing
certificate, without a new linear-programming optimization.

\begin{proposition}[The constructed extension from 18 to 59]
\label{unified:finite-extension}
Take the certified normalized endpoint lifts of the nonnegative-prefix
interval on $[18,59]$, as specified in
\textup{\texttt{cone\_interval\_18\_59.json}}
inside the embedded interval archive. Apply the two explicit
extrapolations in Corollary~\ref{new--new-prefix:strict-enlargement}.
Both new endpoint lifts cancel every prime-log row exactly and
satisfy the weighted positivity budget. The resulting closed
\emph{extrapolated interval} strictly contains the old interval and
has the same least primitive denominator
\[
 q_{\min}=154780615090340473039841749,
\]
attained at numerator $89341795653239106820596473$.
This assertion does not compute the least denominator in the entire
new sharp-budget polytope.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The standard-library verifier \path{verify_window18_extension.py}
reads the specified rational endpoint vectors and regenerates every
residue from the factorial formula. It checks the forty prime rows,
the normalization $q=1$, the output slopes, and the negative-part
budgets at both extrapolated endpoints. The exact positive
extension lengths follow from the formula of
Corollary~\ref{new--new-prefix:strict-enlargement}.
It then checks that both new endpoints remain strictly inside the
original certified Farey-parent bracket. The determinant-one
parent property gives the lower bound $q_{\min}$ for every rational
in that bracket, while the previously certified fraction still
belongs to the enlarged interval. This proves equality of the
least denominator. All comparisons use exact fractions; no digits
of $\gamma$ are used.
\end{proof}

For scale only, the old width is approximately
$1.767715027228\cdot10^{-53}$. The displayed extrapolation extends
it to the left by approximately $3.529919840930\cdot10^{-171}$ and
to the right by approximately $3.120903973075\cdot10^{-174}$.
The exact comparisons, not those rounded decimals, certify the
strict enlargement. Thus this particular constructed interval gives
a positive feasible-region gain without a denominator improvement.
Optimizing the full new polytope is a different finite problem and
has not been performed here.

\section{One-source compilation and embedded exact verification}
\label{unified:reproducibility}

Compile the single TeX file with a standard TeX installation:
\begin{lstlisting}[language={},numbers=none]
pdflatex gamma_consolidated_positive_kernels_and_arithmetic_2026_11_02.tex
pdflatex gamma_consolidated_positive_kernels_and_arithmetic_2026_11_02.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The source has no external \texttt{\string\input},
\texttt{\string\include}, figure, or BibTeX dependencies. Its
post-document comments contain one Base64-encoded ZIP. That
collection preserves the five earlier verification archives
byte-for-byte and supplies a combined runner, the additional
consolidation checks, and a manifest.

The following extractor uses only the Python standard library.
Run it beside the TeX file; the name of the archive is not an
external dependency of compilation.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python,numbers=none]
from pathlib import Path
import base64, hashlib, re

p = Path("gamma_consolidated_positive_kernels_and_arithmetic_2026_11_02.tex")
s = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
meta, rest = s.split("% BEGIN EMBEDDED VERIFICATION\n", 1)[1].split("\n", 1)
expected = meta.removeprefix("% SHA256 ")
payload = rest.split("% END EMBEDDED VERIFICATION", 1)[0]
data = base64.b64decode("".join(
    line[2:] for line in payload.splitlines() if line.startswith("% ")
), validate=True)
if hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() != expected:
    raise SystemExit("Embedded archive hash mismatch")
Path("gamma_consolidated_verification.zip").write_bytes(data)
print("Verified embedded archive:", expected)
\end{lstlisting}

Extract the ZIP into a new directory and follow its \texttt{README.txt}.
The top-level runner checks the inner archive hashes, rejects unsafe
paths and optimized Python, and uses fresh temporary extraction
directories. Any older checkers that generate local reports do so
inside those temporary directories. The source archives are not
modified. Some full lattice checks are substantially slower than
the elementary sanity checks.

\paragraph{What the computational checks certify.}
The collection checks the finite canonical brackets, exact quotient
minima and primal--dual certificates, affine corrections, prefix
signs, transfer identities, binary arithmetic, the finite integer
kernel-image invariants, and the new boundary example. It does not
turn a finite collection of windows into an all-index theorem.
The all-index identities and inequalities are established by the
written mathematical proofs.
